#8923. Infographic | The Cost of Health “Optimization”

If you’re like most people, your answer is probably, “Yes!”

And, you probably want to live not only a longer life, but also a healthier one.

If so, you don’t have to look very far to find claims about how to improve—no, “optimize”—your health.

Want to reverse chronic disease? Extend that youthful glow? Live to 115… or forever? Lots of fitness influencers, authors, and podcasters will tell you how to do it.

But are their ultra-specific, advanced protocols necessary—or even effective?

And just how much effort, time, and money do these methods really require?

Most of all: Are the benefits worth the trade-offs?

By the end of it, you’ll have clarity about how to get the health and longevity you want, while living a life you enjoy.

#8922. Inside the 24-Hour World Record Attempt That Raised Over $500K+ for a Local Food Bank

Ethan Hunger attempts to break the Guinness World Record for the most super-sprint triathlons in 24 hours. (Photo: Grayson Baum/Minus 7, Inc)

Beating the Guinness World Record for the most super-sprint triathlons completed in 24 hours was the goal of my friend Ethan Hunger’s annual community fundraising event. But the record itself was really only a small part of it. The attempt was just one piece of his much bigger, yearlong goal to raise $500,000 for our local food bank – a fundraiser that has been growing through various endurance challenges since 2021.

The idea for his annual “Hunger vs. Hunger” fundraiser was born out of the COVID-related growth of food insecurity in his local area of Bellingham, Washington. What started as a one-year challenge that raised $30,000 has now amassed a total of $1.2 million in donations, and this year’s $500,000 challenge would equate to roughly 7% of the food bank’s annual budget.

The concept and message Ethan shares through these extreme challenges is simple: “No matter how hard a day I create for myself, it will never parallel the struggles of food insecurity.”

For year six, Hunger wanted to go bigger than ever, and a triathlon world record would certainly tick that box while also adding more eyes to the cause. Initially, the record sounded relatively simple when the idea came to light: swim, bike, run, and transition continuously for 24 straight hours – non-stop through the entire night – and beat the previous record of 18 complete triathlons. (Technically, Guinness records the attempt in legs, so he needed 55 completed to surpass the previous record).

However, it quickly became more challenging throughout the buildup. The logistics of putting on a “race” like this at a public park while also adhering to more than 30 pages of Guinness rules began to set in – and that was before considering the largest fundraising goal Hunger had ever attempted.

Here’s how it all unfolded: the behind-the-scenes difficulties of a Guinness World Record, what 24 hours of triathlon actually felt like, how the fundraiser brought it all together, and why he might have stumbled on a revolutionary triathlon idea.

There is a massive difference between saying you broke a world record and having Guinness officially verify it. During the buildup, we found the endless list of verification rules a bit redundant and overly complicated. However, they create a rigorous, no-corner-cutting environment that helps maintain the integrity of the records.

Still, we wished it didn’t cost an estimated $14,000 to send an adjudicator to verify our attempt on-site – which would’ve made everything a lot easier.

Hunger applied for the records six months in advance and was approved. Not everyone gets this approval, as part of the application involves demonstrating that you not only have the experience and skills to attempt something like this, but also the connections and know-how to pull off the necessary verification.

Guinness has a lot of requirements before ratifying an attempt: video, timing, GPS files, logs, photos, and documentation for seemingly everything. So in a feat nothing short of a miracle, we scrambled together seven main cameras to record for 24 hours straight, three additional dedicated cameramen for an upcoming documentary, multiple photographers, timing data, and GPS tracking. But despite all that, one requirement quickly became much more problematic than the others: witnesses.

We discovered late that an individual witness could only cover a four-hour period before needing a four-hour break. We were also further limited in who could qualify, so close friends and family couldn’t simply fill every opening (as we had initially planned).

So, less than a week before a 24-hour event, on top of figuring out nutrition, bikes, course logistics, lights, cameras, batteries, timing, and how the hell any of us planned to stay awake for 24 hours, Ethan now needed to find people willing to stand beside a lake, jump in a safety car for the bike, and on mountain bikes for the run at ridiculous hours of the night and officially confirm that he was, in fact, doing the correct distances.

“If I had to pick one thing that made the event coordination the hardest, it was the witnesses and their four-hour time constraint,” Hunger says.

Somehow, through social media and word of mouth, people volunteered. They came out at midnight, early in the morning, and at all sorts of inconvenient hours. Some of them didn’t know Ethan at all – they simply heard what he was trying to do and wanted to help.

That should have been our first indication of what this event was eventually going to become. The world record might have been Ethan’s, but a lot of people were beginning to feel like they had a small piece of it.

By the end of his record, Hunger had amassed 5.47 miles of swimming, 136.7 miles of biking, and 34.2 miles of running. Yet those numbers are not what he will remember.

I asked him what stands out the most, and his answer goes back to minute one. It paints a picture of the day perfectly:

“The one that lingered for me the longest was likely the starting line. I had been frantically running around for 20 hours trying to get everything set up. I ran over to the start line with my goggles and swim cap, and I looked around with 60 seconds left and finally had the moment sink in of all the incredible people who were there to support me. I saw an older gentleman who I used to volunteer with at the food bank, who I knew had driven 30 minutes to town just to see me start. I saw friends who had flown from around the country. I saw people who currently work at the food bank who came to cheer, and I saw friends who currently rely on the food bank who came to cheer. It was incredibly moving.”

He might have been the one whose name would be attached to the attempt and record, but very quickly it stopped feeling like something he was doing alone. That came partly from the decision to use a real course. From a logistical standpoint, doing the challenge at a pool and track would have been infinitely easier to film, manage, illuminate, and monitor. Every time we left transition on the bike or run course, we disappeared from the main event area, which made everything more complicated.

“There were a ton of moving parts to this, and so many of them were out of my control once the clock started,” Hunger said. “I was able to do my best to get it set up ahead of time and put people in charge of tasks, but then I had to be willing to let it go and hope that it worked out.”

And it did work out: People were joining in on the swim, bike, and run legs throughout almost every reasonable hour (staying behind Ethan to avoid drafting). There was a DJ playing music, food, a campfire, friends sitting around talking, people donating, and strangers coming down simply because they’d heard something ridiculous was happening. Because the distances were short, people could also participate without committing to an enormous endurance challenge of their own. Someone could join one swim, somebody else could do four runs, and others could ride a bunch of the bike legs. Because every leg eventually returned to the same transition area, the group kept coming back together again.

That made the atmosphere completely different from a traditional long-distance triathlon where an athlete might disappear for several hours. If Ethan left on the bike, everyone knew he’d be back in around 25 minutes. If somebody wanted to join the next run, they had a good idea of when it would start.

It helped break the endless cycle of triathlon feeling like such an individual sport and started to feel more like a 24-hour triathlon festival.

We had no idea going in what to expect physically. We’d only practiced this format for about six hours, none of us were truly trained as ultra-triathletes, and sure, we’d completed an Ironman before, but we all safely assumed that somewhere around hour 12 or 15 our bodies would start falling apart.

Weirdly, however, that wasn’t really what happened. Because every individual leg was short and we weren’t moving particularly fast, you’d finish a swim, bike, and run and think, That actually wasn’t too bad. The problem was overcoming the sleep fatigue and the dread of doing specific legs again (and again) with so many hours still ahead.

“My lowest moment was around 3 or 3:30 in the morning,” Ethan says. “I had just finished a triathlon where I was cold the entire time, and I was incredibly sleepy, too. The wind was still causing chop on the lake, and we had headwinds on our bike ride out. I just remember dreading going back in the water because I was already cold, and I knew when I finished the swim, and the wind hit me on the beach, I’d instantly be cold again.”

There were many other smaller obstacles along the way, too. One of which stands out for its irony. Hunger had spent a lot of effort organizing with Outbound Lighting to help illuminate the docks and buoys, to make the night swim one of the coolest parts of the whole experience, yet, in a synchronous moment of shared disbelief, we realized we all had forgotten clear-lens goggles.

On the bike, going from wet to cold to warm meant clothes never quite dried, while chafing, tired hands, wind, darkness, and some sketchy late-night traffic (picture drunk drivers yelling out the window) slowly added up.

Despite that, the hardest part for me might have been the small act of leaving the transition itself: even in the middle of the night, there was a campfire, music, food, and people hanging out, and sitting down beside that fire and prolonging the transition was all too enticing.

Maybe the best way to picture the mental struggle of this challenge is to imagine doing 15 hours of triathlon, getting to 9 a.m. when the sun was finally up, feeling like you’ve survived the hard part – then realizing you still have nine hours left.

For something that had taken 24 hours, the finish felt surprisingly quick. There were lots of people, lots of emotion, and we were all incredibly proud of Ethan. After 22 complete super-sprint triathlons, four more than the previous record, it was finally over.

Then we quickly cleaned everything up and headed to a big party, where Ethan somehow managed to give a speech in front of a few hundred people gathered to celebrate what it was all actually for. The Foodbank.

The number is already over the $500,000 goal, and with still much of the year left, and a documentary release still to come, that should have him far surpassing his expectations.

If you want to donate, you can do so here.

He describes just how much it means to the organization that now helps feed almost 5,000 families weekly in our county:

“My fundraiser is big enough and has been around long enough that the food bank now builds this fundraiser into its annual projection for income. If you combine that with the 2025 federal budget cuts that cost the Bellingham Food Bank around $900,000 and food banks across the country well over $1 billion, the need is there now more than ever.”

There are times when attempting a world record can appear outwardly selfish, done for vanity, to gain attention, or to level up your status. Ethan even received some comments on social media saying so, despite the clear purpose behind the fundraiser. But when you were on-site, you realized there wasn’t much glory in slogging through an attempt like this, and if you dealt with the months of buildup and preparation, you would quickly realize it probably wasn’t worth doing purely for the token of a Guinness stamp.

But doing it for a purpose, and with friends and a community around, made it all worth it. The record gave everyone something ridiculous to rally around; it gave hope, gave purpose, and made every small act feel like it was contributing to something much bigger.

Speaking of bigger, Ethan has already planned next year’s challenge: a 100-mile run around our local track and stadium.

#8921. Is it too late to start strength training at 70? (No. Here’s what happens when you do.)

People in their 70s, 80s, and 90s get meaningfully stronger when they start strength training, and beginners tend to see the biggest response to training.

You also need far less than you’d guess: 30 to 60 minutes of lifting spread across a week is a great starting point.

Here’s the science, three ways to begin, and a client who started at 57 and is still going at 77.

A reader wrote me this week. Her whole email was one sentence:

That hits deep. That fear of: have I missed my window?

I want to share with you what I shared with her, because the science behind this is actually super cool and empowering.

People in their 70s, 80s, and 90s still get stronger when they start lifting. And it meaningfully improves how they move through their lives.

And if you’re someone who hasn’t trained before, or hasn’t trained in a while, I have even better news.

As a beginner, your body is even more sensitive to training. Translation: you get even more reward for your effort!

In the first few weeks, most people feel stronger before they look any different.

That’s because a lot of early strength is actually your muscles and brain learning to coordinate. The movement gets smoother. Standing up from a chair feels a little easier. Etc.

Over a few months, muscle starts to build.

Your bones respond to the load too (strength training is one of the best-supported ways to support bone health as we age.)

You’ll start to feel some muscle in your arms that you didn’t notice there before, like this reader who’s been doing workouts 3x/week and kicking butt with it:

Is every body different? Yes. Does it also depend on sleep, nutrition, and what else life is throwing at you? Also yes.

But the direction is the same for everyone. No matter your age, you can make a meaningful impact in your overall health, fitness, and quality of life!

1) Don’t start with workouts. Start with practice.

Take a few minutes each day to learn and practice a couple of strength moves.

You’re not training yet. You’re getting acquainted.

Try some push-ups off of the wall or the countertop. ​ Sit down in a chair, slow and controlled, and practice keeping your weight evenly spread across your feet (that’s a squat right there!)

Grab a gallon jug, some light dumbbells or canned goods or whatever you have on hand, and practice a one-arm row. See if you can feel it in your upper back as you pull the weight up.

Work within whatever your ability level is, what feels safe and approachable to start.

You’re collecting information about what your body is ready for, and learning exercises like you’re learning a new skill.

30-60 minutes of strength training in TOTAL across the week goes a surprisingly long way.

You can break that up however works best for you. A short 5-10min session most days of the week, inserting some “movement snacks” throughout the day, or a couple of longer sessions 2x/week, etc.

It doesn’t require hours of your day to make serious progress.

3) It’s easier to level up than to cut down

Because your body is more sensitive to strength training, you’ll likely feel more sore in the beginning.

So in general, I recommend you err on the side of less is more.

If you do a few short sessions during the week, and wake up the next day feeling great with little to no soreness, great! You can add a bit more the next week.

Mentally, I’ve also just found it’s way easier to be “leveling up” than having to cut back, which really helps with building that early momentum.

Becky, a Nerd Fitness coaching client, is someone I immediately thought of when I read that initial email. She’s 77, and didn’t start going to the gym until she was 57. Here’s what she had to say:

I couldn’t have said it any better myself, Becky. 😊

No matter your age or where you’re starting from…YOU GOT THIS! 💪

Whenever you’re ready, here are more ways we can help

1) Here’s an article with a bunch of different bodyweight exercises and progressions you can do at home.

2) Our coaches build programs specific to you and your needs. Here’s the exact system we use.

Nerd Fitness cuts through the fitness B.S. to help people get stronger, healthier, and more confident – all with a fun, no-nonsense approach.

Humans featured are exceptional examples and do not guarantee individual success. Your experience and results may vary.

Imagine stepping off a long-haul flight, exhausted and slightly rumpled, and walking into the Park Hyatt Tokyo — the hotel made iconic by *Lost in Translation* — and being handed a room key to a suite with floor-to-ceiling views of Mount Fuji. Or picture arriving at the Park Hyatt Paris-Vendôme, where Haussmann architecture frames your every view and the concierge greets you by name. Or standing in the Park Hyatt New York, 25 floors above Midtown, watching the city sprawl in every direction from a room that costs more per night than most people's monthly car payment. Now imagine paying nearly nothing for it. That's the power of the World of Hyatt award chart — and the Park Hyatt sweet spot is one of the most emotionally resonant redemptions in all of travel rewards. Here's the math that makes the ChooseFI community's collective jaw drop: a single night at the Park Hyatt New York regularly retails for **$1,200–$2,000**. The Park Hyatt Tokyo commands **$800–$1,500** per night. The Park Hyatt Paris? Easily **$1,000+** in peak seasons. Yet every one of these properties sits at **Category 7**, bookable for just **25,000–30,000 World of Hyatt points** per night. At 30,000 points for a $1,500 room, you're extracting **5 cents per point (cpp)** — in a world where most loyalty programs are engineered to deliver 1–1.5 cpp if you're lucky. The CPP range for this sweet spot runs from **2.7 cpp all the way to 6.7 cpp**, meaning even a modest redemption delivers 2–3x the value of a typical points transaction. Why does this gap exist? Because Hyatt uses a **fixed award chart** anchored to categories, not real-time cash pricing. When demand spikes — New Year's Eve in New York, cherry blossom season in Tokyo, Paris Fashion Week — cash rates explode upward while your points cost stays locked. The hotel's revenue management team can't touch your award rate. That's the pricing inefficiency the ChooseFI community is built to exploit. This isn't aspirational travel for the ultra-wealthy. This is FI-minded travel: understanding the system, earning points intentionally, and converting them into experiences that would otherwise require an extra year of saving. A two-night stay at the Park Hyatt Tokyo for 60,000 points — points you can earn from a single credit card welcome bonus — is the kind of redemption that reframes what financial independence actually looks like in practice.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: World of Hyatt prices its awards on a fixed category chart, while Park Hyatt properties punch dramatically above their category ceiling in cash value.

Here's how the Hyatt award chart works: properties are assigned to Categories 1 through 8, with standard award nights running from 3,500 points (Cat 1) up to 45,000 points (Cat 8). Park Hyatt properties — the absolute pinnacle of the Hyatt portfolio, a collection of ultra-luxury city hotels that competes directly with Four Seasons and Ritz-Carlton — fall predominantly into Category 7 (25,000 points/night) and Category 8 (40,000 points/night). But unlike Four Seasons or Ritz-Carlton, which have largely abandoned fixed award charts in favor of dynamic pricing that tracks cash rates, Hyatt has held the line on fixed pricing. This is a rare and increasingly endangered feature in hotel loyalty, which is exactly why the ChooseFI community should be actively using it now.

The transfer path that makes this accessible is Chase Ultimate Rewards. Chase transfers to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio, and the transfer is instant — meaning you can spot availability, transfer your points, and book within minutes. Bilt Rewards also transfers to World of Hyatt at 1:1, also instantly, giving you two powerful earning pipelines into the same program.

This matters enormously for strategy. Chase Ultimate Rewards is arguably the most flexible points currency in travel rewards — earned through cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred and Chase Sapphire Reserve — and the fact that it flows directly into Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio without any degradation is a genuine gift. 30,000 Chase UR points become exactly 30,000 Hyatt points. No conversion fees, no waiting period, no surprises.

Another critical mechanism: World of Hyatt charges zero fuel surcharges on award redemptions. With hotel awards this is less of an issue than with airline programs, but it reflects Hyatt's broader philosophy of clean, predictable award pricing. What you see is what you pay — taxes and fees on hotel awards are typically minimal.

Now layer in Globalist status, and the value compounds further. World of Hyatt's top-tier elite status (earned at 60 qualifying nights per year) unlocks complimentary suite upgrades at check-in (space available) and free breakfast for two guests daily. If you're a Globalist checking into the Park Hyatt New York and you receive a suite upgrade, you've just added hundreds of dollars of daily value to an already exceptional redemption — and free breakfast at a Park Hyatt can easily run $60–$90 per person.

The booking window is 395 days out, which matters for high-demand dates. The Park Hyatt Tokyo during cherry blossom season (late March to early April) or the Park Hyatt New York around major events will see award availability evaporate quickly. Understanding that you can search and book nearly 13 months in advance is your single biggest tactical advantage for locking in prime dates.

Finally, it's worth understanding what you're getting at the property level. Park Hyatt is not Hyatt Regency or even Andaz — it's Hyatt's true ultra-luxury tier, with butler service, marble bathrooms, curated art collections, and some of the best city-view room designs in the world. The points-to-experience ratio here is genuinely exceptional.

Before anything else, inventory what you have. Log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards or Bilt Rewards account and note your balance. You need a minimum of 25,000 points for a Category 7 Park Hyatt night or 40,000 points for a Category 8 property. If you're planning a multi-night stay, multiply accordingly — 30,000 points per night at a Category 7 is a reasonable planning number that covers most Park Hyatt sweet spots.

Decide which property you're targeting. The flagship three for this redemption are:

Go to hyatt.com and use the hotel search. Enter your destination city and dates. In the rate filter, select "Use Points" to display award availability. The site will show you the points cost per night — if you see the Category rate (25,000 or 40,000), availability exists. Note that peak and off-peak pricing can adjust these numbers slightly, so check a few date combinations.

Search flexibly. If your first-choice dates show no availability, shift by a day or two — award inventory at Park Hyatt properties is released in small blocks and replenished irregularly. Use the calendar view to scan multiple dates at once.

This is critical: do not transfer points until you've confirmed award availability exists on your target dates. Point transfers to Hyatt are irreversible. Once you've found open award space, note the exact dates and room type, then move immediately to Step 4.

If you're using Chase Ultimate Rewards: Log into your Chase account, navigate to "Pay Yourself Back" → "Transfer to Travel Partners" → select World of Hyatt. Enter the amount (in increments matching your need) and confirm. The transfer is instant — your Hyatt account will reflect the points within minutes.

If you're using Bilt Rewards: Navigate to the "Rewards" tab, select "Transfer Points," choose World of Hyatt, and confirm. Also instant.

Return to hyatt.com immediately after the transfer confirms. Search your target dates again, select the award rate, and complete the booking. You'll pay any applicable taxes (typically modest for hotel awards) and your points will be deducted. Print or screenshot your confirmation.

Award inventory at Park Hyatt properties is genuinely limited. If you lose availability between searching and transferring (rare, but possible), call the World of Hyatt member line (1-800-304-9288) — agents sometimes have access to inventory not visible online. Alternatively, set calendar reminders to check again; properties occasionally release additional award space within 30 days of arrival as booking patterns clarify. Remember: the booking window opens 395 days out, so planning ahead dramatically expands your options.

The Points Cost: 50,000 World of Hyatt points (25,000 × 2 nights), transferred instantly from Chase Ultimate Rewards.

The bathroom features a deep soaking tub, Aesop amenities, and heated floors. This is the kind of redemption that makes the FI math click in a visceral way. You earned 50,000 Chase UR points — achievable through a single premium travel card welcome bonus — and converted them into nearly $2,500 of genuine luxury. That's the system working exactly as it should.

World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of account inactivity. This is activity-based expiration — any earning or redemption resets the clock. Don't let a large balance sit dormant. A small hotel stay, a points transfer, or earning through a Hyatt credit card all count as qualifying activity.

Hyatt does use peak and off-peak pricing tiers that can push Category 7 awards from 25,000 to 30,000 points on high-demand dates. Always check the actual points cost displayed during your specific date search rather than assuming the standard rate applies.

This redemption is purpose-built for the intentional luxury traveler in the ChooseFI community — someone who has been systematically accumulating Chase Ultimate Rewards or Bilt Rewards points and wants to convert that discipline into a genuinely extraordinary hotel experience, not just a free night at a mid-tier property.

This redemption earns a **moderate difficulty rating**, and it's worth being specific about where the friction lives — because once you understand it, most of the difficulty evaporates. **The earning is easy.** Chase Ultimate Rewards points flow into World of Hyatt at 1:1 instantly, and Chase is one of the most accessible premium rewards ecosystems for new-to-intermediate travel rewards participants. The points pipeline is well-established and reliable. **The transfer and booking mechanics are easy.** The actual process — confirm availability, transfer points, complete booking — is straightforward if you follow the correct sequence. The Hyatt website is functional and the award search is transparent. **The hard part is availability.** Park Hyatt properties are genuinely popular, the award inventory is limited, and the most desirable dates (cherry blossom season, major holidays, Fashion Week) book out fast. This is where most people hit a wall — they discover the sweet spot, feel excited, and then find no availability for their dates. **Three tips to overcome the availability challenge:** 1. **Use the full 395-day booking window.** Plan further ahead than feels natural. If you want Tokyo in April of next year, you should be searching in late March or early April of the current year. 2. **Be flexible by 3–5 days on either side.** Award inventory often opens mid-week when demand is lower. Shifting from a Saturday check-in to a Thursday can unlock availability that doesn't exist on peak nights. 3. **Check repeatedly near the 30-day mark.** Properties occasionally release additional award space as the date approaches. Setting a weekly reminder to re-check your target dates costs nothing. If you're willing to plan ahead and stay flexible on exact dates, moderate difficulty becomes very manageable — and the reward on the other side is worth every bit of the effort.

The Park Hyatt sweet spot is one of the most compelling redemptions in the entire travel rewards landscape. Booking a genuine ultra-luxury hotel experience for 25,000-30,000 points — points that transfer 1:1 from Chase Ultimate Rewards — delivers 2-4 cents per point in value. Whether it is the iconic Park Hyatt Tokyo, the beachfront Park Hyatt Maldives, or the classic Park Hyatt New York, this sweet spot consistently delivers outsized value. For anyone building a Chase Ultimate Rewards strategy, Park Hyatt should be at the top of the aspiration list.

#8919. Over a Tenth of Your Clients Are Dealing With IBS—And Here’s How to Help

This is according to the results of a study of nearly 2,000 people with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).1

In other research, people with IBS said they would take a medicine that carried a one percent risk of sudden death if it would cure their symptoms2—which can include urgent bouts of diarrhea, gas, or persistent constipation.

Some people with IBS experience bouts of abdominal pain they describe as worse than childbirth. These flare-ups can siphon concentration, interrupt sleep, and destroy work productivity.3

As a result, many people with IBS plan their lives around the availability of private, clean bathrooms. Fear of a sudden flare-up leads some to avoid restaurants, get-togethers, even exercising in public.

This pervading worry has a name—gastrointestinal-specific anxiety—and it can affect everything from social relationships to overall well-being. It’s also the main reason people with IBS report worse quality of life than people with other chronic conditions, including heart disease, diabetes, and end-stage kidney disease.4

PN Super Coach Sarah Maughan, certified through Monash University—a global leader in understanding the link between food sensitivities and IBS—has witnessed how lifestyle changes can prevent flare-ups, calm GI anxiety, and allow people with IBS to live the lives they want.

“My hope is for everyone with IBS to know they have options, whether that’s turning to a physician for medication and/or a health coach to learn about lifestyle changes and how to put them into action,” says Maughan.

In this article, we’ll hear more from Maughan. You’ll also learn:

Plus, if you’re a health coach, you’ll learn how to support clients with IBS while safely staying within your scope of practice.

Sometimes referred to as “spastic colon,” IBS is the most commonly diagnosed digestive disorder in the world, affecting about 14 percent percent of adults.5

Unlike Crohn’s and other inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD), IBS doesn’t alter the architecture of the gut. When healthcare professionals use diagnostic imaging, they find no infections, inflammation, damage to the bowel wall, or other evidence of disease.

Years ago, this lack of visible disease led many healthcare professionals to assume that IBS was purely psychological. More recently, however, this thinking has shifted.

Experts now view IBS as a functional neuro-gastrointestinal disorder.

That means the nerves between the GI tract and the brain don’t function optimally, causing the brain to deliver unnecessary pain signals and interfere with typical bowel function.

IBS symptoms can come and go, with some people experiencing months or years of relief only to suffer a severe flare-up that can last hours to weeks.

In addition, not everyone with IBS experiences the same set of symptoms, which can make the condition challenging to diagnose.

The below illustration shows the range of IBS symptoms.

Researchers are still trying to understand why the gut functions differently in people with IBS. However, they do have a few theories.

According to one hypothesis, the nerve endings in the GI tract may be overly sensitive in people with IBS. This can lead to two different sets of symptoms.

▶ Hypersensitive nerves communicate pain signals to the brain, causing people with IBS to notice digestive processes that other people wouldn’t feel. Tiny gas bubbles may be severely uncomfortable for someone with IBS, for example, but not bother someone without the disorder.

▶ Overreactive nerves can trigger GI muscles to contract with too much force, leading to gas, bloating, and diarrhea. If they underreact, the same muscles don’t contract forcefully enough, which slows the passage of food through the intestine and leads to constipation.

Another theory blames disturbances on the gut microbiome, which helps to explain why some people develop IBS symptoms after first having a severe GI illness like the Norovirus.

If you or your client suspect IBS, see a credentialed health professional.

The symptoms of IBS overlap with several other gastrointestinal diseases and health conditions that can require medication, surgery, or medically-supervised lifestyle changes. These include infections, inflammatory bowel diseases, celiac disease, cancer, and food allergies, among others.

It’s especially important to see a medical professional if you or your client notice any of the following:

In addition to ruling out other GI conditions, a healthcare professional will also ask detailed questions about you or your client’s symptoms. This information allows them to pinpoint which IBS “type” you or your client might have:

You or your client’s IBS type will inform what your healthcare professional recommends.

A healthcare provider might suggest a short course of antibiotics and antidiarrheal medicine for IBS-D. On the other hand, for IBS-C, they might recommend a fiber supplement, non-habit-forming laxative, laxative-like medication, or other medicine that reduces the perception of pain and regulates bowel movements.

In order to get the most out of the visit, you can help your client (or yourself) prepare for a healthcare appointment.

A healthcare professional will likely ask the following questions, so consider the responses beforehand:

Another way to prepare for your first appointment?

Well, you might not like it, but it’s a good idea to…

Consider keeping a poo diary for a couple of weeks before your appointment.

In the diary, track the frequency of bowel movements and other symptoms. Use the Bristol Stool Chart (below) to take note of the quality of your poo. This information can help your healthcare professional assess whether you have IBS and which type.

(To learn more about the clues your poos can hide, read: 6 reasons you should care about your poop health)

In recent years, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved several new prescription medicines for IBS, along with a medical device that stimulates the cranial nerves behind the ear.

In addition, thousands of research papers have looked at the interaction between IBS and various lifestyle habits, with many promising findings.

Here are five evidence-based ways to reduce the symptoms of IBS (and bonus, many of them are great for enhancing overall health too).

People with IBS who exercise regularly tend to experience fewer symptoms and flare-ups than people who don’t exercise.

When researchers asked people with IBS to walk moderately for an hour three times a week, study participants experienced significant relief from bloating and abdominal pain within 12 weeks.6

How exercise soothes IBS isn’t fully understood, though.

According to other research, exercise may reduce stress and improve mental health, which, in turn, may help improve communication between the gut and the brain.7 8

Another theory argues that exercise helps encourage the growth of health-promoting gut bacteria, which may help to break down food more efficiently and decrease inflammation.9

Anxiety, stress, and depression all activate stress hormones like norepinephrine (noradrenaline) and cortisol, which can:

Of course, stress doesn’t come with an on/off switch.

Simply telling yourself, “Stop getting so stressed out!” won’t likely help—and may even paradoxically lead to more stress.

That’s why Precision Nutrition-certified coaches like Maughan help clients learn to focus on what’s within their control—such as practicing self-compassion, or experimenting with nervous system regulators like yoga, breathing exercises, and gentle walking.

As the image below illustrates, clients can control how they perceive, respond to, and anticipate stressors—but not always the stressors themselves.

Either way, when clients focus more on what they can control and less on what they can’t, they often feel calmer and more capable.

(If you want to help a client figure out just what’s within their control—and what’s not—try out our free worksheet: Sphere of Control Worksheet)

(Assess your current stress load by taking our free quiz: Do you have a Stress Bod?)

PN coaches have long appreciated and advocated slower, more relaxed eating.

Yes, slow eating helps people fill up on fewer calories—but it also tends to help clients reduce or even eliminate GI woes like acid reflux, bloating, and pain.

For one, slower eating often translates to more chewing. In addition to mechanically mashing food into a pulp, increased chewing also allows the mouth’s digestive enzymes to pre-digest food. As a result, the stomach and intestines have to work less hard.

Plus, eating in a relaxed setting often lowers stress hormones like norepinephrine and cortisol, making it less likely that they will intensify GI pain signals.

According to Maughan, this can be especially important for young parents, as it’s not always easy to eat undistracted and peacefully when tending to little ones.

(Sounds simple, but slow eating is more challenging than people think—and a lot more impactful. Learn more: Try the slow-eating 30-day challenge.)

According to research, people with IBS experience more shallow, less restorative, and more interrupted sleep.13

Because of poor sleep quality, many people with IBS sleep more hours overall than people without IBS—yet feel less rested.

Fatigue can then set off a vicious cycle. When people don’t sleep restfully, stress hormone levels tend to be higher, which can exacerbate gut pain.14

Unrested people also tend to feel hungrier during the day. Cravings for fats and sweets also intensify, driving people to reach for the very foods more likely to trigger IBS symptoms—and wolf them down too quickly.

As with stress, you can’t simply will yourself to sleep more restfully.

However, the first three strategies—exercise, stress management, and slower eating—can all help.

Some PN clients have found that consuming a smaller dinner earlier in the evening gives their bodies more time to digest before bed. Other clients tell us that a relaxing pre-bedtime routine—a few minutes of foam rolling, a guided meditation, a bath, or some journalling—tends to help.

(Find out the best practices for getting better sleep by checking out our infographic: The power of sleep)

While there’s no one-size-fits-all IBS diet, experts have identified several food categories that are more likely to be problematic for many people. These include:

▶ Fermentable Oligosaccharides, Disaccharides, Monosaccharides, and Polyols (FODMAPs), which are a family of carbohydrate-rich foods that are poorly absorbed in the small intestine. Even in people without IBS, these foods tend to slow digestion and attract water. When gut bacteria ferment them, they produce gas, which can stretch the intestinal wall. For most, this slowed digestion and gas isn’t especially noticeable; In people with IBS, it can lead to intense pain. High-FODMAP foods include wheat, rye, barley, onions, garlic, beans, dairy, honey, cashews, some processed meats, and many fruits and vegetables. (More about FODMAPs in the next section.)

▶ Caffeinated beverages and foods, especially coffee, which trigger the release of stress hormones, stimulate the production of stomach acid, increase muscle contractions in the colon, and irritate the lining of the intestine.15

▶ Alcohol and spicy foods that irritate the gut.16 17

▶ High fructose corn syrup and sugar alcohols such sorbitol and mannitol, which have been linked to gas, bloating, and diarrhea in susceptible people.18 19

▶ Fatty, greasy foods, which can slow digestion and attract water, leading to loose stools, bloating, and gas.20 21

If the idea of giving up all the foods and beverages on the above list has you in a cold sweat, know this…

Not everyone with IBS is sensitive to the same foods and beverages.

“Everyone can have different triggers,” says Maughan. “That’s why it’s so important to figure out what makes your body feel good and what doesn’t.”

Some people struggle with apples but are okay with berries. Others can drink green tea but not black. One person might be able to consume five to eight ounces of beer but not 12. A gluten-free diet may work great for some but not others.

Similarly, many people find relief by avoiding certain high-FODMAP foods. However, you may only be sensitive to some FODMAPs and not others. If so, eliminating all FODMAPs would be unnecessarily restrictive and difficult to follow consistently.

For this reason, it can be helpful to try an elimination diet to see which foods and beverages are problematic—along with the quantities you can safely tolerate, says Maughan. You’ll learn more about elimination diets in the next section.

(Want someone to walk you through exactly how to do an elimination diet? Read: How and why to do an elimination diet.)

In our online coaching communities, we often see people asking some version of the following question:

“My client just told me that she has IBS. Am I allowed to continue to coach this person?”

As we mentioned, Maughan specializes in helping people with digestive problems. Coaching someone with IBS is no different than coaching a client with any other nutritional goal, she says.

“Because IBS is often largely associated with what someone eats, it’s within a coach’s wheelhouse—with some caveats,” says Maughan. “You can’t diagnose your client with the condition, and you should make it clear that you’re not prescribing a diet for them. In addition, you should encourage clients to seek care from a medical professional, especially if you suspect something other than IBS is going on.”

To stay within your scope of practice, follow these do’s and don’ts.

Elimination diets do what the name suggests: They exclude certain foods for a short period—usually three weeks. Then, you slowly reintroduce specific foods and monitor your symptoms for possible reactions.

Elimination diets work a lot like a science experiment that helps you identify problematic foods.

The phrase “elimination diet” may sound scary and off-putting, as if you’ll be living for months on bland food you have to slurp through a straw.

However, there are many different types of elimination diets, with some much less restrictive than others.

This is an excellent option for people who suspect they already know which foods and beverages trigger symptoms.

It goes like this: You eliminate up to four foods for several weeks. Then, slowly reintroduce them one at a time to see if your symptoms return.

Let’s say, for example, from experience, you know you feel bad whenever you eat dairy. On the lite elimination diet, you’d eliminate just dairy for three weeks. Then you’d reintroduce it to see how you feel.

If you’re unsure of how food interacts with your GI tract—but aren’t ready for a super restrictive eating plan, our Precision Nutrition elimination diet is likely the way to go.

Created by PN and approved by several registered dietitians, the plan removes many of the foods most likely to cause problems, while still including a variety of vegetables, fruits, starches, legumes, nuts, seeds, and meats, so you can continue to eat a well-balanced diet.

To learn more, download our FREE Ultimate Guide to Elimination Diets. This ebook has everything you need to be successful, including an at-a-glance chart that helps you easily follow the diet, along with recipes, meal ideas, and tip sheets.

Over several years, researchers at Monash University in Australia have developed and extensively studied a low-FODMAP elimination diet for people with IBS.22

Unlike other types of elimination diets, the FODMAP diet is a highly specialized form of medical nutrition therapy. The FODMAP diet’s list of problematic foods (shown below) is anything but intuitive, and the reintroduction phase is more complex than other elimination diets.

As a result, if you’ve been diagnosed with IBS and suspect you have a FODMAP issue, seek the expertise of a FODMAP-certified practitioner. You can also download Monash University’s FODMAP Diet app, which will help you navigate low-FODMAP eating.

In isolation, more knowledge doesn’t always lead to more power.

For example, there’s a difference between knowing that dairy messes with your gut and doing something with that knowledge.

Similarly, you might know that you feel better when you eat a small dinner earlier in the evening, but you may struggle to plan your life so an early dinner happens regularly.

This is where a certified health coach can help.

“Many of my clients already have an idea of the foods that tend to cause them problems,” says Maughan, “But they’re nervous to know for sure because they fear that the knowledge will make eating more challenging.”

Even if you do an elimination diet and you learn your favorite food is contributing to your IBS, you don’t have to do anything with that information.

You can choose to continue to eat your favourite foods if you want, AND you can choose to avoid them when it’s really important for you not to experience IBS symptoms, she says.

“With knowledge, you have choices,” says Maughan.

#8918. How to Start a Workout When You Really Don’t Feel Like It (The Bridge Task Method)

If you can’t get yourself to start a workout after a long day, the problem might not be the workout itself. It’s the gear shift from “couch” to “go.”

A bridge task is a small, neutral action (not fun, not hard, just…meh) that you put in between the two so the jump is smaller.

Below is the 5-step version one of our coaching clients uses with her own students, plus a free worksheet to map your own.

A few weeks ago I was talking with Tabitha, a Nerd Fitness coaching client, about a challenge a lot of people face. ​ Some quick context: Tabitha is an executive function coach. She helps neurodivergent students and their families build the skills and systems that support their academic and personal goals. ​ And she noticed something: ​ The challenge of getting started on a workout is almost identical to the challenge her students face when trying to start homework. ​ This might sound familiar. You get home after a long day, mentally fried, and all you want to do is veg out on the couch. ​ In that state, getting up to cook a healthy dinner or go do a workout can feel really freaking hard.

Switching from a “YEAH!” task (chilling on the couch) to a “NAH!” task (workout/homework), is often harder than the task itself.

If we can make that gear shift less dramatic, it can make a big difference!

Instead of going from YEAH! to NAH!, you insert at least one task that’s just…MEH.

If you’re struggling to start your workout, don’t fight the gear change. Bridge it.

Add a little MEH to the mix and see what happens.

Tabitha put together a free worksheet that walks you through mapping your own task initiation sequence. Your personal YEAH -> MEH -> NAH.

Try it this week, and keep me posted on how it goes. ​ You got this. ​ -Matt

2) Want a coach who builds a plan and walks with you each step of the way? Learn about NF Coaching.

#8917. How Yin Yoga Bananasana Can Transform Your Swimming

Swimmers spend plenty of time working on stroke mechanics and building upper-body strength, but mobility of the side body, particularly the intercostal muscles between the ribs, can affect how freely you can breathe, especially as fatigue sets in.

Bananasana, a gentle yin yoga pose, stretches the side body. A supported side-lying pose, with blocks under the ribs and head, creates a more targeted stretch that can help expand your ribs for three-dimensional breathing.

While Bananasana offers a relatively subtle lateral stretch of the obliques, intercostal muscles, and IT band, a supported side-lying variation increases the sensation and may help ease fascial tightness.

Fascia is a network of connective tissue that surrounds and connects muscles, nerves, bones, and organs. When fascia’s layers glide well, the body moves freely. However, training load, injury, prolonged postures, and other factors can contribute to stiffness or reduced mobility. Restriction in the rib cage and side body can make a full, expansive breath feel harder to achieve.

Give your shoulders and lats attention, but don’t overlook your ribs and side body. Add these stretches to your regular mobility routine to build breath awareness and find more ease and efficiency in the water.

#8916. A WorldTour Rider Shared His Tire Pressure. It’s Lower Than You Think.

His answer was striking even in an era when road tire pressures keep dropping.

An Instagram Reel featuring world tour pro Luke Plapp (Team Jayco-AlUla) talking about tire pressure appeared in my Instagram feed and caught my attention, mostly because many pro riders either won't tell you or don’t know their tire pressure, and most team mechanics won’t openly share that information with the press. Now, I’ve been on the lower-is-generally-better tire-pressure train for many years. I routinely run my road bike tires between 50 and 70 psi, depending on the bike, tire, and wheel setup. I was still struck by how low Plapp’s number was, even by modern standards.

The clip comes from the September 23, 2026, episode of Stanley St. Social podcast. Plapp says he gets the same reaction whenever he tells people what pressure he runs. “This is actually one where every single time I tell people what tire pressure I run, every punter all over the world just can't believe it, so we're running 32mm tires at 3.7 to 3.8 bar.” That works out to 53.7 to 55.1 psi.

Plapp calls them 32mm tires. But the team is using CADEX Aero 30mm, so his quote likely refers to their mounted width. I haven’t measured the exact setup of the CADEX Ultra 50 wheels, which use a hookless rim with a 22.4mm internal width and 30mm external width with the CADEX Aero 30mm tire. But I’ve ridden these particular tires and reviewed the CADEX 50 Ultra for Bicycling. In my test, a nominal 28mm CADEX Race tire measured close to 30mm on the 22.4mm internal rim. So it’s very reasonable to assume that a labeled 30mm tire would inflate closer to 32mm. You can read my CADEX 50 Ultra wheelset review here.

The biggest piece of information that we don’t have from this clip is Plapp’s actual weight. His Pro Cycling Stats page lists him as 158.75 lbs, which may or may not be accurate. But using that as an estimate puts Plapp firmly on the lower end of the tire-pressure spectrum, as I would expect someone that weight to run closer to the low-sixties psi based on various tire pressure calculators. That means Plapp is either a bit lighter than PCS thinks he is, or he simply prefers the added comfort and grip of running lower pressure.

But why is any of this interesting? For one, I generally agree with Plapp’s inferred assessment that many riders still run too much tire pressure. That’s generally been true when I talk to folks in my riding circles. Because of this, I think many riders simply don’t understand just how low performance-oriented riders have gone with their tire pressure. So if you don’t want to hear it from me, I hope hearing it from Plapp, who has raced the Tour de France for the last two years, will be more convincing.

Finally, the brief quote also highlights that if you care about your performance and optimize your tire pressure, you shouldn't take the labeled tire size at face value. Instead, you need to actually measure your tires inflated on the wheelset you are using. Just because something is labeled as 30mm doesn't mean it will measure 30mm on your wheels, and that can change the tire-pressure math in a meaningful way.

If you don’t know where to start with tire pressure, read this story, then check out my recommended tire-pressure calculators to dial in your setup.

#8915. Does Soreness Mean a Good Workout? No. Here’s What It Actually Tells You

Soreness is not an indicator of a good workout, and not being sore doesn’t mean your workout didn’t count.

That day-after ache (DOMS) mostly tells you that you did something new, not something effective.

Progress is more reliably measured in your training log: more weight, more reps, more control over time, sore or not.

Rachael (a reader and all-around amazing person) sent me a question about this so well-organized it came with multiple choice answers. 😃

I LOVE this question, because almost everyone who’s getting started (or starting again) wonders the same thing:

Quick definition first. That achy, stiff, “why does it hurt to sit on the toilet” feeling that shows up a day or two after a workout has a name: DOMS, or Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness.

It usually peaks somewhere around 24-72 hours after you train.

Severe soreness is NOT an indicator of a good workout.

It’s a sign that you did something new that your body isn’t used to yet:

But it’s also not something to be afraid of, especially if you switch up your routine and are mildly sore for a day or two.

Your body is adapting quickly! And as you adjust to the new exercises, you’ll be less and less sore from it.

So when is soreness helpful, if ever? ​ Soreness can give us a useful signal that we worked a muscle we were trying to target and hadn’t felt before.

But if you’re SUPER sore? Like, can’t get out of bed the next day and have to waddle around like a newborn giraffe sore? That’s a sign the jump was bigger than your body needed.

And the real cost (beyond the discomfort) is that it gets in the way of your next couple of workouts. Either because your technique gets sloppy because everything hurts, or you’re so wrecked that you don’t want to show up at all.

The best way to lower your odds of severe DOMS is to ease into a new program slowly.

Start with fewer sets and lighter weights than you think you need, and build from there. 💪

Yes! You DO need to push yourself over time in order to make progress:

That’s the law of progressive overload, and there’s no getting around it.

Sometimes adding that extra bit will make you sore. Other times, it won’t.

But it’s the underlying principle that matters: are you asking a little more of yourself over time? Not: did it hurt afterward?

So why do we care so much about soreness?

Here’s what I think we’ve fallen into with fitness in general.

We as humans operate really well with feedback. If we touch a hot stove, we get burned and know not to do that again.

We want to know, immediately after doing something, whether it worked or it didn’t.

And with strength training, you don’t feel stronger the next day. It takes time to build up.

So we reach for proxies that close that feedback loop.

It’s exactly like the story of minty toothpaste.

As the story goes, toothpaste manufacturers had a hard time selling their product until they added mint.

Suddenly, there was a tingly clean feeling you could latch onto. “Oh, this IS working.”

The mint doesn’t clean your teeth. But it’s associated with the thing that does, and it gave people something to feel.

It’s not the REASON you’re getting stronger.

But it can be associated with the work you do, especially as a beginner who is new to exercise, so we’ve learned to chase the tingle.

✅ How much weight, how many reps, how many sets are you doing?

✅ Do you feel more stable and controlled with the exercise than you did last month?

Then great! It’s working. Doesn’t matter if you never get sore.

And if you do end up super sore after trying something new, it’s not that you “failed”.

Just take it as a cue to introduce things more gently next time. 😊

So, back to Rachael’s multiple choice question.

C is really close. But I’ll add an fourth option:

D) Soreness tells you what was NEW. Your training log tells you what’s WORKING.

No extra fitness points for being sore. No points off if you do end up sore, either.

All the points gently ramping things up over time, and showing up again next time. 🔥

Is it bad if I’m never sore? No. If your weights, reps, or control are improving over time, your training is working, sore or not.

How long does DOMS last? It usually peaks 24 to 72 hours after the workout and fades over a few days. If you’re regularly wrecked for longer, ease the jumps in your program.

Should I work out while sore? Mild soreness is fine to train through, and easy movement often helps. If you’re severely sore, target a different part of the body, scale down, or take another rest day; what we don’t want to do is have sloppy technique because we’re SO sore we can’t perform the exercise normally.

#8914. New Pedals, No Problem: How to Install Pedals Without Damaging Your Bike

Avoid stripped crank threads and costly repairs with this step-by-step pedal swap guide.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

There are few part swaps I have seen cause more damage on a bike than an incorrectly installed set of pedals. I’ve seen experienced and beginner cyclists make a pedal installation mistake causing damage to both the pedal and the crank—resulting in anywhere from a little under $100 of damage to over $500. In some cases threads can be cleaned up and parts can be saved, but too many times this small part install can lead to hundreds of dollars in repairs.

Two of the most common ways I have seen this mistake happen are from a pedal going in at an angle into the threads of the crank or the pedals being installed on the wrong side of the cranks. If the system is damaged beyond repair, then parts need to be replaced.

Another way this can go wrong is if the pedals are not fully torqued during the installation to the cranks. When I ran a shop I’ve had customers come in that tried to install pedals at home, but the pedals backed out mid ride. When this happens it can be both a safety issue for the rider and cause damage to the bike. The good news is when done right this is a straightforward install process that can be done at home. The right tools, an easy-to-follow guide, and some attention are all you need to avoid some of the most common pedal installation issues. Below we have your guide on everything you need to know about installing your new pedals.

One thing to note on this method—I always begin the removal process and the final torquing of the pedals with the bike on the ground. This is because the torque that goes into the removal of the pedals and to meet the final torque specifications can cause stress on the frame and seatpost if the bike is clamped in a stand—especially for carbon posts and frames. When removing the pedals, put the bike in the stand after they don’t require force to loosen. Conversely, take the bike out of the stand during install after the pedals are properly screwed into the cranks, but before they get their final needed torque.

Pedal Wrenchor 5 or 6 mm Hex Wrench/Allen KeysBicycle Grease

To reduce the chance of damaging your bike, Bicycling always recommends consulting the manufacturer’s recommended torque setting and using a torque wrench when installing or servicing bike parts.
