#8898. The beliefs these Master Health Coaches had to unlearn (and you might too)

For example, in Motivational Interviewing, an effective communication style used in coaching and counseling, there is something called the “righting reflex.”

The righting reflex is the instinct to help or “fix” a client, as well as give them directions on how best to change. Often, the righting reflex is particularly strong in people who really, really care.

Sounds like a great instinct to follow if you’re a coach, right?

Motivational Interviewing describes how this (beautiful, well-intentioned) instinct to help can actually hinder a client’s progress.

That’s because when we swoop in to fix, correct, or steer, clients often do the exact opposite of what we’re hoping for: They dig in and get defensive.

Push someone the “right” way and, paradoxically, they’ll start advocating for the very habits they came to you to change. You end up being the one arguing for change—which leaves them to argue against it. Everyone walks away a little more frustrated, and the client feels more stuck than ever.

Instead, great, experienced coaches learn to get curious instead of corrective. (They might even encourage the client to explore not changing!)

That’s just one example of an upside-down skill that separates a good coach from a masterful one. But it’s certainly not the only example.

We asked some of Precision Nutrition’s most seasoned PN Level 2 Master Health Coach Certified coaches a simple question:

What’s something you were sure about early in your career that you later had to unlearn?

Their (honest, and sometimes humbling) answers are below, plus the wiser way forward they adopted, and are now sharing with you.

Our first lesson to unlearn comes from PN in-house coach Jeremy Fernandes, PN2-MHC.

With over 14 years of coaching experience, Coach Jeremy is known for his friendly, comfortable, “talk to me like I’m your buddy” coaching style. Which is ironic, because as you’ll see, he started off his career leaning heavily on a rigid structure that was actually pushing clients away.

At the beginning of my career, when I’d been a personal trainer for a year or two, I had a friend ask if I offered nutrition coaching. And my first move was: Here are all of the forms. And when I say “all of the forms,” I mean all of them—I probably sent this person 20 pages to fill out.

Three weeks later I had to hunt them down, and we ended up filling them out together—which took two and a half grueling hours.

If not for those forms, we could have started actually coaching, like, 20 days earlier.

Not long after, another friend showed up at my door with this white-hot intensity: “Tell me what to do, I’m ready,” they said. And I immediately dumped a metaphorical bucket of ice water on them with those darn forms. It was radio silence after that.

The problem was that I was operating like my sole job was to extract information from a person and then solve the mystery—as if I had some advanced pattern recognition about you that you didn’t have about yourself.

And unfortunately, I kept on that terrible path for a while.

What finally prompted a change was going through the Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification.

Going through that course, I saw there was a better framework—one that doesn’t rely on me robotically extracting information.

I learned to let the client take the lead, and then just listen and maybe ask a few good questions. And it works so much better—for everyone.

Now I work from the assumption that my client knows themselves better than anyone. One of my most valuable questions is simply:

“What have you tried before, what did you like about it, and what didn’t you like?”

When I let people take the floor, they nail the really big stuff more often than not—in a way my paperwork and my detective work never facilitated.

Honestly, the forms were me projecting professionalism, because back then I didn’t feel like a professional. My identity as a coach never felt natural until after L2. Now, just letting someone talk feels like coaching. We start with a connection, and then I just let them fill in the gaps.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN Director of Community Engagement and in-house coach Kate Solovieva, PN2-MHC.

With over 16 years of coaching experience, Coach Kate is known for her honesty and incisiveness. She has a way of dropping realness on her clients that may first feel like a shock, but ultimately ends up getting her clients to the heart of the matter much faster. But one hard truth she had to face was her own.

You know the story: You reach the healthy weight, the habits lock in, and the weight just stays stable on its own. You hit “save” and move on with your happily ever after.

At least most of the time. It’s true, some goals really are like that. If you want to run a marathon, you can pick a race date, follow a training program, show up to the start line, run it—and then you never have to run again and you will still have achieved that goal. That’s a real destination; you cross the finish line once and check the goal off.

But weight loss, muscle gain, body recomposition, building a habit of movement or eating well—those aren’t like that. Especially when the goal means working against a chronic tendency, like a predisposition to high blood pressure, or to hating exercise, or to living in a larger body than you’d prefer.

Those goals come with a pretty good amount of ongoing and intentional maintenance—daily, weekly, monthly. There’s no save button.

This realization didn’t come from one single client or one moment for me. It came through a collection of observations, including observations of myself. But once I saw it, it changed how I coach.

I realized that if there’s no real finish line, then my job is to manufacture finish lines along the way. That way, my clients continually feel like they’re accomplishing something satisfying.

I take the big goal and break it into something specific and daily—and then I insert smaller outcome goals into the journey.

For instance, someone going from sedentary to wanting to lose 100 pounds is facing a huge goal, full of behaviors and identities they’ll have to grow into. So along the way, we might set a goal of running a single mile without stopping. Strictly speaking, that doesn’t have much to do with the bigger goal—but it also has everything to do with it. It’s checkable. Achievable. Ideally it’s also something they’re a little excited about: fun, interesting, maybe even a little scary, but still within reach.

Because here’s the thing: It’s very hard to motivate the human brain to work out three times a week for the rest of their life to “get healthier.” “Being healthy” isn’t tangible, it’s not immediate—you can’t feel that far-off outcome in your body.

But striving towards a fun, achievable goal in the next three to six months? That’s real. It also builds in structure, and provides those little spikes of motivation—the hit of dopamine you get from working hard at something and actually accomplishing it.

Health isn’t something we ever fully “accomplish” or check off. So we have to give ourselves these little concrete goals along the way that we can feel and see and be delighted by.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN content creator Azul Corajoria, CPT, PN2-MHC.

With over nine years of coaching experience, Coach Azul’s coaching fingerprint is empathetic, relatable, and endlessly encouraging.

While these traits always came naturally to her, for a long time, she thought she had to adopt an opposite style to help certain clients (and herself) to “get back in line” when habits didn’t go as planned.

Early in my coaching career, I thought that if someone wasn’t following through on what they said they would do, it’s because they needed more structure or just to get their “head in the game.”

I couldn’t understand why someone would invest in coaching and then not do the things we planned.

It was especially confusing because most of my clients had “discipline.” They were successful, responsible, hardworking people who showed up for their jobs, families, and everyone else in their lives.

Meanwhile, I was also “disciplined” in many areas of my life—yet I also struggled with eating well and exercising consistently.

At this time, I felt this lack of consistency was my fault, and went straight to being really angry at myself. I thought I was just missing the “perfect something” (the perfect workout, the perfect diet) to help me change, so I’d just move from thing to thing, but each one would bring fresh disappointment.

I was incredibly frustrated by this cycle, and my response was to get stricter and harsher with myself.

It’s hard to say when it all changed. It wasn’t an overnight epiphany; it was a culmination of years of getting curious, being open to different methods, like the Body Positivity Movement and Intuitive Eating. I dove into self-compassion and positive psychology research, and I went through the PN Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification.

I applied everything I learned, and I noticed that the more open and curious I was, the better my clients responded. Slowly, that turned into the realization that the more open and curious I was with myself, the better I would respond.

I stopped binge eating. I started enjoying exercise more. I took more career risks.

I learned that when we can respond to a setback with curiosity instead of punishment, we’re much more likely to stay engaged. When I allow myself to be disappointed by an action, take responsibility for it, and remain on my own side, I feel safer reflecting and taking risks. The more I do that, the more likely I am to achieve the things I want.

Sometimes the most helpful thing we can teach a client (and ourselves) is not how to push harder or “just be more disciplined.” It’s how to make a mistake, remain on our own side, and keep going.

Because self-compassion is not the opposite of accountability; it’s often what makes accountability possible. (I call it “compassionate accountability.”)

None of us will ever be the “perfect” coach, and we don’t have to be. The more human I’ve allowed myself to be, the better relationships I’ve had with my clients. My biggest goal as a coach is to create an environment my client feels safe to come back to with not only their wins, but their losses. The safer they feel being honest and open with me, the safer they’ll feel to try new things—and over time they’ll build the confidence to do it themselves.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN in-house coach and Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification instructor Dom Matteo, PN2-MHC, NBC-HWC.

With over 16 years of coaching experience, Coach Dom stands out for his non-judgemental attitude and excellent listening skills. For Dom, these traits are relatively inherent, but they’ve also been carefully developed and honed, in part by letting go of what he calls the “coach’s ego”—the assumption that he already knew what a client’s success should look like, and that he was the one who got to keep score.

I took that stated goal at face value, and treated whatever number they gave me as the measuring stick, as the most important thing to work towards.

But then, I’d see a client struggling to do their actions even 50 percent of the time, and I’d think: ‘This person is never going to be happy, because this won’t get them to the goal weight they told me they wanted.’

Remember, I assumed the number was the real goal.

However, again and again, those same clients would turn out to be genuinely happy with their progress, not because they hit their exact goal, but because they felt so much better about themselves and their lives.

What I learned is that the stated outcome was almost never the true goal for many of them. When they said ‘lose 50 pounds,’ what they really meant was: I want to feel better. And being consistent even half the time, over a year, netted results they were thrilled with. Because they felt better. They felt different.

So the thing I had to let go of was my own scorecard. Who am I to tell a client that what they’re doing isn’t good enough, if they’re happy with how things are going?

My new definition of progress became less about approaching a specific final number and more about another question: “Am I a little better today than I was yesterday?”

These days, I spend time up front helping a client build what we call a “wellness vision.” We clarify their values, and what success actually looks and feels like to them.

Then, instead of assuming I know how to measure their progress, I’ll ask: “How will you know if this is helping? How do you want to measure success?”

The result is that even a client who’s fixated on the scale can see other signs of progress long before the scale actually changes. And often, those other signs are the things they really wanted to change in the first place.

It turns out the most useful thing I can provide isn’t a judgement about whether a client is succeeding. Instead, it’s to help them determine and notice their own success, by their own measures.

The next lesson to unlearn comes from PN in-house coach and Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification instructor Jason Bonn, PN2-MHC, NBC-HWC.

With over 18 years of coaching experience, Coach Jason’s clients describe him as patient, observant, and deeply dedicated. He has a knack for spotting a client’s potential—though as you’ll read in this story, Coach Jason learned that getting too focused on a specific version of that potential sometimes kept him from seeing other ways his clients could grow and thrive.

For me, progress felt like a puzzle to solve: I’d play with adjustments to exercise volume or intensity, calorie or protein intake, eating more slowly, eating to 80 percent fullness, all the fundamental stuff.

But then, because of one client I still think about, I began to shift how I thought about “progress.”

He was in our PN coaching program. He lost 40 to 50 pounds in his first six months—which was great—but then everything stalled.

We tried adjustment after adjustment for the next two and a half years. We added more protein, more cardio, and worked through his particular peccadillo, eating corn chips at night. But none of it moved his numbers.

What got me was that he kept showing up anyway: three straight years, re-enrolling each time, even though the scale had plateaued.

That told me something was working for him—it just wasn’t something I recognized yet.

In his third year, we stopped looking only at the gym and his diet, and started looking at his whole life. He was a landscape painter, so we built his practices around that instead: make a sketch or work on a painting daily, anything that sparked some joy or interest. Within a couple of weeks, he was getting on his bike and riding out to further places for different scenery to paint.

In part because of this client, I’m now a lot more cognizant of coaching the whole person, and considering their Deep Health. Weight and performance numbers are just one piece of a much bigger picture that includes relationships, emotional wellbeing, and what someone finds meaningful.

I’ve also stopped zeroing in on “problem” behavior.

I try to understand a person’s life overall—not just the behavior I’ve been hired to help with—because there’s a connectedness to it all, and behavior tends to emerge within the context of someone’s life.

I’ve also stopped treating the coaching relationship as a means to an outcome and started treating it as the main thing—the sun that everything orbits, the glue that holds it all together.

That client kept coming back for three years because the relationship mattered to him. By the end, I’d stopped thinking I was failing him. The weight loss was such a small part of the success. The relationship was the bigger piece.

Coaching mastery isn’t about stockpiling more information. (Your clients can Google information or ask a chatbot, and so can you.)

It’s about developing the judgment to know when to use what you know, when to set it aside, and when the most helpful thing you can do is nothing at all, except be there.

But that kind of judgment is hard to build alone; it takes practice, expert feedback, and a few humbling moments with real clients—which is exactly what the PN Level 2 Master Health Coach Certification is designed to offer.

With enough practice, self-awareness, and the right training, you can gain the wisdom and skill of the above coaches.

But the best coaches, it turns out, are defined less by what they know than by what they’ve been willing to unlearn.

Ready to move from competent to truly masterful—in 20 weeks?

The PN Level 2 Master Health Coaching Certification is an advanced, practice-based program designed for coaches who want to work at a deeper level—and do it sooner than the traditional 5–10 year path.

It’s a mentored, small-group experience that prepares you to:

#8897. Stop Cramming Bikes in Your Car. These 10 Editor-Tested Hitch Racks Make Hauling Easier and More Secure

Our editors hauled bikes for thousands of miles to find the easiest, sturdiest hitch racks.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Cramming your bike into your car or SUV gets old quickly. Removing wheels and getting mud or grease all over your interior is no fun, and transporting your bike inside your car also leaves less room for passengers, luggage, or gear. Hitch-mount racks are the easiest, most secure way to carry your bike to your riding destination without mess or hassle. They’re ideal for heading to your local mountain bike trails, taking a road trip with friends, or going for weekend rides with your kids.

Hitch racks mount to the receiver on your vehicle’s bumper, making hitch racks easier to load than roof racks—hoisting a heavy bike onto an SUV’s roof after a long ride is never fun. Plus, you don’t need to remove your front wheel. Unlike roof racks, you can also drive into parking garages and drive-thrus with bikes on a hitch rack. And importantly, in an era of sky-high fuel prices, hitch racks typically impact your gas mileage less than roof-mounted options.

While hitch racks usually cost more than simple, low-cost trunk-mount racks, they can last for many years with proper care and maintenance. Hitch-mount carriers can also carry heavier bikes, like electric bikes or full suspension rigs, than trunk racks and are more stable at highway speeds.

Our editors and test team evaluated dozens of hitch racks to see which ones perform best. Our staff has used some of these racks on their own vehicles for years, safely transporting bikes over tens of thousands of miles. Our picks for the best hitch-mounted bike racks vary in features like position, trunk access functionality, bike capacity, and price—but all are dependable options for your next cycling trip.

Based on price, weight capacity, and ease of use, Thule’s Outpace ranks as our current Best Overall pick. The Outpace is lighter and more compact than most hitch racks, which makes it easy to install and remove. At only 28 pounds, it’s light enough to carry across the garage and slide into the receiver tube. Setup takes less than a minute, so you can mount it on the car when you need to haul your bikes (rather than it semi-permanently living on your bumper).

The rack can accommodate a wider range of bike wheel sizes, making it great for families. The rack adapts easily to any size bicycle in either position. The tradeoff for this versatility is that it takes a bit longer to load than bulkier racks with cinch-style clamps. But for something that can carry all of our bikes, and is so quick to install or remove that it never has to be a permanent fixture, that’s a small price to pay.

Our tester noted the Outpace’s receiver arm is on the short side. It fit snugly against the bumper with about two inches to spare, but on another vehicle, it wouldn’t fit without a hitch extender.

The Trail Rider is a great, lower-cost alternative to premium racks. It holds two bikes in fixed wheel mounts, secured with a single ratcheting arm that clamps down over the frame. The upright beam (which holds the frame holders) folds back and out of the way for trunk access; it’s also handy for loading up two bikes. We could fold it down, set a bike on the rack closest to the car without lifting it up and over the arm, then lift the arm back into place and position the second bike.

The trade-off for the Trail Rider’s low price isn’t stability or strength, but adjustability: The bikes are positioned in a fixed location. You have limited ability to separate them if two bikes don’t fit well together. That said, you can stagger the wheel cradles so the bars and saddles don’t interfere.

The Swagman XTC2 is one of the most affordable 2-bike racks we recommend. This no-frills rack is a solid choice for budget-conscious riders. It fits both 1¼-inch and 2-inch receiver tubes, and it accommodates wheel sizes from 20 to 29 inches. However, with a total weight capacity of 70 pounds (35 pounds per bike), it’s not suitable for e-bikes.

As expected at this price, the rack has some trade-offs. The wheel hoops are adjustable, but not as smoothly or precisely as on more premium racks. The rack doesn’t tilt away from the vehicle when loaded, limiting access to tailgates or liftgates. Lastly, you must remove the center support bar to load a bike on the inside tray.

Yet, the XTC2 is lightweight, durable, and very reasonably priced. If you’re willing to trade a bit of convenience for significant savings, the Swagman XTC2 is a reliable and practical option.

The Piston Pro X is our runner-up for Best Overall hitch rack; its construction, features, and style make it a standout pick in the category. Aside from the high price, the Piston Pro X is almost the perfect hitch rack for most users.

With the Piston Pro X, Küat elevated the rack from something purely utilitarian to a desirable piece of gear that’s easier to use than other racks. The rack includes smart features (such as integrated brake and turn-signal lights) and can carry more wheel sizes (and more weight) than almost any other rack on the market.

The top-end Pro X model costs more than almost any other hitch-mount rack, but it has proven extremely durable and maintains its good looks. It's also available in 3- and 4-bike models. Küat also offers a slightly cheaper Piston Pro variant, which ditches the Kashima coating on the pistons and the integrated brake lights and turn signals.

If you like the Küat racks but $1,600 is out of your price range, the brand offers several other hitch-style racks that could meet your needs. One great option is the Sherpa 2.0 model.

While the Sherpa doesn’t have the features or carrying capacity of Küat’s more expensive racks, it has two big upsides—color options and low weight. The Sherpa weighs only 32 pounds (claimed) in the 2-inch hitch configuration (1.25-in. also available). Küat offers the Sherpa in three colors: black metallic (with a silver accent), grey metallic (with orange), and pearl white (with silver).

The Sherpa carries two bicycles weighing up to 40 pounds per tray. So it’s ideal for non-electric road, gravel, and mountain bikes. It has an integrated cable lock to secure your bikes during rest stops or meal breaks, and it features a foot-operated lever to lower the rack into position for loading bikes.

It’s often difficult to carry e-bikes that are equipped with racks and fenders on traditional hitch racks. That’s because many hitch racks secure the bike with extending arms that clamp one or both wheels. However, Thule’s EasyFold XT model holds your bike by its frame.

Another feature that makes the EasyFold ideal for e-bike owners is the included ramp. This makes loading or removing your bikes much easier; no more wrestling with heavy bikes or front wheels or handlebars flopping as you load them onto the rack. And the ramp attaches to the rack when you’re finished.

Thanks to the rack’s 45-pound weight, it’s easy to remove it from your vehicle when you’re not using it. It folds down and features casters (which make moving it around your garage easier). The EasyFold XT’s biggest drawback is that Thule only rates it to 65 pounds per bike. While that will accommodate many e-bikes, some fat tire models may weigh too much.

When Thule debuted the T2 over a decade ago, it raised the bar for what cyclists expect from a hitch-mounted bike rack. Over the years, Thule updated the rack to accommodate wider tires and different wheel sizes. It also improved the T2’s look and made it easier to operate. One of the best recent upgrades is a wide-trigger handle that allows you to raise and lower the rack (and dip it out of the way for access to rear hatches) with one hand.

Integrated cable locks help keep your bikes secure for quick stops, and each tray can hold a bicycle up to 60 pounds and tires up to 5 inches wide. This makes the T2 a good option for all but the heaviest e-bikes. The T2 Pro’s arms have wide, comfortable grips that slide easily to secure the front wheel. Instead of using a bolt, the rack secures to your hitch receiver with an expansion wedge that tightens with a locking knob. The system makes installing and removing the T2 easier (though it weighs 52 pounds), but it’s not foolproof.

Yakima’s StageTwo two-bike rack goes head-to-head with premium offerings from Küat and Thule at a lower price. In about 2,500 miles of on-car testing, the StageTwo impressed us with its ease of use and flex-free performance. This rack is only rated up to 35 pounds per tray, so it’s not made for transporting e-bikes. However, it’s one of only two racks on this list that accommodates wheels as small as 16 inches.

The StageTwo’s trays are offset, which means less chance of contact when carrying two similarly sized bikes (however, bikes sit more widely apart, so watch those tight parking spaces). The rack includes two SKS locking cables (they don’t auto-retract, so tuck them back in when not in use). The StageTwo also includes an integrated lock loop for extra security when parked or locking your rack off the vehicle.

The rack is offered in 1.25- and 2-inch sizes. The 2-inch variant can accommodate four bikes with an add-on kit. Also, check Yakima’s fit guide before buying—One of our testers experienced a hardware fitment issue.

If you travel to mountain resort towns (or have been around trailheads or bike parks lately), you’ve probably seen behemoth racks like these on the back of vans and trucks. Since modern mountain bikes are bulky, racks like Thule’s ReVert make sense if you’re hauling a full load with a single vehicle.

The ReVert holds six bikes, loads quickly, and sticks out no farther than a standard 2-bike horizontal rack. Its carrying capacity makes it ideal for large families, race teams, or ride groups.

At over 87 pounds, the ReVert is undeniably heavy. However, a few smart features make the rack manageable. Dual hydraulic dampers assist with lowering the rack when it’s fully loaded, so you don’t have to wrestle with it. Once in the lowered position, even shorter riders and kids can lift their bikes high enough to slot them into the baskets. Individual bikes are spaced 11 inches apart, giving you plenty of room to carry any combination—flat bar, drop bar, even cruisers.

1UP USA has built a cult-like following with its industrial-looking racks that take a simplistic approach to securing your bike. This model features two ratcheting arms that clamp down on your wheels—no hooks or straps necessary.

The Equip-D’s pivot mechanism is smooth and reliable even after years of abuse (although an occasional shot of WD-40 White Lithium Grease Spray goes a long way in keeping the release mechanism running smoothly). A T-handle release positioned at the end of the hitch bar means you don’t need to reach through the rack to fold it up. Tiered trays position bikes closer together, and the rack rides out of the way of most exhaust pipes. 1Up also offers the Equip in a single-bike version for a sleeker look.

Hitch racks are bicycle carriers that attach to your vehicle’s hitch receiver. Popular models carry one to four bikes, but some hanging-style hitch racks can haul up to six bikes.

A hitch is a standard feature on most trucks and many SUVs. However, if you have a car or wagon, a hitch can often be added. If your vehicle doesn’t already have a receiver, it’s easy to have one installed. (U-Haul is a reliable and affordable option for installation.)Receivers come in two sizes: 1¼-inch and 2-inch (measured across the inside of the square opening). Most trucks and SUVs use a 2-inch receiver. Many racks are available in both sizes, but heavier-duty racks—and racks that carry three or more bikes—often require the larger 2-inch receiver for added strength and stability. Racks rated to carry heavyweight e-bikes also typically require a 2-inch receiver.

If the rack will live on your vehicle year-round or see frequent use, invest in the most durable model your budget allows. While all racks listed here secure bikes effectively, higher-priced options tend to have sturdier moving parts—ratchets, straps, buckles, and locks—that stand up better to long-term use.

Not all hitch racks are rated for the extra weight of e-bikes. Those that aren’t suited for heavier bikes are clearly noted in our reviews.

Some racks are quite heavy, which contributes to their strength but can be inconvenient if you plan to remove and reinstall the rack frequently.

For most vehicles—aside from sedans—accessing the trunk or tailgate is restricted when the rack is in use or folded up. Many of our top picks offer tilt-down designs that allow you to open the back of your vehicle even with bikes loaded. For full access, swing-away adapters like the Küat Pivot v2 Swing-Away allow the entire rack to pivot 90 degrees, completely clearing the rear of your car or truck.

Need more clearance? Sometimes a simple hitch extender can do the trick. For added stability and peace of mind, we also recommend using an anti-rattle clamp with any rack you choose.

Pros: Hitch racks strike the perfect balance between the ease of access of a trunk rack and the security of a quality roof rack. They slot into your car’s hitch receiver, relying on no flimsy straps or sketchy hooks. They’re also positioned behind your car, which is great for gas mileage and roof-collision prevention (low standing height). Better yet, many are modular, allowing you to add extra trays, locks, and even bottle openers for more personalized functionality.

Cons: These racks are the most consistently expensive out there—quality materials and a confidence-inspiring construction unquestionably affect their price. Furthermore, they can be a pain to remove, as most options weigh well over 40 pounds and need tools to detach. Furthermore, with bikes on the rack, they add significant length to your vehicle, which could prove tricky if you need to parallel park. And most critically, not every car has a hitch, which means you’ll either need to install one yourself or forego this style entirely.

Our editors drove hundreds (and in some cases, thousands) of miles with their bikes on these racks. We hauled road bikes, mountain bikes, e-bikes, and city bikes. We carried bikes with disc brakes, big wheels, and fat tires. Our test team used these racks for months, in various environments and conditions. We tested them in the salty winters of Pennsylvania, the high mountains of Colorado, and the gritty Arizona desert.

These racks in this story stand out for their ease of installation and use, lack of play in key areas, manageable weight, and bike capacity. We also looked for sharp prices and deals.

Whether you’re a roadie on the way to your next fondo, a mountain biker heading to the trailhead, or loading up the family for a weekend adventure, our rack picks will cover whatever needs you and your riding crew may have.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

Picture this: you're settled into your seat on a United flight out of LAX, the Pacific stretching endlessly outside your window, and you know — you genuinely know — that the person next to you paid $400 for this exact seat while you paid **7,500 miles**. That's the Hawaiian sweet spot, and it's one of the most quietly powerful redemptions available to anyone building a travel rewards strategy. Hawaii has always been the aspirational American vacation. It's the honeymoon destination, the bucket-list family trip, the anniversary getaway. And because of that demand, flights from the mainland — especially during spring break, summer, and the holidays — rarely go on sale. A round-trip economy ticket from Los Angeles to Honolulu will routinely run **$400–$700**, and during peak travel windows, prices can push past $1,000 for a family of four. That's real money. FI-community money. Now consider what Turkish Airlines Miles & Smiles charges for that same seat: **7,500 miles one-way**. At the low end of cash pricing ($200 for a one-way), you're extracting **2.7 cents per point**. At the high end ($500 during peak season), that same 7,500 miles is worth **6.7 cents per point** — a figure that makes even seasoned travel rewards enthusiasts do a double-take. For context, most people in the points world consider 1.5–2 cents per point a solid redemption. **Getting 6.7 cents per point is extraordinary.** It's not a fluke or a loophole — it's a structural pricing inefficiency baked into the Turkish award chart, which treats all short-haul domestic U.S. flights (including Hawaii, which is technically a domestic route) at the same rock-bottom rate. This is the fundamental insight behind every great travel rewards redemption: **loyalty programs price awards based on their own logic, not cash fares.** Turkish Miles & Smiles sees LAX→HNL as a short Star Alliance partner flight. The fact that cash fares on that route are elevated because of destination demand is irrelevant to their award chart. That gap — between what Turkish charges in miles and what the market charges in dollars — is exactly where you save. For a ChooseFI community member who already holds Citi ThankYou Points, this redemption is within reach right now. You don't need to fly Turkish. You don't need to connect through Istanbul. You just need availability on United, 7,500 miles, and about 20 minutes.

The magic here comes down to one core concept: Star Alliance partner pricing on a domestic U.S. route.

Turkish Airlines is a Star Alliance member, and like most alliance programs, they allow their members to book award flights on partner airlines — including United. Where Turkish gets interesting (and generous) is in how they price those partner awards. Their award chart uses a fixed, distance-based or zone-based structure, and for short-haul U.S. domestic flights, the price bottoms out at 7,500 miles one-way in economy.

Here's the pricing inefficiency in plain language: Turkish Miles & Smiles doesn't care that Hawaii is an aspirational, high-demand destination. To their award chart, LAX→HNL is just another short domestic United flight. Meanwhile, United's own MileagePlus program charges significantly more for the same route — often 13,000–22,500 miles one-way depending on the fare bucket. Turkish is pricing the same seat at less than half what United charges its own members. That's the gap you're exploiting.

No fuel surcharges — ever. This is a critical detail that makes Turkish a standout program. Many European programs (we're looking at you, Lufthansa Miles & More) pile on hundreds of dollars in fuel surcharges that nearly erase the value of the award. Turkish charges zero fuel surcharges on any award flight, including partner redemptions. Your out-of-pocket cost when booking this redemption is taxes and fees only — typically $5–$15 for a domestic U.S. itinerary.

The most accessible path to 7,500 Turkish miles runs through Citi ThankYou Points, which transfer to Turkish at a 1:1 ratio. The transfer is instant — meaning you can see award availability, confirm your plan, and have the miles in your Turkish account within minutes, not days. That speed matters because Hawaii saver availability can disappear quickly.

You can also transfer from Bilt Rewards at 1:1 (also instant), or Marriott Bonvoy at a 3:1 ratio (takes 1–5 days and is far less efficient — avoid Marriott for this transfer unless you have no other option).

The best Citi cards for earning ThankYou Points include the Citi Strata Premier, which earns 3x on dining, groceries, hotels, and airfare — categories that make accumulating 7,500 points genuinely fast for most households.

Turkish's award chart is fixed, meaning the price doesn't fluctuate with demand, time of year, or how close you are to departure (beyond the booking window). A saver economy award on a short domestic U.S. United flight is always 7,500 miles. No dynamic pricing surprises. No "off-peak vs. peak" tiers to navigate. This predictability is itself a feature — you can plan around it.

The booking window opens 355 days in advance, giving you nearly a full year of search runway to find the availability you need.

Here's exactly how to execute this redemption from zero to booked.

Before you transfer a single point, confirm that saver economy availability exists on your target route and dates. Go to united.com, enter your origin and destination (for example, LAX to HNL), and select your travel dates. When the results appear, look specifically for fares labeled "Saver" — these are the award inventory buckets that partner programs like Turkish can access. Standard or Everyday awards will NOT be bookable through Turkish.

Search for "Saver" fares in economy and note the exact flight numbers, dates, and times. Take a screenshot — you'll need these details when you move to the Turkish website.

Tip: United's calendar view lets you scan a full month for saver availability. Use it. Flexibility of even 1–2 days can be the difference between finding a seat and hitting a wall.

Go to turkishairlines.com and navigate to the Miles & Smiles award booking tool. Search the same route and dates you identified on United. Turkish's search engine pulls real-time Star Alliance availability, so what you see here is what you can book. If the saver seats from Step 1 appear, you're ready to move.

Important: If you don't yet have a Turkish Miles & Smiles account, create one now — it's free and takes just a few minutes.

Once you've confirmed award availability, transfer your points. Log into your Citi ThankYou account (or Bilt Rewards account), navigate to the transfer partner section, and select Turkish Airlines Miles & Smiles. Enter the amount — 7,500 points per one-way flight — and confirm.

Citi and Bilt transfers to Turkish are instant. Your miles will appear in your Turkish account within minutes. Do not transfer until you've confirmed availability in Step 2 — points transfers are one-way and non-refundable.

Return to the Turkish award booking tool with your miles now loaded. Complete the booking for your confirmed flight. You'll pay only taxes and fees at checkout — typically $5–$15 for a domestic U.S. itinerary. Enter your payment details for that small amount and complete the reservation.

You'll receive a booking confirmation from Turkish. The actual ticket is on United metal, so you'll also see the reservation appear in United's system using your confirmation code.

You pull up United.com and search LAX→HNL for mid-April — not peak spring break week, but the week after, when families have gone home and the island is quieter. The points price: 7,500 Turkish Miles & Smiles miles per person, plus roughly $11 in taxes and fees. For two people, you're spending 15,000 miles and about $22.

You already have 20,000 Citi ThankYou Points sitting in your account from everyday spending on your Citi Strata Premier — groceries, dining, a couple of utility bills. You transfer 15,000 points to Turkish Miles & Smiles (instant transfer), log into the Turkish booking portal, and complete both seats in a single transaction.

Your CPP on this redemption: $389 ÷ 7,500 = 5.2 cents per point. That's more than three times what most people consider a strong redemption.

Now for the experience itself: you're flying United Economy on a widebody aircraft — typically a Boeing 767 or 777 on the Honolulu route from LAX. The flight is approximately 5.5 hours. Economy isn't business class, but United's Pacific routes are comfortable — you'll find decent legroom in Economy Plus if you want to upgrade your seat selection for a modest fee, complimentary entertainment, and meal service on this longer domestic segment. The flight across the Pacific, even in economy, has a different feel than a 2-hour domestic hop. The water below you turns that impossible shade of blue. You land in Honolulu at mid-morning, cleared customs quickly (domestic flight — no customs required), and you're at your hotel before lunch.

Total cost for two one-way tickets: 15,000 miles + $22. Cash equivalent: $778. Money saved: $756. That's a car payment, a month of groceries, or a head start on your next investment contribution — redirected from airline revenue to your FI journey.

The 7,500-mile rate is available year-round — Turkish doesn't have a separate peak pricing tier for this redemption. But United's saver inventory dries up fast during summer, spring break, and the December holidays. Target September through November and January through mid-February for the best combination of availability and lower cash prices (which tells you demand is lower). Mid-week departures (Tuesday, Wednesday) consistently show better saver seat availability than weekend flights.

Turkish's booking window opens 355 days in advance. United releases the bulk of its saver award inventory when the schedule first opens — roughly 11 months before departure. If you have a specific date in mind (say, a milestone anniversary trip), start checking 355 days out and move fast when you see availability.

Book the outbound through Turkish (LAX→HNL, 7,500 miles) and then search for a separate return award. Turkish allows open-jaw itineraries, so you could theoretically fly into Honolulu and return from Maui if routing works. Piece together two one-way awards for maximum flexibility.

This is the single most common mistake. Points transfers to Turkish are irreversible. If you transfer 7,500 points and then discover saver availability has disappeared, those points are in Turkish's system with no easy path back. Always confirm availability on the Turkish booking portal before initiating any transfer.

Marriott Bonvoy transfers to Turkish at a 3:1 ratio and takes 1–5 days. You'd need 22,500 Marriott points to get 7,500 Turkish miles — a terrible rate. Stick with Citi ThankYou or Bilt at 1:1, both instant.

If you're combining this Hawaii redemption with an international Turkish itinerary, Turkish allows free stopovers in Istanbul on connecting itineraries. That's a separate strategy, but worth knowing as your travel portfolio grows.

Turkish miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. Even one small miles transaction — earning or redeeming — resets the clock. Transfer a small batch of points or book a cheap award every few years to keep your account alive.

Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles uses a distance-based award chart that treats Hawaii as a domestic U.S. destination. Since flights from the West Coast to Hawaii are under 3,000 miles, they fall into the lowest pricing tier at just 7,500 miles each way. Compare this to United MileagePlus, which charges 22,500 miles each way for the same route through its own program. The Turkish chart effectively gives you a 67% discount for the identical seat on the identical United flight. This pricing anomaly is one of the most valuable in travel rewards and has persisted for years.

Register for a free Miles&Smiles account on the Turkish Airlines website. You will need this account to receive transferred miles and book award flights.

Before transferring miles, verify award space exists. Search on United.com for saver-level award space to Hawaii on your preferred dates. If United shows availability at the saver level, it should be bookable through Turkish.

Transfer Citi ThankYou Points or Capital One Miles to your Turkish Miles&Smiles account at a 1:1 ratio. Allow 24-48 hours for transfers to process. Only transfer once you have confirmed availability.

After booking, you will receive a Turkish Airlines confirmation. Add your United MileagePlus number to the reservation for elite benefits. You can manage the booking through either Turkish or United once ticketed.

Yes. Turkish Miles&Smiles prices United-operated flights to Hawaii at 7,500 miles each way in economy because its award chart treats Hawaii as a domestic U.S. route. The same seat through United's own program costs 22,500 miles — three times more.

The most practical path is through Citi ThankYou Points, which transfer 1:1 to Turkish Miles&Smiles. The Citi Premier card earns 3x on travel and gas, making it a strong earning tool. Capital One Miles also transfer to Turkish at a 1:1 ratio.

Availability depends on United releasing Star Alliance partner award space (sometimes called "saver" availability). Searching 2-4 months in advance, on weekdays, or during shoulder season (April-May, September-October) significantly improves your chances.

Yes, but the miles cost increases with distance. From the East Coast, flights to Hawaii price at 10,000-12,500 miles each way depending on routing distance. Still an excellent deal compared to United's own pricing, though the West Coast offers the absolute lowest redemption.

This redemption was built for the ChooseFI member who's just starting to take travel rewards seriously — someone who has a Citi credit card, has been accumulating ThankYou Points on everyday spending, and wants their first "I can't believe this worked" moment.

Families planning a Hawaii vacation. At 7,500 miles per person, a family of four needs just 30,000 miles one-way — an achievable balance for anyone who's been strategic with a single Citi card for 6–12 months. The savings versus paying cash for four tickets can easily hit $1,500–$2,000, which is serious FI-community money.

Couples looking for a meaningful but accessible trip. Hawaii is aspirational without requiring long-haul international travel. This is the redemption that converts skeptical partners into believers.

West Coast residents (California, Washington, Oregon, Nevada) who have direct United service to Hawaii from nearby airports. The further you are from direct Hawaii service, the more complex positioning becomes.

Minimum points balance needed: Just 7,500 Citi ThankYou or Bilt points per one-way flight. That's genuinely achievable — even a single welcome bonus on an entry-level Citi card exceeds this threshold.

This redemption is less ideal for travelers on the East Coast (positioning flights eat into the simplicity), anyone without access to Citi or Bilt points (other transfer paths are inefficient), and travelers who need guaranteed availability on specific peak dates — the saver inventory just isn't reliable enough for inflexible itineraries.

This redemption is rated **Easy** in category but carries a few specific friction points worth understanding before you start. The **earning side is straightforward** — 7,500 Citi ThankYou Points is a modest target that most people hit within a few months of regular spending on a Citi Strata Premier. The transfer to Turkish is instant and simple. The **main challenge is availability**. United's saver economy inventory to Hawaii is genuinely limited, especially during popular travel windows. You may search your ideal dates and find nothing. This isn't a bug — it's just the nature of partner award bookings. The program prices this incredibly cheaply *because* the airlines release limited seats at this level. The **booking interface** adds minor friction. The Turkish Miles & Smiles website works, but it's not as polished as booking directly on United.com. Expect a slightly clunky experience — search patiently, and don't be surprised if you need to refresh or try slightly different date combinations. **Three tips to overcome the main challenges:** 1. **Be flexible with dates.** Saver availability is the limiting factor. If you can move your trip by 2–3 days, your chances of finding a seat increase dramatically. 2. **Search early.** Start 10–11 months out. The availability you can't find at 3 months may have been wide open at 11 months. 3. **Confirm before you transfer.** Check the Turkish booking tool *first*, then move your points. This keeps the process clean and stress-free. If you're willing to be slightly flexible on dates, this redemption is genuinely beginner-accessible — and the payoff, especially for a family, makes the modest extra effort completely worthwhile.

The Turkish Miles&Smiles sweet spot for Hawaii flights is one of the most dramatic value plays in travel rewards. Booking the exact same United flight for 7,500 miles instead of 22,500 United miles is a 67% savings, and at cash values of $400-$800+, you are getting 3-5 cents per mile in value. While the booking process can require a phone call and some patience, the savings are substantial enough to make this one of the first sweet spots every travel rewards enthusiast should learn. If you hold Citi ThankYou or Capital One points and want to visit Hawaii, this is your move.

#8894. The Science of “Extreme” Exercise During Pregnancy

The author attended the Tanenbaum Institute for Science in Sport Conference in Toronto to hear directly from Margie Davenport and Michelle Mottola, key researchers shaping the upcoming 2027 International Olympic Committee guidelines. The resulting piece analyzes their latest clinical and survey data on pregnant athletes engaging in heavy weightlifting, high-intensity intervals, endurance sports, and rock climbing.

Back in 2019, I wrote about a new set of guidelines for exercise during pregnancy. These guidelines were revolutionary—up to a point. Advice from doctors at the time was often extremely conservative, like never letting your heart rate exceed 140 beats per minute. But solid evidence now suggested that consistent moderate exercise—at least 150 minutes spread over at least three days per week—was not just safe for most pregnant women but was actually beneficial for both mother and fetus, dramatically lowering the risk of conditions such as gestational diabetes, pre-eclampsia, and depression.

Sign up for a ten-part email series from Alex Hutchinson on how to train, fuel, and recover. Each week, Alex covers a new topic, including strength training, supplements, and more!

Beyond that threshold, though, the deadlines dared not tread. Moderate exercise? Sure. Lifting heavy weights, or running marathons, or going rock climbing? That’s a trickier question, because no scientist wants to send a pregnant person out to do something that could potentially harm her or her baby. But ignoring it doesn’t make sense, because many female athletes do continue participating in their sports while pregnant, regardless of what the guidelines say. And those who stop or dramatically reduce their activity may suffer declines in both physical and mental health.

It’s important, then, to understand what the evidence says about the risks and benefits of more extreme forms of exercise. In 2018, the answer was “not much.” But in the years since then, there has been a steady flow of research on pregnant athletes doing hard things. In fact, the International Olympic Committee is planning to release a new and dramatically revised set of guidelines for pregnant athletes in 2027.

At the Tanenbaum Institute for Science in Sport Conference in Toronto last week, I had a chance to hear two key authors of both the old and new guidelines—Margie Davenport of the University of Alberta and Michelle Mottola of Western University—speak about their research. They couldn’t yet reveal what’s in the new guidelines, but they did share some of the key research that informs them. Here are some highlights from the extreme frontiers of exercise and pregnancy.

Any sort of heavy lifting is frowned upon during pregnancy, and particularly lifting while lying on your back, which could compress key blood vessels. But this advice, Davenport points out, is based on expert opinion and workplace studies, where heavy lifting is different from lifting in the gym where you control load and recovery.

To start, she and her colleagues surveyed 679 recreational weightlifters and CrossFit athletes who were pregnant and habitually lifted at least 80 percent of their one-rep max. Those who continued heavy lifting had a 51 percent reduction in complications compared to those who obeyed the guidelines and dialed back their training. They were also roughly half as likely as normal to report postpartum depression after delivery.

Of course, survey studies have limitations: maybe complications caused people to stop lifting rather than the other way around, for example. But those initial positive results paved the way for bringing 10 pregnant women into the lab and having them do squats, bench press, and deadlift for 10 reps at up to 90 percent of 10-rep max. They monitored maternal and fetal heart rate, umbilical blood pressure, glucose and lactate levels, and various other health markers, and compared the results to those of ten non-pregnant controls; there were no causes for concern.

A heart-rate limit of 140 is outdated. Still, the 2019 guidelines remain cautious. “Vigorous” exercise, they suggest, should top out at around 169 beats per minute for women 29 and younger, and 162 beats per minute for those 30 and older.

In a 2023 study, Davenport and her colleagues put that ceiling to the test. They had 15 volunteers, at an average of 27 weeks pregnant, do either a 30-minute moderate bike ride or 10 x 1:00 intervals at above 90 percent of their predicted maximum heart rate. The women ended up reaching a peak of 96 percent on average during the intervals, with some getting as high as 105 percent of max. (This isn’t Spinal Tap: the standard estimate of max heart rate, 220 minus age, was clearly off for these women.)

Once again, the researchers took a bunch of measures of fetal and maternal physiological responses. There were no relevant differences between the moderate and intense exercise sessions.

This was another survey study: 331 women who, on average, were 33.2 years old and had completed 2.1 pregnancies. All had engaged in exercise bouts lasting at least an hour during their pregnancies; 80 percent had continued long-duration exercise throughout their pregnancies, but in most cases had gradually decreased overall training as the pregnancy progressed.

Davenport and her colleagues divided the respondents into two subgroups: those who continued to do at least 300 minutes of exercise per week during their third trimester, and those who were below that threshold. Those in the high exercise group had a lower risk of complications during delivery, but a higher risk of diastasis recti—a separation of the stomach muscles—after delivery.

The overall conclusion was that long-duration exercise well above guideline recommendations “appears to be well tolerated” by people who are already used to that level of training.

Here’s where things get interesting, because it’s hard to wave away the hypothetical dangers of a hard fall. But do these risks justify telling people not to climb?

Davenport has led a couple of studies exploring this issue. One involved interviewing 11 elite climbers who continued to train or compete during pregnancy about their perspectives on risk. Climbing, one of the climbers said, was actually safer than walking down the street: “I’m less likely to fall because I’ve got three points of contact on, compared to one when I’m walking… So I feel like I’m more likely to trip over something in the dark on the street than falling while climbing up a climbing wall.”

The second study surveyed nearly 700 climbers who had climbed through pregnancy, logging a cumulative total of 64,000 hours of climbing and suffering 155 self-diagnosed “hard falls.” Here there were two adverse events (one vaginal bleeding, the other undeclared), but both births were healthy. Climbing isn’t without risks, Davenport says, but the findings suggest the risks are lower than previously thought. Of note, 96 percent of respondents were “happy” or “very happy” they had continued to climb.

There’s more—Davenport has also studied contact sports like soccer, for example—but you get the picture. Some of these activities clearly involve theoretical risks, but those theoretical risks need to be balanced against the measurable mental and physical benefits of continuing to train and the risks of stopping. One of the best predictors of post-pregnancy injury, for example, is having reduced your training by more than 50 percent during pregnancy.

The focus of the upcoming IOC guidelines will be “athlete-centered decision-making”—not an ironclad set of rules about who can do which types of exercise when, but a framework about how to weigh the pros and cons in different contexts. It’s an important update, because it recognizes what’s already happening in the real world. “Our current public health guidance is fantastic and sets our baseline,” Davenport says. “But most athletes—well, all athletes—are going to vastly exceed current recommendations.”

#8893. Can’t get back into working out? It’s not a motivation problem.

Recently, I asked you: where are you feeling most stuck with your fitness right now?

Hundreds of you wrote back. Thoughtful, honest answers. Thank you.

And one theme jumped out at me IMMEDIATELY.

One reader, let’s call her Supergirl, said it this way:

If you’ve ever had a great run (for a few days or a few years) and then couldn’t find your way back, this one’s for you, too.

I’ve heard this so many times in my coaching career. You were in a really good groove. Something knocked you off. And getting back on track feels incredibly difficult, and you don’t know why.

I’ve experienced this myself! I was in a groove with food logging. It felt easy. Then I took a break, and when I tried to start up again, I couldn’t get it going with any consistency for the life of me.

Here’s my take after nearly two decades of coaching: I doubt this is a motivation thing.

You were cruising at 70 miles an hour. You made a pit stop, and now you’re trying to jump the car straight back to 70. Instantly.

Another reader put it really well in their message to me:

That’s driving with your eyes on the rearview mirror. And it makes anything smaller feel like it doesn’t count.

But smaller is how you get back up to speed.

After multiple false starts with food logging, I realized I was falling into the same trap. And instead of forcing myself to weigh and measure anything, I gave myself a different on-ramp. Protein and veggies at each meal? Check. That allowed me to build back up again and find the groove that worked for me in this current phase of life.

Previous success can feel like a scorecard that you have to grade yourself against.

But what worked before might not work for you right now.

And it’s important to remember that most of us needed an on-ramp the first time, too. That part didn’t change after some time off.

You know what you “should” be doing. Let’s put that aside for now.

Instead, let’s shrink down what our focus is. We don’t have to figure out the whole routine. Not the whole week. Let’s work on today.

Try this thought experiment with me: if you didn’t have any expectations of what this “should” look like, what is one thing that feels doable today?

Maybe it’s performing your warm-up routine. Or doing the first round of exercises in your workout.

Maybe it’s batch cooking some protein tonight, or running to the grocery store to stock up on some easy fruit and veggie options.

Try it out, and see how that feels. Is the resistance still there? If it isn’t, you’ve found the start of your on-ramp. 🙌

And if it still feels hard to start? That’s OK, too. We can choose a different entry point and try again.

If you’re in that camp of “I know what to do. I can’t get myself to start,” give yourself a different, smaller on-ramp.

But it may be exactly what you need right now.

Hit reply and let me know what yours looks like.

#8891. That Mysterious Bike Creak Is Driving You Crazy—Here’s How to Check Your Bottom Bracket

Simple checks to pinpoint bottom bracket creaks before they become bigger repairs.

As cyclists, we hear a lot of sounds when riding. Usually, the noises come from chirping birds, the wind rustling leaves, or your bike’s tires rolling over your favorite trail. But sometimes the noises sound bad and come from your bike, and those noises can range from annoying to anxiety-inducing as you ponder the cause.

Bicycle components are moving parts that wear out and sometimes need adjustment. These squeaks, creaks, clicks, and other strange sounds are often a sign that something on your bike needs repair or replacement. And if your bike seems extra noisy, it might be time for some routine maintenance.

Noises on bikes are sometimes frustrating and mysterious. It’s often a challenge to figure out exactly where the sound originates—especially if it’s hard to reproduce when not riding. When I ran a shop, we would have customers come in and they would be certain that a noise was coming from one spot—only to find the culprit be somewhere else. Many times a noise would originate at the cranks or bottom bracket, so that’s what we’ll focus on here.

It’s worth checking on the lowest hanging fruit before we dig into the bottom bracket. The most common noisemakers are loose parts or bearings requiring adjustment, cleaning, or replacement. Performing regular preride bolt checks helps keep components tight and noises at bay. Several spots on your bike use bearings to rotate smoothly, including your headset, bottom bracket, hubs, and suspension linkages on mountain bikes. Keep these bearings properly adjusted to cut down on squeaks and knocking sounds.

Before checking if the noise originates from your bottom bracket, check that the crank bolts (which affix the crank arms to the BB on many bikes) are sufficiently tight. You might hear a clicking when these bolts loosen. And if a crank bolt entirely backs out, it can cause a crankarm to fall off while riding or damage your crank or frame. Grab a torque wrench and tighten the bolts to the manufacturer’s recommended specification.

After you are sure the noise is not from a loose crankarm, stand next to your bike and grab both brakes. Then, put your foot on the pedal closest to you and press inward. If the bike still creaks or ticks when you put weight on the pedal, the problem likely comes from your bottom bracket.

If the clicking sound isn’t from your drivetrain or pedals (see below), your BB may be loose, or the bearings may be worn. Many bikes use a non-adjustable cartridge or press-fit BB that must be replaced when the bearings wear out. Some systems (such as SRAM DUB and Race Face Cinch) use a preload ring to add preload to the bottom bracket bearings. These rings can loosen and cause a click while pedaling. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions to tighten it back up.

If you don’t hear anything, the problem is likely the bearings in your headset, hubs, or suspension parts. Bearings can wear out after a season, especially if you live somewhere wet or sandy. Your local bike shop can help you order and install new ones.

It’s also possible you simply need a new bottom bracket in the bike. Bottom bracket standards are a deep rabbit hole and can feel overly complex if you aren’t familiar with the system. Different frames and different cranks require different bottom brackets. Before searching Amazon for the best deal on bottom brackets, consult the technical specifications for your specific bike and component group or visit your local shop for direction.

I have seen bottom bracket issues actually cause issues on carbon frames as well. I’ve seen this specifically on older carbon frames with press-fit bottom brackets that were not maintained over time. All the bikes that I saw frame issues from bottom brackets fell into the same category: older carbon road bikes with press-fit bottom brackets that were not maintained for years. Eventually the customer would hear a noise, but keep riding. Then that noise would turn into knocking in the crank. By the time they got to our shop, the space in the frame for the bottom bracket was no longer a perfect circle. That circle shifted into an oval over time—which more times than not resulted in a new frame being needed. If you have a creak in your bottom bracket, get it checked out (or inspect it yourself) before it becomes something bigger.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. #8890. Triathlon News, October 2026: Ironman Crashes, NYC Tri Returns, Middle East Racing

Tim Heming highlights the biggest news in triathlon in October 2026. (Photo: Triathlete)

In October, the triathlon world turned its eyes to the Big Island for another epic edition of the Ironman World Championship, but that didn’t stop the rest of the multisport world from serving up its usual mix of drama, debate, and headline-grabbing news.

From analyzing the sparse participation numbers at New York’s long-awaited race return to tackling safety, transparency, and course caps following a scary collision on the Queen K, October delivered plenty of food for thought. And, as always, contributor Tim Heming is here to digest it with you.

The first line of Sarah Wassner Flynn’s article about the return of the iconic New York City Triathlon, published earlier this year, reads: “For more than two decades, the New York City Triathlon was one of the sport’s most iconic races. Debuting in 2001, it quickly became a bucket-list event for age-groupers and pros alike.”

The piece previewed this year’s race return, renamed the Big Apple Triathlon, under new ownership of Alpha Win, formerly known as HITS Endurance, with Tommy Struzzieri taking over the company from his father, Tom.

Alpha Win, based in Saugerties, New York, is no novice when it comes to race hosting. They have put on over 200 races, but making a success of this one offered the sternest test of their credentials to date.

Held on October 10, the day when most eyes in the triathlon world were focused almost 5,000 miles west on the Big Island of Hawaii, would it prove enough of a draw to justify the set-up costs of a swim in the Hudson River, a bike up the closed West Side Highway, and a run through Central Park?

Since its halcyon days, the event has been beset by problems, with participation tumbling from a peak of almost 4,000 during its time as part of the Life Time Fitness Series in 2010. In 2024, it was canceled by new owner Supertri before registration even opened, with organizers saying they couldn’t find a suitable date. It didn’t return in 2025 either, which, given Supertri’s focus on producing stylish, short-course events in major urban areas, had to be a worrying sign.

“We’re just trying to bring back something that athletes have been asking for,” Struzzieri said in March, noting that numbers would be capped at 2,500. If that felt optimistic, a New York Post piece on the eve of the event recounted its troubled history and asked: Is this time the charm? stating that around 1,300 athletes were expected to start, with prices ranging from $350–$650.

The results, however, show fewer than half that number: only around 600 finishers across all formats, the lowest the event has seen since it began in 2001. “Every year that there’s an issue with this event, it hurts the event the following year,” Scott Nilson, Supertri’s U.S. general manager of events, told us in 2024. Perhaps this year it will be the simple economics of numbers.

Registration for the 2027 event is now open with early-bird pricing (including processing fees) at $548.90 (Olympic distance) and $383.90 (sprint distance). Triathlete reached out to Alpha Win for comment.

For the majority, the Ironman World Championship is a day of celebration and achievement. It’s a once-in-a-lifetime experience, the ultimate triathlon dream. For Trish Byron, that dream turned into a nightmare.

Byron was struck by a male cyclist from behind almost 30 miles into the bike leg, leaving her with seven fractured ribs, a broken collarbone, a punctured and partially collapsed lung, a concussion, a laceration requiring stitches, and extensive road rash.

It’s understood the cyclist stopped and spoke with volunteers before continuing the race, but Byron’s daughter Cassie Anne put out a plea on Facebook for more information, saying: “We’re hoping to gather firsthand accounts, identify the cyclist involved, and better understand what happened.”

Accidents happen, but the incident raises questions about transparency when serious collisions occur during races. Should such incidents be publicly reported, both to demonstrate that appropriate safety protocols and follow-up procedures have been followed and to help triathletes better understand the risks involved in signing up?

Cassie Anne’s post received a response from Judy Daggett, who said: “This exact scenario happened to me on the bike about mile 85, causing me to crash also. The guy who hit me kept going. Another athlete helped me to my feet.

“I immediately had double vision and said, ‘Yes, I need help,’ but there was no one around. I managed to get back on the bike and ride to T2, praying my vision didn’t completely leave.

“When I got there, they took me by ambulance to the ER for a CT of my head, thinking I could possibly have a brain bleed. Thankfully, I did not, but I also have fractured ribs, a hip and shoulder injury, and a concussion.”

Daggett went on to say she’d reached out to Ironman but was yet to hear from them, stating it was her first DNF in 30 years and that the “men were so aggressive, they need to let them go first”.

Her final point relates to the questions raised about the scheduled swim start waves that interspersed the men’s and women’s age-group divisions in Hawaii, whereas previously, the men had been started earlier in one cohort, followed by the women.

It also brings into focus the broader question (that has continued to surface since the announcement of the return to one day of racing) of whether Ironman should cap numbers on the course for both fairness and safety reasons.

While it might seem that Trish Byron’s family shouldn’t have far to go to find answers, as Anna Grosz, who also responded to the post, explained, it might not be that simple: “I provided medical support for the race. We are bound by patient confidentiality laws. You should reach out to Ironman through official channels. The medical director may be able to communicate directly with the affected athlete, but course volunteers cannot do so.”

Triathlete has contacted Ironman for comment.

Championship season is not quite over in the world of triathlon. The T100 Tour still has three events on the calendar, with Dubai and Saudi Arabia in November ahead of the T100 World Championship Final in Qatar. The action in the Middle East will also continue with the 2026 World Triathlon Multisport Championship in Abu Dhabi.

The headlines will be the professional races over 100K where Hayden Wilde looks to be the odds-on favorite to retain his title, and it’s wide open on the women’s side. But there is also shorter-distance racing and representative age-group competition throughout.

Despite conflict in the region and the cancelation, postponement or relocation of other major sporting events, particularly in Saudi Arabia, both World Triathlon and the Professional Triathletes Organization are, for now, proceeding as planned. That’s perhaps to be expected, with contingency decisions often left until the last possible moment. But if the events do go ahead, it will be interesting to see how much appetite international athletes have for traveling to the region.

Conversations around weight can be a sensitive topic: triggering to some, frustrating to others, and almost irrelevant to others. And Susan Kitchen’s article on why we shouldn’t be concerning ourselves with post-race weight gain will no doubt grab the attention of athletes who might have concerns about how they can be heavier after doing all that exercise.

While Kitchen spells out the reasons here (which, spoiler alert, can be perfectly natural as your body recovers), it also made me think that perhaps the concern shouldn’t be how much you weigh, but why, in the days following an incredible endurance feat, you’re not off celebrating somewhere, rather than hopping on the scale.

You may not find an answer as to which is better, but there is plenty we can learn from Jordan Blanco’s roundtable discussion with triathlon legends Flora Duffy and Jan Frodeno when it comes to their appreciation for the pinnacle events in our sport – including that the 2008 win in Beijing was Frodeno’s first-ever elite victory!

But if there is one takeaway, then it’s probably that following your heart is the first step, and the financial rewards will follow. Doing it the other way around might just be a little tougher.

What do we learn from the Kona bike mechanics recounting tales from the Big Island?

Number one: That most of us should probably invest a bit more time in understanding how to fix our own bikes.

Number two: That whatever daft mistake you’ve made, it won’t be the dumbest thing they’ve seen (one athlete rolled up with two front wheels and no back, another with two back wheels and no front).

Number three: If you do have a problem, get to the mechanics early (the day before race day was the busiest).

And number four: Have a little patience. “That’s really the hardest part of Ironman week – managing athletes’ timeline expectations,” Taylor Bushong, a traveling race mechanic working out of Bike Works Kona, told Sara Stover. “Managing the unrealistic ‘can you just’ requests. The understanding of the level of the request seems to be outside the scope of recognition.”

But while being a bike mechanic sounds like a thankless task, it has some upsides. The real kicker, featuring five carbon wheels and the town’s dump, is cleverly left until the final line.

Some charitable sporting endeavors fall flat while others just fly, and often there seems to be no logic as to which cause will capture the public mood.

Thankfully, for Ethan Hunger, the idea to complete a world-record number of super sprint triathlons within 24 hours to raise money for his local food bank in Bellingham, Washington, really took off.

If ever there was a classic case of nominative determinism, then this is it. Hunger v. Hunger actually started following the COVID pandemic, but as Travis Mundell found out, this year’s challenge was the most ambitious yet, helping push the initiative’s total fundraising beyond $1.2 million.

It’s life-affirming to see such dedication in action, not just from Hunger, but from the community that rolled out to support him, where putting all the proper procedures in place so the record could be ratified by Guinness reads as more grueling than all that swimming, biking, and running.

There’s probably not much more that needs adding to one of the most dramatic Ironman World Championship races in living memory. Having written a reaction piece on how the house (in this case, the Big Island) always wins versus the gambler, I’ve reflected more on how it just seems such a difficult race to get right. My first thought: If the pros can’t do it (see the DNF files here), what chance do the mere mortals have? Follow-up thought: Nobody racing here could ever be described as a mere mortal anyway.
