What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds

What $10,000 grows to at different rates over 30 years — the rate difference matters more than you think.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Future value (FV) is the projected worth of an investment at a specific point in the future, based on an assumed rate of growth. It answers the most practical question in investing: "If I invest this money today, what will it be worth in 10, 20, or 30 years?"

Future value calculations rest on compound interest — the principle that your returns earn their own returns over time. Albert Einstein reportedly called compound interest "the eighth wonder of the world," and while the attribution is debatable, the math is not. The difference between simple interest (returns on your original investment only) and compound interest (returns on your investment plus accumulated returns) becomes enormous over long time horizons.

The basic future value formula for a lump sum investment is:

For example, $10,000 invested at 8% for 20 years:

FV = $10,000 x (1.08)^20 = $10,000 x 4.661 = $46,610

The table reveals two critical insights. First, small differences in return rates produce massive differences over long periods — $10,000 at 6% grows to $57,435 over 30 years, while the same amount at 10% grows to $174,494. That 4-percentage-point difference triples the outcome. Second, time is the dominant variable. At 8%, your money doubles roughly every 9 years — so 30 years gives you more than three doublings, turning $10,000 into over $100,000.

Most people do not invest a single lump sum and walk away. They invest regularly — monthly or per paycheck — over decades. The future value of a series of regular contributions uses a different formula called the future value of an annuity:

Where PMT is the periodic contribution, r is the periodic rate, and n is the total number of periods.

In practice, you do not need to calculate this by hand. The insight that matters is this: regular contributions are far more powerful than most people realize because each contribution starts its own compounding clock. Your first $500 contribution compounds for the full 30 years, while your 360th contribution (at month 360) compounds for just one month — but together they build wealth that dwarfs a single lump sum.

A person investing $500 per month at 8% for 30 years accumulates $745,180 — from total contributions of only $180,000. That means $565,180, or 76% of the final balance, came from compound returns rather than your own deposits. This is the engine of wealth building.

Every future value calculation should be done twice — once in nominal terms and once in real (inflation-adjusted) terms. The nominal return is the raw number your investments earn. The real return subtracts inflation, showing you what your money will actually buy.

Historically, the S&P 500 has returned roughly 10% nominally and 7% after inflation. The difference matters enormously over long periods:

That $1.13 million in nominal terms has the purchasing power of roughly $610,000 in today's dollars — still excellent, but nearly half less than the headline number suggests. When planning for FI, always use real returns (6-7%) rather than nominal returns (9-10%) to avoid overestimating what your portfolio will actually support in retirement spending.

The Rule of 72 is the simplest and most useful mental math tool in investing. Divide 72 by your annual rate of return to estimate how many years it takes for your investment to double:

This works in reverse too. If you want to know what rate of return you need to double your money in 15 years: 72 / 15 = 4.8%. The Rule of 72 is an approximation — it is most accurate for rates between 5% and 12% — but it is remarkably precise within that range and far faster than pulling out a calculator.

The FI community uses future value calculations as the backbone of retirement planning. The process works in three steps:

The table shows how starting balance and monthly contribution interact. Notice that increasing your monthly contribution from $1,500 to $2,500 (a $1,000 increase) with a $100,000 starting balance cuts 3.5 years off your time to $1 million. This is the savings rate lever in action — the amount you save each month matters more than any other variable you control.

A common question is whether it is better to invest a lump sum now or spread contributions over time (dollar-cost averaging). The math is clear: lump sum investing wins approximately two-thirds of the time because markets trend upward over the long term. However, dollar-cost averaging reduces the psychological risk of investing a large amount right before a downturn and provides a behavioral advantage that keeps many investors on track. For most FI-seekers, the question is academic — you invest each paycheck as it arrives because you do not have a large lump sum sitting on the sidelines.

When projecting your portfolio growth for retirement planning, use real (inflation-adjusted) returns of 6-7% rather than nominal returns of 9-10%. A $1 million nominal balance in 30 years has the purchasing power of roughly $550,000 in today's dollars at 2% average inflation. Planning with real returns ensures you are targeting a portfolio that can actually support your desired spending level.

Track your actual spending for 3 months and annualize it. Multiply by 25 to get your FI number using the 4% safe withdrawal rate. If you spend $60,000 per year, your FI number is $1,500,000.

Add up all retirement accounts (401k, IRA, Roth IRA, HSA), taxable brokerage accounts, and savings. Exclude home equity and non-liquid assets. This is your starting balance for the future value calculation.

Subtract your monthly spending from your monthly after-tax income. Include employer 401(k) match and any other automatic savings. This is your periodic contribution amount for the future value formula.

Use the future value of a lump sum plus annuity formula, or a simple online calculator, to project when your current balance plus monthly contributions will reach your FI number. Use 7% real return (after inflation) for conservative planning.

Test what happens if you increase contributions by $200/month, $500/month, or $1,000/month. Seeing the concrete impact of a savings rate increase — often shaving 2-5 years off your FI timeline — makes the trade-offs tangible and motivating.

For long-term stock market projections, use 7% for inflation-adjusted (real) returns or 10% for nominal returns based on the S&P 500 historical average. For a more conservative estimate, use 6% real. For bond-heavy portfolios, use 3-4% real. Always specify whether you are using nominal or real returns — mixing them up is one of the most common planning mistakes.

Future value calculations show what WOULD happen if returns were constant every year. In reality, markets fluctuate — you might earn 25% one year and lose 15% the next. Over 20-30 year periods, average returns tend to converge toward historical norms, making future value projections reasonably useful for planning. Treat them as directional estimates, not guarantees.

Future value asks: "What will $10,000 today be worth in 20 years?" Present value asks the reverse: "What is $50,000 in 20 years worth in today's dollars?" They use the same variables but in opposite directions. Present value is useful for evaluating whether a future payout (like a pension or annuity) is worth the cost today.

The Rule of 72 works for any compounding rate, including inflation. At 3% inflation, prices double every 24 years (72 / 3 = 24). This means $50,000 in annual spending today becomes $100,000 in 24 years in nominal terms — your purchasing power is halved if your income stays flat. This is why investing in assets that outpace inflation is essential.

For FI planning, future value is more intuitive — it tells you what your portfolio will grow to. However, the most practical approach is to calculate future value using real (after-inflation) returns. This effectively gives you a future value stated in today's purchasing power, which is what you actually need to know for spending planning.

In tax-advantaged accounts (401k, IRA, Roth IRA, HSA), your investments compound without tax drag, so the standard future value formula works directly. In taxable accounts, capital gains taxes, dividend taxes, and tax-loss harvesting all affect your real return. A rough adjustment is to reduce your assumed return by 0.5-1.0% for taxable accounts to account for ongoing tax drag.

Future value calculations are the most practical tool in the FI planner's toolkit. They turn abstract concepts like compound growth and savings rate into concrete dollar amounts and specific timelines. The key takeaways are straightforward: use 7% real returns for conservative planning, always account for inflation by using real rather than nominal returns, and remember that your monthly contribution rate has a far larger impact on the outcome than chasing an extra point or two of return. The Rule of 72 gives you instant mental math for any investment decision — how long to double, what rate you need, and how inflation erodes purchasing power. Combined with a clear FI number and a disciplined savings rate, future value projections show you exactly when financial independence becomes reality. Run the numbers, test different scenarios, and let the math motivate you to increase that monthly contribution whenever you can.

#8875. 4 Things You’re Doing in Yoga That Might Worsen Lower Back Discomfort

Monica Bright is a yoga teacher whose continuing education centered on injury mechanics and movement. She breaks down the common yoga mistakes that could be worsening lower back discomfort, and offers options for relief. You can also learn more about yoga poses for your lower back.

Lower back discomfort is one of the most common pain points among people worldwide. If you fall into that category and also do yoga, chances are you’ve expected the practice to bring you relief. But certain movements in yoga, and how you approach them, can sometimes have the opposite effect of the lower back release that you were hoping to achieve.

Learning to recognize what triggers tightness in your lower back can help you make more supportive choices on and off the mat. That way, you’re still working toward undoing your discomfort, but without accidentally worsening it.

Whether you’re in class or at home, or even moving throughout your everyday life, notice whether any of the following approaches to movement worsens your lower back sensitivity—and explore the following alternatives that might help relieve your discomfort.

Some people’s lower back strain is aggravated by moving too quickly. This is often the case with forward rounding. Think Seated Forward Bend or reaching down to pick something up off the floor. Moving slowly allows you to pay attention to the sensations in your body and ensures you’re not accidentally forcing yourself to move too far into a stretch and tweak your lower back.

What to try instead: Throughout your yoga practice, and even during your day, ask yourself, “How does it feel when I move more slowly?”

The “neutral” position of your spine that you commonly hear yoga teachers mention includes several curves, including one in the lumbar spine that is concave, meaning it curves inward. But many students have a tendency to round the lower back during certain poses, such as forward bends and Chair Pose, which can have the effect of flattening the lower spine and causing tension.

What to try instead: Maintaining that neutral spine can be more beneficial than “flattening” it for some students with a track record of stiffness and soreness in the lower back. That comes into play in several common yoga poses.

In Chair Pose, for instance, there is a tendency to draw the core toward the spine so much that it counteracts the natural curve in the lower back. Maintaining a neutral spine means keeping the length in your lower back rather than tucking the tailbone.

In Standing Forward Bend, keeping a neutral spine means being aware if you are rounding your lower back as you reach forward and, instead, hinging at your hips, perhaps bending your knees, and not being concerned with how far forward you fold.

However, some students find a greater sense of ease in the lower back by rounding forward. Ask yourself, “Does my lower back feel better, or worse, with rounded forward folds?”

If your lower back is sensitive, your yoga practice might look different from the person’s on the mat next to you—and that’s okay. The goal in yoga isn’t to push past discomfort, but to find the alignment in which your lower back feels good. And sometimes that means taking variations.

What to try instead: Explore variations of poses—some of which might include using props, such as blocks—to help support your movements. Take Happy Baby, for example. Drawing your knees toward your chest and holding the backs of your thighs might feel more supportive to some. When sitting in a forward bend, placing a blanket underneath the lowest part of your back to slightly elevate your hips and provide more room for your lower back might be your preferred version. Finding the movement options that feel tolerable for you can be enormously helpful while you’re learning to prioritize your lower back.

Stress, poor sleep, a sense of being overwhelmed, even anxiety surrounding practicing certain movements can put your body on high alert and cause your nervous system to brace for impact. This has the potential to turn up the volume on physical discomfort. Understanding how to downregulate your nervous system, on the other hand, can help your entire body relax.

What to try instead: You’re likely familiar with some of the practices that activate your parasympathetic nervous system, including resting in poses such as Child’s Pose, Legs Up the Wall, or Crocodile and practicing various pranayama (breathwork) techniques, including Box Breathing or simply lengthening your exhalations. Even slowing the pace of your practice and taking the variations that feel good to you are ways of signaling to your nervous system that you’re safe. Experiment with one or two calming exercises prior to your next yoga class or at-home practice.

Practicing with these ideas in mind will ultimately help you recognize how to support your body when practicing yoga. This doesn’t mean you need to have to have all of the answers. It simply, but it does means that you are present, aware, and listening to your own body’s signals.

#8874. Stop Chain Skipping: How to Adjust Your Rear Derailleur for Smoother, Cleaner Shifts

A step-by-step guide to cleaner shifts on mechanical and electronic rear derailleurs.

Many of us have been there—try to shift and the chain just does not want to get up into that next gear. That frustrating click click click as the chain can’t make the jump is like nails on a chalkboard.

The rear derailleur is a key piece of equipment on the bike—especially with the gaining popularity of single chainring setups. The good news is that adjusting a rear derailleur is a fairly straightforward process.

On bikes with cable-actuated derailleurs keep in mind that as you ride (especially after getting a new bike or a new rear derailleur cable installed) the rear derailleur cable will settle into the bike—you’ll hear shops call this cable stretch. Over time you’ll need to add a little cable tension to the system to make sure your shifting stays tight and crisp.

Below we’ll go through everything from how to do a quick cable tension adjustment to how to spot a bent derailleur hanger so you can keep your shifting smooth for your next ride.

Your rear derailleur moves your chain across cogs and maintains proper tension on the chain with every gear change. How? The chain runs around two jockey pulleys on the rear derailleur. When you shift to a larger chainring or cog, the shifter cable pulls the rear derailleur forward, causing the pulleys to push the chain onto the larger sprockets while keeping chain tension in check.

When you shift to a smaller cog, the shifter cable releases the rear derailleur, which swings outward, taking up chain slack and causing the pulleys to pull the chain onto a smaller sprocket. If everything is set up correctly, your rear derailleur should make one clean shift for every click of your shifter.

Before adjusting anything on the derailleur, first ensure that your rear derailleur hanger is straight. A bent hanger is often the cause of rear derailleur shifting woes.

The derailleur hanger is the part of the frame to which your rear derailleur mounts. Derailleur hangers are made to bend or break under impact and not destroy your expensive frame or drivetrain. On carbon and aluminum frames, this hanger is often replaceable. If bent inward, you can very gently align it. But your best remedy is to have your local shop use a special hanger alignment tool to fix it, or replace the hanger entirely. Universal derailleur hangers have gotten more popular, but different frames need different hangers. Pick up an extra hanger to keep at home, but make sure you have the right one for your bike. This small and relatively inexpensive part will come in handy when you need it in a pinch.

If your chain doesn’t move when you shift, or it skips cogs, your rear derailleur may be out of alignment. Hop off your bike and do this: Shift your chain into the biggest chainring and smallest cog, then loosen the cable clamp bolt (where the cable attaches to the derailleur).

Look for the high and low adjusters on the derailleur—often marked with an H and an L. Adjust the high-gear screw by turning it until the jockey pulleys line up with the smallest cog. Your chain should move smoothly around the cog and pulleys when you turn the pedals.

To check alignment with the largest cog, rotate the pedal forward and push the rear derailleur so that the chain shifts to the largest cog. If the pulleys take the chain beyond the largest cog, screw the low adjuster inward until this stops. Reattach the cable and tighten the clamp.

Fine-tune with the barrel adjuster, located where the cable housing enters the rear derailleur. For the best performance, position the guide pulley roughly 6 to 7 mm away from the cogs. If your chain skips when you shift to a lower gear, give the barrel adjuster a half-turn counterclockwise. (Tip: Think L for lower and for left turn.) A higher gear? Try a half-turn clockwise.

Sometimes the cause of a skipping-feeling of your shifting is a stiff chain link. This happens when one or more chain links doesn’t properly articulate, either from corrosion or damage to the chain. This can be mitigated by cleaning your chain and adding a few drops of lube to each of the rollers and pins. This creates a smooth and efficient chain and allows your rear derailleur to move through the cogs without hesitating. To check for a stiff link, gently backpedal the chain and pay attention to how the chain rolls off the derailleur pulleys. If any links skip, work some lube into the link and gently flex the link until the chain moves smoothly.

Also check your chain for excessive wear—an overly worn chain can also cause poor shifting. As a chain is ridden, the bushings and rollers in the chain wear out, causing slop to develop and the distance between the pin centers to increase. (This is commonly called “chain stretch,” though the metal in the chain hasn’t really stretched.) Generally, when a chain “stretches” by 0.5 percent, it is time to swap the chain.

The easiest way to test for wear is a chain checker tool. But you can also use a ruler. A fresh chain measures 12 inches from pin center to pin center. If it measures more than 12 ¹⁄₁₆ inches, change your chain.

After cleaning, add a few drops of lube to the pivot points. (there are eight) of the parallelogram linkage, cycle through a few shifts, then wipe off any excess lube. When you clean your chain, clear any muck from the inner and outer surfaces of both pulleys—it collects at the base of their teeth. Make sure to wipe away all the excess that may reside on your chain, pulleys, and pivot points.

First, remove the chain. Many chains use some sort of quick removal link to make this easy, so look for that first. If not, break your chain with a chain tool or, if your chain is joined by a connecting pin, by removing the pin (use a new pin to rejoin the chain). Loosen the cable-clamp bolt on the rear derailleur and pull the shifter cable out. Undo the hex bolt that attaches the derailleur hanger from the rear dropout.

Make sure your new derailleur is compatible with your bike’s shifters; eight- through 11-speed shifters must be matched with the same manufacturer’s equivalent derailleur. Attach the new derailleur to the hanger using its hex bolt. Reattach the cable and loop the chain through the jockey wheels before reconnecting the chain. Shift through all gear combinations to make sure everything is running smoothly. If it isn’t, turn the barrel adjuster on the derailleur in or out to fine-tune shifting.

While your electronic rear derailleur operates on the same principles as the mechanical version, the biggest difference is the electronic rear derailleur has a tiny motor doing the work of pushing and pulling rather than a cable. That motor is powered by a battery that sends and receives signals from either a wireless or wired connection to the rear derailleur.

With an electronic system, shifting is managed by firmware, so it shouldn’t go out of alignment once it’s set up—though it may be adjustable through an app or other software tool (and it may need firmware updates). If you’re having trouble with your electronic derailleur, first check to make sure the battery has enough charge. Make sure any cables are fully connected as well.

When electronic derailleurs are shifting poorly, one of the first things I check is the hardware. Bent derailleur cages, hangers, or damaged derailleurs can all cause poor shifting, so assess those parts while your firmware updates.

There are a few important steps to be aware of prior to adjusting or fixing your rear derailleur. Identify which brand of electronic drivetrain is on your bike. Each brand has a different procedure on how to troubleshoot or adjust your rear derailleur.

Once identified, confirm whether it is wired or wireless. Then, double-check that the battery or battery interface is connected or has power. The following steps are unique depending on which brand of drivetrain you have.

Step 1: Charge your battery and check the coin-cell batteries in the shift levers (as basic as this sounds, it’s often the issue when a SRAM AXS or Shimano Di2 drivetrain suddenly stops shifting).

Step 2: Download the manufacturer’s mobile app.

Step 3: Check for any derailleur or shifter firmware updates.

Step 4: Follow the manufacturer’s instructions for derailleur and shifting adjustment (often there are step-by-step instructions in the app or check the brand’s website for details).

#8872. Jess McClain Took a 2-Year Break From Running—and Came Back Faster Than Ever. Here’s What You Can Learn From Her Impressive Return.

The most important strategy for making a strong comeback.

About six years ago, Jess McClain went out for her scheduled workout—1,000-meter repeats—like any other day. She felt like she was going full send, but was frustrated to see that each rep actually clocked in about 45 seconds slower than her goal time.

The experience was the straw that broke the camel’s back, so to speak, after slowly losing motivation and excitement for competing professionally. “I ended up walking home and I texted my coach that day and said, ‘I think I need to shut this down,’” she recalls. He responded that a week off sounded like a good idea, to which she said: “No, I think I need to shut it down for good.”

Luckily, her professional running break only lasted about two years, during which she met her now-husband, reconnected with old friends, and got married.

In 2022, just after her honeymoon, McClain saw an ad for the Mesa Marathon in Arizona, happening a few days before her 30th birthday, and signed up on a whim. “I actually built a playlist that was two hours and 45 minutes long and I was like, ‘I’d be really stoked if I finished the race before this playlist ended,’” she says.

She finished in 2:32—and won. But the best part? “I was like, ‘damn, that was so fun,’” she says. “I probably still have Mai Tais in my system from my honeymoon and I’m running 2:32 and I ran 45 to 55 miles a week and I felt awesome and I just had so much fun. This is when I knew there’s that competitor still in me.”

That experience was the jump-start she needed to get back to the sport professionally—but with a promise to herself that she would always find joy in the process going forward.

“I think I had a lot of joy running in college, but then I think as a professional, I took it so, so seriously that it was almost like all I had and all I poured myself into,” McClain says. “Taking time away from the sport gave me a lot of perspective and reminded me why I love it.”

Clearly this mindset shift is working for her: Since the Mesa Marathon, McClain has run some of the best races of her life, including placing fourth at the Olympic Marathon Trials ahead of the Paris Games, setting the American course record at this year’s Boston Marathon with a time of 2:20:49, and placing second at this year’s New York City Marathon—the first American woman to podium at the race in eight years—with a time of 2:24:42.

McClain isn’t the only example of an athlete who took time off after feeling burned out, rediscovered the love of the sport, and made an insanely impressive comeback. And you don’t have to be a pro to gain the benefits of running for fun, including leading to your best race performances.

It may sound abstract—and not like your typical training tactic—but here’s why and how adding more joy to your running just might lead to the breakthrough you’re looking to achieve.

Sometimes taking a break is what athletes of all levels need in order to rediscover joy in their sport—and possibly come back stronger than ever. Figure skater Alysa Liu temporarily retired after the 2022 Olympics because of burnout, then came back to win two gold medals at the Milan Cortina Games in 2026 after restarting the sport initially for fun.

Part of the reason taking a break can ultimately have a positive effect on performance could be because the athlete is exercising their autonomy, says Erin Ayala, PhD, a sports psychologist, certified mental performance consultant, and founder of Skadi Sport Psychology.

“When an athlete is able to choose to step away, that helps with motivation because they feel like they’re in charge of their athletic identity,” she says. “And then they’re also usually able to reconnect with what they loved about running because when we take off that pressure, it lights that fire inside of them again where they’re like, ‘oh yeah, this is why I got into it.’”

A break also allows athletes to lean into other parts of their identity, whether that’s as a partner, sibling, parent, cook, or otherwise. “When we only see ourselves as an athlete or a runner, we’re more vulnerable to burnout, depression, anxiety, [and] spirals when running is not going well,” she says.

However, catching the early signs of athletic burnout could help you to prevent it from manifesting and necessitating a long break.

There’s a difference between true athletic burnout and normal training fatigue. Here are a few signs it’s the former, according to Ayala:

Whether you’re burned out or not, making running more joyful can benefit every runner. Looking forward to your runs not only keeps you consistent—a key factor for race-day performance—but can also improve your speed and your endurance.

When Ayala works with clients dealing with burnout, the first thing she does is help them rediscover their why—and it’s something you can do yourself, too, Ayala says. “Think about when you first started doing this, what was driving you, what was getting you excited to get out of bed in the morning or to go for the run?,” she asks.

Greg Laraia, a running coach at Motiv in New York City, says that most people will have five to 10 “whys” if you dig deep enough. A client might say the reason they’re running the marathon is to PR so he’ll ask why they want to PR. “They’re like, ‘Well, because [I want to be] faster than last time,’ and I’m like, ‘Well, why?’ If you can keep asking why and just pull them a little bit deeper than, ‘I want to run fast,’ a lot of times they’ll actually realize either they do really care about this or it’s so superficial that it doesn’t really matter,’” he says. “I think that’s a huge piece of what can help preserve enjoyment, too, and then being able to tap back into that.”

Ayala says that the ways to tap into and preserve fun are often tied to community, self-improvement, or time for yourself.

Again, autonomy is key to helping prevent burnout and there are small ways you can exercise it on the regular. For example, build in more of your favorite kinds of workouts, even if they’re not “ideal” or exactly what’s on your training plan, Ayala says. “If it’s bringing you more joy, it’s totally worth it. Having more agency over [your] training is really important and it is really effective.”

This might look like running your local free 5K in the park or joining your friends for their track workouts.

McClain says that prior to 2020, she was very focused on the outcome. “In practice, I’d get spun up if I was off a few seconds on a rep and then I think that just snowballs into overanalyzing and overthinking racing and worrying about the things I couldn’t control,” she says. “Now I’ve relinquished a lot of that and I just focus on what I can control and I really try to enjoy the whole process. I think that’s lent itself to just feeling a little bit more free while running.”

No one wants to get to a race like the marathon, in which you put in 16 to 20 weeks of training, have it go poorly and look back thinking you didn’t enjoy the build, McClain adds. If you actually enjoyed getting to the start, the finish line in itself is just an extra sweet payoff.

Ayala helps her clients set process goals—where they focus on how they want to execute the race or training instead of just the splits, times, or the paces—for this exact purpose. “That might be showing up on race day with a tutu and sparkles and giving as many high fives as possible or volunteering with an organization,” like Girls of the Run, she says.

Earlier in her career, McClain says she was “bad” at celebrating small wins. “I was just so addicted to setting PRs and hitting my highest mileage week and I think there’s so many things along the way that you can celebrate,” she says. “Don’t take yourself so seriously and have fun along the way and then celebrate all the small milestones and the big ones.”

For McClain, those small wins include celebrating being able to get in 90 grams of carbs per hour on a long run or simply being able to get up on the first alarm during the summer.

These days, McClain says she’s focused on listening to her body and adapting her plan accordingly. “The goal is to get the workout done as it’s written on my plan, but there are a lot of times where I’m pulling audibles and adjusting the pace based on how my body feels on the day,” she says. “I think that’s also made it more fun because my body’s just agreeing with the training and what I’m doing instead of doing three days of high intensity and a ton of mileage.”

In general, McClain focuses on two hard days and about 82 to 85 miles a week, which she says also gives her time for other stuff in her life.

Ayala points out that this flexibility is a great way to work against burnout: “We also know, unfortunately, perfectionists are more vulnerable to burnout,” she says.

“I think it’s good to practice adaptability also because in a marathon, you just never know what’s going to happen and you can feel so different in one mile to the next,” McClain says. “So also practicing how you’re talking to yourself when things get hard, that’s really important to strengthen those muscles in your workouts and your long run.”

Ignoring the data for a short time can help you decompress without reducing training load, Laraia says. That could look like starting your watch but not looking at it until your workout is over (rather than constantly looking at your heart rate, pace, etc.), he says. Or just go out for an hour-long run and don’t even start your device.

“Today, I think we’re surrounded by so much data and information that it’s really easy to get caught up in numbers and stats and either compare them to yourself or you compare to your friends,” Laraia says. And you know what they say about comparison being the thief of joy…

Laraia recommends that his clients jot down their emotional state after workouts and races just as they might keep track of more quantifiable metrics. “How did this long run feel? How did your mind feel? What were you thinking about in the workout or in the race? Those are things that I think are really important because it helps guide where to push them or pull back,” he says. Even without a coach, you can notice patterns in your own notes.

The key is to look for a mismatch in how you felt and how you performed. If your runs are feeling easy but your heart rate is higher, you may be pushing paces you aren’t ready to run.

On the flip side, if a workout felt really hard but your heart rate was lower, that could mean something else is going on (potentially even an early sign of mental burnout) that’s worth paying attention to if it’s repeated (versus just one or two runs).

“Eat more than you think you need—that's my biggest tip,” McClain says. “I feel like the amount that I’ve fueled and eaten on and off the runs in the last two or three years [has] kept me super healthy alongside a few other things, but I think fueling is so important,” she says. “Making sure you’re taking care of your body on the nutrition front is really, really big.”

Think about it: You’re not having fun when you’re hangry, right?

READ OUR COMPLETE GUIDE TO MARATHON FUELING

Now, when McClain travels for races, she builds in time for fun with her husband. “That’s been a huge additive mindset to this whole elite racing thing—you can have a great time,” she says. “You don’t have to be holed up in your hotel room and you can lean into all the fun appearances and the shakeout runs. It’s energy adding instead of energy sucking for me.”

By taking time to enjoy the experience, even if the race doesn’t go exactly as she hoped, McClain still revels in the fact that she enjoyed the trip and the experience.

Some seasons of life necessitate more R&R, and you need to give your body enough time to absorb the stress of training, Ayala points out. She experienced this firsthand on the heels of COVID-19 when a close friend died, and she felt super burned out in general. She took two months off from cycling—the first in almost a decade of consistent training—and ended up setting a new PR within eight weeks of getting back to it.

“I'm really convinced that it was because I just finally listened to my body and took the pressure off and just took a break,” Ayala says. “It led to a huge boost in performance in one of my best seasons afterward, which was pretty cool.”

Sometimes, even a shorter break—like five days—can be enough to circumvent burnout, Laraia says. “It could be as simple as dropping a hard run or taking an extra day off or reducing mileage or just doing an easy run instead of that hard workout.” Whatever break you need to come back with excitement is worth it.

#8871. 7 Knee-Strengthening Exercises That Prevent Pesky Knee Pain

Don’t let a twinge slow down your pedal stroke—or keep you out of the saddle.

Because cycling isn’t a high-impact sport, you’d be forgiven for thinking your knees are safe. But Tara Parsons, a USAC-certified cycling coach and Rapha Women’s Ambassador says she hears riders complaining about knee pain all the time. In fact, 23 percent of riders experience knee pain, according to a study of 116 professional cyclists—and you can bet that number is higher among amateurs.

The knee acts as a hinge between the hip and the ankle, so just think about how many times you flex and extend your knees during a ride. “If you’re missing 5 percent of your range or in a position that’s slightly less than ideal, a small issue can turn into a big problem for someone who's averaging 50,000 reps a weekend,” says Dane DeLozier, the biomechanics lab director at and co-founder of Revo Physiotherapy and Sports Performance in Boulder, CO.

“This, in combination with a lifestyle that involves sitting at desks all day, can cause the weakening of muscles of the trunk, such as the core, glutes, and hips,” adds Parsons.

From there, it’s a domino effect: “When those muscles become weak or underused, they can become inactive or underactive. And when that happens, the muscles that you use a lot on the bike, such as the quads, end up overcompensating. This overcompensation causes poor knee tracking and poor alignment throughout the pedal stroke, which can lead to knee pain,” says Parsons. And that’s not even considering the stress you’re putting on your knees if your bike isn’t fit correctly or if you’re positioning in the saddle is out of whack.

Pay attention to pain in the patellar tendon, the tendon right on the front of the knee, and the IT band, which goes from the hip down to the knee, says DeLozier—those are common areas for pain, irritation, and inflammation that can hamper knee movement. “If that irritation persists, it’s probably best to go see a PT or your physician to figure out what the root cause is,” he adds.

Whether you’re currently dealing with pain or not, it’s important to build up strength around the joint. Strength training off the bike is crucial to developing those muscles. Plus, “your weekly strengthening routine should involve not just strengthening and activation, but also foam rolling or other type of soft tissue manipulation and mobilization” to keep your muscles in peak condition, says Parsons.

Not sure where to start? These knee-strengthening exercises will help you pedal on pain-free.

How to do this knee-strengthening exercise: Perform 2 to 3 sets of each exercise two times per week. You will need a resistance band loop, a Bosu trainer, and a medium weight. An exercise mat is optional.

The exercises in this workout are demonstrated below by Noam Tamir, certified strength and conditioning specialist and founder of TS Fitness in New York City, so you can learn the proper form. Follow along in the video above with Brian Levine, USAT Level 1 coach and endurance athlete.

Place a resistance band loop around legs just above the knee. Lie on your left side with knees bent, and ankles, knees, and hips stacked. Rest your head on left hand to avoid straining your neck and rest right hand on mat in front of you. Keeping your heels together, rotate right knee up toward ceiling as much as possible. Return to starting position. Complete 15 reps, then repeat on right side.

Lie faceup on the mat with a resistance band loop around your legs just above the knees and knees bent, heels close to butt, arms at sides. Contract glutes, and press into heels to lift hips up toward ceiling so your body forms a straight line from shoulders to knees as you simultaneously press knees out to keep them in line with hips and maintain tension on the band. Pause. Lower and repeat for 10 to 15 reps.

Start standing on a Bosu trainer with hands on hips for balance. Take a big step back with left foot and lower into a lunge with right leg forming a 90-degree angle. Press through right heel to return left leg to start. Complete 10 reps, then repeat on other leg.

Place a band around ankles and stand with feet hip-width apart so band is taut. Lower into a micro squat, then step out to the left. Bring right foot in so feet are hip-width apart again; continue walking, taking 15 steps to the left before reversing to take 15 steps to the right, keeping the band taut the entire time.

Start standing and holding a kettlebell or medium weight in right hand. Shift weight onto left leg and micro bend left knee. Hinge at the hips as you lower weight to floor and extend right leg back behind you for balance. Continue lowering the weight until you are about parallel to the floor while keeping back straight. Return to the starting position. Repeat for 10 to 15 reps then switch sides.

Start on all fours with wrists under shoulders, knees under hips, toes tucked, and back flat. While keeping knee bent, lift right heel up as if to “stamp” your footprint on the ceiling. Return to starting position. Complete 15 reps then repeat on left side.

Start on all fours with wrists under shoulders, knees under hips, toes tucked, and back flat. Extend right arm and left leg straight out until they’re parallel to the floor. Maintain a flat back, level hips, and focus on pulling your belly button toward your spine. Return to all fours, then raise left arm and right leg. Continue alternating for 90 seconds.

#8870. The Fastest Shoes at the 2026 NYC Marathon

Eight brands cracked the top 10, but Nike and Adidas “hyper shoes” took the overall top spots.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

The defending champs were in the mix all the way to Central Park, but in the end there were some surprising upsets. Andreas Almgren, in his debut, became the first European man to claim victory at the NYC Marathon in 30 years. And Jess McClain outsprinted Hellen Obiri to take second place overall. There were even bigger surprises—at least in the eyes of the RW gear team—as there was good parity among shoe companies among the fastest runners. Even Xtep got into the mix. Let’s take a look at what the top 10 men and women laced up for their dash from Staten Island to Central Park.

You can’t get this shoe until January 2027, but Nike’s top pros are already having some good success on the roads with the $360 racer. It has two Air units stacked under the forefoot and a zero drop. Lighter and more aggressive than an Alphafly, the Apex is being positioned as Nike’s elite-level marathon shoe, while the Alphafly 4 is being turned into a marathon racer for the masses. I took an Apex demo pair out for a short run last month and found they feel aggressively propulsive—you’re immediately tipping forward off those Air units as soon as you touch down.

On had a big day on the streets of the Big Apple. Even though Hellen Obiri didn’t repeat as champ in the women’s division, the brand’s top racing model with the robot-sprayed upper was seen a lot among the pro fields.

Personally, I love that the collar of the upper is designed more like a normal shoe—the taller cuff of the first version rubbed my ankle and I had to cut the upper.

Xtep might be a new name to you, but it’s one of a handful of exciting brands coming out of China right now. The shoes are tough to get here in the U.S., but we’ve received a few of Xtep’s models for testing recently, including the 160X 8.0 Pro. “This is a rocket ship of a shoe,” said RW shoe tester Josh Davis. “It really shined in intervals where I was pushing it at 5:30+ pace, but it is downright uncomfortable at easy paces.” Mofolo rode this thing in the sweet spot today.

This shoe has been cleaning house at the World Majors Marathons. Today was one of the rare days when the featherweight, $500 speedster didn’t land on the podium. Bonus: Adidas just refreshed stock so a few pairs are still available. Hurry. If that shoe sells out, the next fastest option is the Adios Pro 5.

The Ray is Asics’s ultralight racer, using an exceptionally soft A-TPU midsole foam with a see-through upper that really does little more than hold the foam to your sole. It’s a lot of fun if you’re dashing in a straight line, but gets squirrelly if you have to turn.

Muhumed laced up a black-on-black prototype that Hoka got approved by World Athletics within the past week. It’s hard to see much detail here but, given the silhouette of the sole, it looks like it might be the successor to the Rocket X 3 (the Cielo has a more pronounced rocker shape).

Nike recently released the Alphafly 4 and announced the Apex, which you saw finish further ahead in the pack. But Kamworor reached for the Alphafly 3, which has been discontinued. That’s the beauty of this sport: Our preferences are highly individual and you have enough choices to reach for the shoe that works best for you.

The blue color looks like the Ray we saw earlier, but zooming in on the image it appears there are two layers of foam—the top layer is a little more yellow-tinted—and the upper looks to be the slightly thicker mesh found on the more traditional racing duo. The use of two foams (PEBA and A-TPU) gives the Sky better stability and a firmer feel underfoot.

As we expected, Chepkirui (the 2024 champ) and Hellen Obiri (2025 champ) went toe-to-toe all the way into Central Park. In the end, it was the Pro Evo 3 once again taking the top spot in a WMM race.

The World Athletics site lists two development prototypes, one named “hyperion Green2” and one simply called “RED.” That latter shoe was approved for use at the end of September, ahead of the fall marathon season. We’re not sure which of these is the shoe McClain wore to claim a podium spot, but earlier in the week Brooks told us that she was planning to race in a prototype disguised to look like the currently available Hyperion Elite 6. That’s the same tactic Clayton Young used at the Chicago Marathon last month when he ran the second-fastest marathon ever by an American.

The 46-year-old delivered another stunning performance in NYC. On her feet were Puma’s speediest racing shoes with a carbon-fiber plate that extends out past the toes for extra leverage.

The Cielo is Hoka’s bounciest marathon shoe, with a much more aggressive rocker shape. If you prize a slightly firmer or more stable experience, the Rocket X 3 may be more your speed. The Cielo carried Chelangat to a top-five showing.

The second American woman finisher laced up the Edge, a marathon racer that is designed for “cadence” runners—those who speed up by taking faster steps rather than lengthening their stride.

The two layers of PEBA foam in this racer are just a little firmer and more controlled than found in the Cielo. The rocker, too, is more easygoing and doesn’t feel quite so propulsive. But it’s clear that the shoe can still get up and move.

Jeff is Runner-in-Chief for Runner’s World and the director of product testing. He has tested and reviewed running shoes, GPS watches, headphones, apparel, and more for nearly two decades. He regularly tests more than 100 pairs of shoes each year, and once had a 257-day streak running in different models. Jeff can usually be found on the roads, racing anything from the mile to a marathon, but he also enjoys racing up mountains and on snowshoes. When he’s not running, you’ll probably find him hanging from a ladder making repairs and renovations to his house (he’s also director of product testing for Popular Mechanics).

If a picture is worth a thousand words, then our posture speaks volumes. Poor carriage of the torso—rounded shoulders, sunken chest, and a downward cast of the eyes—generally suggests a negative state of being. Good posture, on the other hand—shoulders rolled back and down, chest lifted, and an energetic carriage—demonstrates confidence and a sense of purpose.

All the backbending yoga postures help create this physical expression of assurance. You feel better, have more energy, and benefit from an enhanced respiratory system. The internal alignment of the organs is refined as we adjust and improve the external alignment.

The postures actually have the potential to positively and profoundly affect you on all levels: physical, mental, emotional, and spiritual. Approaching your asanas with this awareness is the key to the enrichment of your practice.

The repertoire of backbending postures, or hyperextensions of the spine, is vast. In this article, we are going to focus on one of the more basic back-bending poses, Grasshopper or Locust Pose (Salabhasana). There are several variations of this posture, according to different systems or styles of hatha yoga. We will practice two versions of Locust, beginning with Salabhasana One as described in B.K.S. Iyengar’s Light on Yoga.

Locust is excellent for correcting poor posture, as well as for counteracting the development of kyphosis, the rounding of the upper back. It tones the whole posterior of the body, strengthens the abdominals, and enhances digestion.

Begin by lying face down on your mat, with your arms at your sides near your hips, palms facing upward. Tuck your chin in, forehead on the floor.

Engage your abdominals by drawing your navel in and up, to stabilize your lower back. Contract your buttocks and quadriceps. Keep the knees, legs, and feet together. Exhale the breath as you simultaneously raise the head, chest, arms, and legs. Look forward and up. Hold and breathe for five to 10 seconds. Keep the abdominals firm so you feel the support from underneath.

Exhale as you come out of the pose, returning to base position. Turn your head to the side and completely relax. Repeat once or twice more.

Full Locust begins in the same base position, but with the arms outstretched at shoulder level, perpendicular to the body. The palms are facing down, and the chin is on the mat. The knees, legs, and feet are together.

Engage your abdominal muscles by drawing your navel in and up; contract your buttocks and quadriceps. This time, inhale the breath as you raise the arms, chest, head, and legs. Look forward and up. Breathe naturally as you hold the posture for five to 10 seconds. Keep your shoulders away from your earlobes as you continue to stretch your arms back and slightly upward. Palms remain facing the floor. The idea is to lift the entire body upward as you balance on the center of your abdomen.

Exhale as you come out of the pose, returning to base position, and relax. Repeat once or twice more.

If your lower back is sensitive or you are prone to chronic neck tension, you may want to practice the pose in the following stages.

Lie on your stomach, face down, arms at your sides near your hips. Palms are facing up, the chin is tucked in, and the forehead is on the floor. Legs are hip-distance apart. Firm the buttocks and abdominals as well as the quadriceps.

Inhale the breath. Exhaling, raise just the arms to about hip level, keeping the palms facing up. The head remains on the floor. Lengthen the neck and focus on strengthening your back muscles. Feel your shoulder blades pull down your back and slightly together.

Keep the abdominals, buttocks, and legs firm. Exhale and lower down.

Next, repeat what you’ve just done and add the lifting of the chest. The neck and head will come up as well, but keep looking downward so the neck remains extended rather than arched. Inhale in your base position. Exhale and raise the arms only. Inhale and hold. Ex-haling, raise the chest. Again, hold and breathe rhythmically for five to 10 seconds. Exhale as you lower down.

In the same beginning position, inhale the breath, and exhale raising the arms up. Hold and inhale. Exhale, raising the chest. Hold and inhale. Finally, exhale and raise the legs. Hold and breathe. Keep looking at the floor, focusing on lengthening the body from the top of your head to your fingertips on down to your toes. When you’re ready, lower down on an exhalation. Turn your head to the side, release the pose completely, and relax.

A natural inclination after performing a back bend is to pull your knees to your chest. So after your last repetition, you may want to got into Child’s Pose: Kneel back onto your heels, folding your torso over your thighs with your head resting on the floor in front of your knees. Arms are at your sides with palms facing up.

If your head doesn’t rest on the floor easily, simply fold your arms underneath your forehead for support.

#8867. The Best Bike Lights for Triathletes in 2026, Tested and Reviewed

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Bottom Line: Each of the bike lights in our Best Bike Lights of 2026 list below has been tested on long rides by an experienced triathlete for many miles. Our reviewer is unbiased, with no brand relationships, meaning no brand has paid to appear in our list.

It’s that time of year again. You glance at your training plan, realize your post-work ride slot will now be taking place in the dark, and suddenly “bike light” jumps to the top of your shopping list. The good news is that bike lights in 2026 are significantly better than offerings from just a few years ago. You could even say they are light-years ahead (pun intended) of the bike lights from the 20th century. They are brighter, lighter, and – critically for triathletes – easier to mount on your bike than ever before.

But before you order the cheapest bike light on Amazon, there’s a bit more to think through. The cheapest option is far from the best, but you also don’t need to take out a second mortgage to buy a bike light either. Here’s what actually matters when buying lights as a triathlete, followed by the best options on the market right now.

As a light-toting triathlete, your goal isn’t just to see the road ahead of you; it is also to be seen. Public roads are far from perfectly safe, especially in today’s phone-addicted world filled with distracted drivers. But thankfully, having a bike light is one of the best ways to gain the attention of nearby drivers, reminding them to slow down and give you space as they pass by.

When shopping for a bike light, you want to consider two different design priorities, and pay close attention because most lights optimize for one or the other. First, you want a bike light that shines a powerful beam down the road, illuminating your path at speed in the dark. Second, you want a light that is designed to be seen. These lights use wide-angle optics, lateral emission, and attention-grabbing flash patterns to make you visible to cross-traffic and drivers approaching from the rear. Ideally, your bike light(s) do both.

For triathletes specifically, the lighting challenge runs deeper than a single unit on your bicycle. You might actually want three different lights for the corresponding sports. The ideal setup might include front and rear coverage on the bike, a headlamp or chest light for early-morning runs, and some form of visibility for open-water swims, especially those before sunrise. Each sport requires different hardware, but in this guide, we’ll focus on bike lights. Let’s help you figure out how to sort and sift through the hundreds of options on the market.

The standard brightness unit for sports lights is lumens. The higher the number, the brighter the light. But brighter isn’t always better. Some brands love to advertise max lumens at maximum output, but that can drain the battery in under two hours. Always check the light’s runtime at the mode you’ll actually use.

Consider the type of darkness you’ll be riding in, and how much light you’ll need. Not every triathlete will train in pitch darkness, so here is a quick reference of what you’ll find on the light market:

A pinpoint beam aimed straight ahead is great for one thing, and that’s seeing directly in front of you. But if you’re riding in the dark, you also want to have side visibility, not just from your own perspective, but for other riders and drivers to see you. The best bike lights have a wide spread beam that alerts drivers approaching from angles, not just head-on. Some lights now use multiple LEDs, which is worth considering if you ride in the dark year-round.

This is one of the most important aspects of a bike light because if the battery dies while you are riding in the dark 20 miles from home, you are SOL. Most bike lights are USB-C rechargeable, but runtime varies enormously. If you don’t get a light with a low-battery warning (ideally with several minutes of reserve before shutdown), make sure you keep tabs on how long you’ve been running it before it’s time to recharge.

This is where triathletes diverge from road cyclists. Aero bars, clip-on extensions, and non-standard cockpit shapes make standard clamp mounts useless in many setups. When shopping for lights, you’ll want to look for options that come with flexible silicone straps, GoPro-style mounts, or Garmin quarter-turn compatibility. Silicone straps cover the widest range of setups and are easy to transfer between bikes.

In the 2026 bike light market, there are a number of smart features that come with some of the more pristine options. Some of the features are just bells and whistles, but a few are genuinely helpful, especially for triathletes. Radar integration (Garmin Varia), ANT+ connectivity, automatic brightness adjustment, and brake-sensing technology are popular features that help improve function and safety on the bike. These are not marketing gimmicks – radar in particular can dramatically improve your confidence when riding on open roads with traffic.

Front light placement can be the trickiest part of lighting your tri bike. You can choose between below the basebar (the most aerodynamic option), midway down the aerobars (if the light rotates that direction), and arguably the best solution: adding a computer bridge to your aerobars and mounting the light on top or below it. Whatever you choose, test it on a bumpy road during daylight hours before relying on it in the dark. Remember that you’re not only looking for the light to stay attached, but also for the angle to remain stable as the light illuminates the road in front of you.

Rear lights are much more forgiving, with the seatpost being the most ideal spot for a rear-facing bike light. If you have limited seatpost access, you can mount a light on the seatstay. Just make sure your light is pointing backward rather than toward the sky or floor. If you have bottles or other gear mounted under or behind your seat, make sure they don’t block the bike light when they are fully loaded.

Output: 1,300 lumens front; 90 lumens rear

Battery life: 1.5 hrs front; 4.5 hrs rear

The Ion Pro and Flare bike lights do much more than illuminate through darkness. The paired set uses ANT+ to link the front and rear lights together, and you can control both from a compatible Garmin or Wahoo head unit. Up front, the Ion Pro has up to 1,300 lumens, which is more than enough for most low-light situations. It also has a clean beam pattern with solid front and side visibility, with a few hours of battery life across various power settings. In the rear, the Flare can be used with a 16-degree offset mount option that helps solve one of the most common triathlete problems: mounting a rear light on an angled seatpost or seatstay. The mount is sold separately, but it only costs $5.

Pros: ANT+ integration, offset rear mount solves tri-bike seatpost issues ($5 cost), strong front output Cons: Pricey for a set; front light only has 90 minutes of runtime at max output

Output: 130 to 1,000 lumens with six different modes

Battery life: 120 hrs on ECO FLASH; up to 2 hrs at max output

The Blinder has earned its spot on best-of lists for years, and the 2026 version is no exception. IP67 waterproofing and six different light modes make the Blinder 1000 suitable for a wide range of weather and light conditions, including midnight rain-riding. At low outputs, the Blinder 1000 lasts for days on a single charge. GoPro-style and standard handlebar mounts are both included, making it versatile on almost any tri cockpit.

Pros: Fully IP67 waterproof, versatile mounts, solid build quality, side window visibility

Cons: Heavier than some competitors at the same lumen output

Battery life: 1 hr at max output; up to 60 hrs at minimum output

If your friends call you “Nightrider,” then the AMPP 2200 might be the perfect bike light for you. With a max output of 2,200 lumens, the AMPP 2200 obliterates darkness in a way that can make you feel like you’re riding during the daytime. This is the light for those who ride in pitch darkness at speed, or those who live in extreme daylight climates such as Alaska or Iceland. While its top-end output is impressive, the AMPP 2200 includes different light modes that are ideal for riding in the dusk rather than the pitch black. At 500 to 800 lumens, the AMPP 2200 becomes a practical all-night light with sufficient battery reserve. Its included mount is quite secure, even on rough pavement. The trade-off is weight; at 211g, it’s the heaviest option on this list.

Pros: Exceptional max output, wide runtime range, secure mount, high-quality build

Cons: Heaviest light on this list; 2,200 lumens if overkill for those who don’t ride in complete darkness

Battery life: 4 to 80 hrs (front); 3 to 60 hrs (rear)

If you’re only looking for a pair of lights that will help you be seen, the Knog Frog combo could be the perfect fit. The front light output isn’t enough to illuminate a dark road, but not every triathlete wants to ride in the dark. Sometimes, you just want to be seen by drivers and cross-traffic, especially in low-light conditions. The combo’s battery life is fitting for the price point, and the pair is so light that you won’t even notice them. They come with a flexible silicone strap that wraps around virtually any tube shape, including aero bars. While they won’t light up a country road, the Knog Frog combo is great for being seen in the city, on the bike path, or on a foggy training loop.

Pros: Aero-bar compatible, extremely lightweight, very affordable, easy to use

Cons: 40 lumens won’t illuminate a dark road; not a standalone solution for night riding

Battery life: 16 hrs (day flash mode); 6 hrs (solid mode)

The Varia is a rear light that also functions as a vehicle radar. In terms of safety and security, it is one of the best bike lights on the market. When paired with a compatible Garmin head unit or Varia app, the light alerts you to vehicles approaching from behind, before you can even hear them. It is an incredibly useful safety feature, especially if you frequently ride in groups or on busy roads. If you get nervous riding on open roads, the Varia RTL515 could be the best option for you. While the light function itself isn’t anything special, the radar is the reason to buy it.

Pros: Vehicle radar is a game-changer on open roads; lightweight, impressive battery life, pairs with Garmin ecosystem

Cons: Expensive for a single rear light; radar requires a compatible head unit or phone mount

Battery life: 12 hrs constant; 30 hrs flash

In terms of bang for your buck, it’s hard to beat the Gravity Plus, which uses an accelerometer to detect braking and automatically increases brightness when you decelerate. It is effectively functioning as a brake light, and it is one of the cheapest options on this list. For triathletes who ride out of town, train with unpredictable stop-and-go conditions, or frequent group rides, the brake-sensing rear light is surprisingly effective. Runtime is excellent for a budget light, and you probably won’t even notice the added weight.

Pros: Brake-sensing technology, outstanding battery life, lightweight

Cons: 100 lumens is modest; a brighter light is necessary for riding in complete darkness

#8866. Jess McClain’s Coach—Record-Setting Ultramarathoner David Roche—Shares a Key Training Tactic for Fighting Late-Race Fatigue

This simple long-run tweak can help your legs stay strong when the late miles hit.

Many runners think of the climbs as the toughest part of a hilly race. Uphills send your heart rate soaring and slow even the strongest runners to a grind, while descents offer a chance to catch your breath and let gravity do some of the work. But David Roche, ultramarathoner and coach to New York City Marathon women’s runner-up Jess McClain, says those easier-feeling downhills can come at a cost later in the race.

And Roche knows the importance of late-race performance, which is why he integrates strategies into his training to fight fatigue through long distances.

Take McClain’s finish in New York City as an example: She outkicked reigning champ Hellen Obiri just feet from the finish line to take second place by mere seconds, clocking 2:24:42 and becoming the first American woman to reach the podium in NYC since 2018.

Roche’s fatigue-fighting tactics take him even farther in his own races. The two-time Life Time Leadville 100 winner—and course record holder—covered the famously demanding trails in 15:12:30, averaging roughly 9:07 per mile. Yet he rarely relies on extremely long, arduous training runs to prepare for conquering late miles.

Instead, Roche uses downhill workouts to reproduce some of the muscular stress that can cause runners’ legs to fail in an endurance event. “Downhills are the gateway to fatigue resistance in these really long events,” Roche tells Runner’s World.

The best part is, you don’t have to be an elite like McClain or Roche to benefit from his advice. He shares how purposeful downhill training can help runners preserve their strength, form, and pace deep into a race. Plus, he offers his go-to workout to add to your buildup.

Running downhill may provide some relief to your cardiovascular system—by lowering your heart rate a bit as gravity naturally carries you downward—but it puts much more strain on your musculoskeletal system. To keep you from tumbling down the hill, the quads must repeatedly brake the body’s momentum.

Braking action involves eccentric contractions, meaning the muscles produce force while lengthening under load, Roche explains. Eccentric contractions occur during many activities—including simply walking down stairs—but running a lengthy descent can deliver thousands in succession, significantly increasing the load on your muscles.

When the body isn’t accustomed to the stress caused by downhill running, the aftermath can wreck you. Roche explains that while a runner may feel relatively normal after their first downhill running workout, they end up developing significant soreness within a day or two. “That feeling of, ‘Oh man, I have no quads right now,’ a few days later is also what happens to your quads in an ultra,” Roche says—and even a marathon.

The initial downhill running effort, however, also triggers an adaptation known as the repeated bout effect. A review published in 2024 on the subject describes the repeated bout effect as a form of skeletal-muscle memory in which the first eccentric challenge activates protective responses that make the muscle more resistant to damage than subsequent ones.

Scientists haven’t identified one physiological mechanism that fully explains the effect. Instead, the review suggests several adaptations may work together. The nervous system may distribute the load more effectively across the muscles, while changes to muscle fibers, tendons, and the extracellular matrix—the structural network surrounding the cells—may help the tissue tolerate force. The inflammatory response may also become better regulated after the body has encountered that stress before.

Basically, the more downhill running you do in your training, the less sore your legs will become after each workout, Roche explains. Using the downhill bout effect to your benefit in this way helps keep your legs stronger later in races as they handle similar impact.

Research shows this phenomenon in action: In a study published in 2022, 10 recreational male runners completed the same 30-minute treadmill run at a 20 percent decline twice, with three weeks between sessions. Following the second run, the athletes experienced a smaller rise in creatine kinase—a blood marker commonly used to assess muscle damage following exercise—along with less soreness and a smaller reduction in maximal force. Their running mechanics were also less disrupted after the second session.

The practical takeaway: With the appropriate exposure, the legs can learn to handle downhills with less fallout. That makes downhill training particularly valuable for ultrarunners who spend multiple hours in a race descending hills, but Roche believes the same principle applies to road runners, too.

At mile 20 of your marathon, your limiting factor isn’t always your heart or your lungs. You could simply lack the muscular strength to keep the same mechanics or pace. Downhill running is Roche’s solution to prepare for that problem without requiring immense volume, and his go-to workout is simpler than you might expect.

For most runners, Roche’s downhill workout isn’t a complicated interval session. It’s an easy long run with a deliberate change in pace when you reach a decline. Roche uses variations of this downhill workout twice per week in his own training, recommending most athletes start with one session and progress from there based on how they recover.

“Because the aerobic demand [of the run] is low, it’s just about pushing the steeper terrain in a way that causes eccentric muscle contractions,” Roche says.

Instead of trying to stack as many miles as possible to mimic race-day conditions, Roche recommends runners focus race-day muscular demand into a 16-mile effort. The faster descents repeatedly load the quads, while the surrounding easy running provides the aerobic work that’s crucial for long-distance racing, says Roche.

According to Roche, in an ideal scenario, you should aim for downhills as steep as—or steeper than—those in your goal race. Running these downhills faster than your race pace ensures your muscles can take on the challenges your goal race will present.

While Roche’s recommended 16-mile run is generally reserved for experienced athletes preparing for marathons or longer, you can scale the same principle to nearly any experience level or race distance by shortening the overall run.

The purpose of downhill training isn’t to leave the quads wrecked every week. Initial sessions may cause soreness, but over time, the same type of descent should become less disruptive, allowing you to recover more easily and withstand greater late-race fatigue.

The workout succeeds not because of how much punishment the quads absorb during one run, but because they’re still capable of working when the race delivers the same punishment as you approach the finish line.

Matt Rudisill is an Associate Service Editor who has been with Runner's World since 2025. Matt was also heavily involved in communications efforts for Penn State football, men's basketball, and women's gymnastics. In his role with Runner's World, Matt has interviewed Olympians, world champions, and countless experts in the field to create service content that helps runners of all ages and experience levels train smarter and race faster. #8864. Once Was Enough for the NYC Marathon—Here’s Why I’ll Never Run It Again

Running the race tested my limits, revealed my grit, and brought me full circle with the city that shaped me.

Probably the most excruciating breath I’ve taken in my life was in Lenox Hill Hospital on East 77th Street. It was my first breath on Earth, and my lungs must have wondered what had hit them. Forty-three years later, it seemed fitting that I’d come back to you for another challenge to my lungs and body: my first marathon.

I have lots of memories of you, starting from those early years on Manhattan’s Upper East Side. Then there were holiday visits and sleepovers with my grandmother in Stuyvesant Town, special days in Dad’s office in Washington Heights, Mom’s gallery openings in the Village. There were the fits and starts of my early professional career when I lived in Brooklyn and then Alphabet City, using most of my paycheck for rent, the rest for food. And of course, after I moved away in my late 20s, when I’d see you a couple of times a month for work.

If I’m being honest, you’ve always been a bit of a headache and a challenge. Back when I was just starting out, I couldn’t tolerate your high prices and abrasive attitude, and your tendency to “never sleep.” Which is why I ditched you for a less exhausting life in the country. Even today, I stress out just thinking about seeing you.

But on an unseasonably warm November Sunday, NYC Marathon day, you challenged me more than ever before—and revealed a level of grit I didn’t know was in me.

On the Verrazzano Bridge, I was overcome with emotion at having made it to the starting line. Surrounded by scores of runners from all over the world, with the open waterway below and the iconic skyline in the distance, I felt like a part of something huge and meaningful. It literally brought tears to my eyes.

Running through Brooklyn, I was in a zone. I was able to stay on pace and hit the halfway mark in decent shape, so I forced a smile at the throngs of cheering spectators. I’ve never been one to smile during races, and even your generous Brooklynites couldn’t get me to light up a genuine grin.

Then came the 59th Street Bridge. Long Island City, with its dull stretches of low-slung warehouses, is perhaps one of your most charmless neighborhoods. Nothing against the spectators who did their best in the streets leading up to the bridge, but that endless, gradual incline in the eerie quiet with the wind blowing up off the East River is where I started to unravel.

The screaming wall of people on First Avenue did nothing to energize me. This is where I began to feel like perhaps a marathon is just too long a run to be considered a wise choice.

And, sorry. Even if the Bronx had welcomed me with confetti and a marching band, it wouldn’t have mattered. Once I got to the Willis Avenue Bridge, I regretted not bringing money or a MetroCard so I could duck out and just go home. With every step, my feet, my quads, my knees threatened imminent shutdown. Worse was the shivering that seemed to consume my whole body, like when you lie feverish in bed, begging for the Tylenol to kick in.

Harlem was a fleeting boost, lifting me up ever so briefly at Mile 22 with its gospel choir, its Jamaican ska, its salsa beat. New York, here is where you started to shine and where I started to believe in myself. Your Harlem spectators literally reached out their hands and told me, “You can do this” and “You look strong.” They warmed me with their smiles when my body was wracked with chills. They let me pet their Bernese Mountain Dog, a wagging gift of comfort when all I wanted was to curl up on the sidewalk. They watched me cry tears that were a strange mixture of homesickness, pride, and self-pity. And they saw me smile a genuine smile for the first time all day.

The high was short-lived, but that’s okay. Marathons are not meant to be easy. I had no illusions that I’d skip along Fifth Avenue with my arms in the air. But I was able to hold on to that smile, the one I picked up in Harlem, that was as real as I’ve ever smiled in a race. And friends told me later that I looked strong and was even passing other runners on that stretch just south of 110th Street.

Central Park made my head spin. It was so close to the finish, yet it felt like endless circles. I was ready to be done with you, New York. But you had other plans. After I crossed the finish line (at 4:44, roughly 15 minutes slower than my hoped-for time), you sent me into the arms of a mom-like volunteer named Kate on whose shoulder I blubbered and drooled and snotted until she led me into a medical tent where I collapsed in a shivering heap, and was caught by a dreadlocked medic named Ishmael with gentle eyes who covered me in woolen blankets and placed me next to a heater and fed me hot soup and salt and Gatorade until I could stand up again and hobble back to the hotel and my family and my peaceful life.

And though you raised the stakes in a big way, New York, that day, you made me grateful for the chance to prove to myself that I can do hard things. Even if we don’t see eye to eye, you helped make me who I am. I never believed I could run this distance, that I’d be up to the challenge. But looking back on our history, I’m pretty sure you knew I had it in me all along.

This article originally appeared in the Winter 2025 issue of Runner’s World.

A will (technically a "last will and testament") is a legal document that specifies how your assets should be distributed after your death. It must go through probate — a court-supervised process that validates the will, pays debts and taxes, and distributes assets to beneficiaries. A living trust (specifically a revocable living trust) is a legal entity you create during your lifetime that holds your assets. When you die, the successor trustee distributes those assets according to the trust terms — without court involvement.

You need both: A trust does not name guardians for minor children (only a will can do that), and a trust only controls assets that have been formally transferred into it. A pour-over will acts as a safety net — it directs any assets not in the trust at your death to pour into the trust, where they are distributed according to the trust terms. The pour-over will still goes through probate, but it ensures nothing falls through the cracks.

The term "living trust" almost always refers to a revocable living trust — one you can change, amend, or dissolve at any time during your lifetime. You remain the trustee, manage the assets as you always have, and pay taxes on trust income using your personal Social Security number. For income tax purposes, a revocable trust is invisible — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist.

An irrevocable trust is fundamentally different. Once established, you cannot easily modify it, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. This permanence provides two powerful advantages:

The federal estate tax exemption is $13.61 million per person ($27.22 million for married couples) in 2026, but this historically high exemption is scheduled to sunset after 2025, potentially dropping to approximately $7 million per person. FIRE households who have built $3 million to $10 million in net worth through decades of saving and investment growth should monitor this sunset closely. If the exemption drops, irrevocable trusts become relevant at much lower wealth levels.

For most FIRE households with $1 million to $5 million in net worth, a revocable living trust provides the right balance of control, flexibility, and probate avoidance. Irrevocable structures become compelling only when estate tax exposure is real or asset protection needs are elevated.

Estate planning is governed primarily by state law, and the value of a living trust versus a will varies significantly depending on where you live.

Nine states are community property states: Arizona, California, Idaho, Louisiana, Nevada, New Mexico, Texas, Washington, and Wisconsin. In these states, most assets acquired during marriage are owned 50/50 by both spouses regardless of whose name is on the title. At death, only the deceased spouse's half passes through their estate plan.

The remaining 41 states follow common law (also called "equitable distribution"). Ownership depends on whose name is on the title. This distinction affects how assets pass at death and whether a trust or will provides better spousal protection.
