#8853. Cold, Dark, Rainy? The 10 Best Editor-Tested Indoor Bike Trainers Keep Your Training on Track

Our editors tested the best indoor bike trainers for winter miles, Zwift rides, and every budget.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Well, friends, it’s that time of year again. Colder temperatures and shorter daylight hours mean indoor riding season is right around the corner for many of us—if it hasn’t already arrived where you live. But thankfully, newer trainer tech and digital connectivity make those boring nights spent staring at your basement wall or garage door while endlessly spinning the pedals a thing of the past.

Smart trainers—some priced under $500—connect to Zwift and Rouvy, popular platforms that feature virtual worlds, group rides, and even organized races. Plus, lower prices on nicely-equipped indoor bikes mean you no longer have to wrestle with putting your bike on the trainer or ruining pricey components with sweat.

Our editors test trainers year-round, from budget-friendly units to the most advanced smart bike models currently available. We do workouts and ride a ton of base miles; some staff even compete at a high level in virtual racing leagues, giving us important feedback on trainer accuracy, stability, and durability.

The Wahoo Kickr Core 2 with Zwift Cog and Click is our Best Overall Indoor Trainer because it’s the perfect choice for most riders. It combines Wahoo’s excellent base-model direct-drive trainer with Zwift’s singlespeed cog and virtual shifting. The system sets up easily and works with almost any bike, regardless of gear range or number of speeds. (You can easily swap the Zwift Cog with a cassette if you don’t like the virtual gearing.) This enables multiple riders in a household to share one trainer, even if their bikes have different drivetrains or gearing.

I used the first-generation Kickr Core as my home setup for four years without any issues. Wahoo’s recent updates to the Core only make an already great smart trainer even better. Test Editor Dan Chabanov recently used the new Kickr Core 2 for three months after switching from the more expensive Kickr V6. He said, “Honestly, I can’t say I’ve noticed any kind of downgrade.”

On paper, the Kickr Core 2 has lower maximum wattage, less grade simulation, and slightly less claimed accuracy. In practice, the ride feel is almost identical on both models. Like the Kickr V6, the Core now features Wi-Fi (along with Bluetooth and ANT+) for smooth connectivity and faster data transmission for online events. “Truly, the only reason to opt for the pricier V6 is that it folds slightly smaller and is easier to move around,” Chabanov concluded.

The Zwift Cog uses virtual shifting to change gears instead of your bike’s shifters and derailleurs. Unfortunately, virtual shifting only works in Zwift. If you plan to ride without Zwift (or on another platform), purchase the Kickr Core 2 with a cassette.

Tired of putting your bike on the trainer every time you want to ride indoors?

Dedicated training bikes, such as the Zwift Ride, are a great option for indoor riding. This way, you have a bike on the trainer that’s always ready to ride. No more fumbling to remove your wheel or wearing down tires. The Ride’s adjustment range also makes it easy to set up and share with multiple riders in a household.

“After more than a year of heavy use by my wife and me, the Zwift Ride has proven to be a durable, impressively quiet alternative to abusing our 'good' bikes on a trainer, with excellent Zwift integration and easy adjustability for our multi-rider household,” said Senior Test Editor Matt Phillips.

Zwift’s recent updates addressed our criticisms of the original Ride. The V2 now fits more riders (4’10” to 6’6”), adds saddle adjustability, and increases the bar diameter. It also includes Zwift’s multi-position crank with lengths from 160mm to 175mm, which used to be a $100 upcharge.

If you ride indoors and want a dedicated setup that integrates with Zwift out of the box (and don’t want to spend thousands of dollars for a premium indoor bike), the Zwift Ride is an excellent option. Zwift sells the Ride Smart Frame alone (without a trainer) for $800 if you already have a direct-drive trainer.

Since launching in 2012, the Wahoo Kickr has consistently been one of the best indoor trainers and a favorite of Bicycling’s staff. While the sixth version of the venerable smart trainer is more of an update than a wholesale redesign, the changes help the Kickr rank ahead of other high-performance smart trainers.

The latest iteration features the same flywheel as the previous one, so the two units look virtually identical. As a result, both generations experience the same ride feel. The Kickr ramps up smoothly and correctly as you accelerate. Power accuracy is very good, and most riders will find the claimed 1-percent accuracy to be true.

Despite its high price and lack of cassette-sizing options, the latest Kickr is a solid choice. It’s the best option for performance-minded cyclists who push big watts or racers who require accuracy and improved connectivity for online events.

If you need a basic, budget-friendly trainer that gets the job done in a pinch—and offers compatibility with third-party apps like Zwift—the Tacx Boost Trainer Bundle is a solid option. With its magnetic roller, you can manually adjust resistance across ten levels. And because the Boost uses magnetic resistance instead of fluid or fans, it stays relatively quiet. The loudest sounds you’ll hear are your drivetrain and the tire on the roller.

The bundle includes a Garmin speed sensor and a front wheel block to keep your bike level while riding. It also folds up easily for compact storage. For an easy-to-use, low-cost, no-frills setup, this one covers the essentials.

The Saris Fluid2 is a good trainer at a reasonable price. This makes it a solid pick for riders who need something basic to keep up with their training plan on rainy days, rehab from injury, or get back into riding before heading outside onto the bike path, road, or trails.

The Fluid2’s wheel-on design means you don’t need to fumble with your drivetrain to set it up, and the fluid resistance provides a smooth, progressive ride feel. Although this version isn’t compatible with Zwift, Rouvy, or other online platforms, the Saris combo kit (for $40 more) includes a wheel sensor that adds connectivity. Also be sure to get an adaptor kit if your bike has a thru axle rear wheel.

Instead of buying that no-name $50 or $80 trainer, spend a little more for a proven trainer from a trusted brand. While it looks similar to Saris’ Fluid 2 (above), the Mag Plus uses a magnetic sensor to provide resistance instead of fluid. This saves a little money and gives you a linear feel (versus the Fluid’s progressive resistance). However, a big downside is that they tend to wear out tires pretty quickly, especially pricey, high-performance rubber.

Mag trainers have been around for decades (I’ve had several from different brands over the years); the tech hasn’t changed much and they don’t have any smart features. If you plan to ride Zwift or Rouvy, you need to install a wheel sensor. If you need a super basic trainer that gets the job done for only $100, the Mag Plus is your best bet.

The Neo 3M matches the Wahoo Kickr in power measurement (up to 2,200 watts with 1% accuracy) and maximum simulated gradient (up to 25%), but it has two unique features. The Neo generates its own electricity, so you can use it without external power (though it works best when plugged in). And, like an old-school Nintendo Rumble Pack, the Neo 3M vibrates to simulate a wide range of road surfaces—from gravel to cobblestones to concrete slab roads—when you’re riding Zwift.

Unlike other direct-drive trainers that use belts or rollers to transmit power, the Neo 3M uses a metal flywheel with magnets that interact with electrical coils to moderate resistance. Combined with the built-in motion plates, the trainer has an impressively realistic ride feel. However, the Neo 3M lacks a native high-speed data transfer mode or built-in Wi-Fi—a great feature for competitive virtual racing—but Garmin offers a separate adaptor.

The Wahoo Kickr Bike Pro is the indoor trainer of choice for riders seeking the best possible experience—and who have the space for a dedicated setup. At $4,000, it’s like investing in an extra bike that you can’t even ride outside. However, for many riders, the price is worth it since it’s always ready to go. You don’t need to install a bike or connect any devices. Plus, highly corrosive sweat and salt from trainer rides won’t damage your outside bike.

The Kickr Bike Pro adjusts to almost all bike fit measurements. Or, if you had a Guru, Retül, or Trek bike fit, you can plug the dimensions into the Wahoo app for more precise setup. Since the Bike uses virtual shifting, you can program it to any Shimano, SRAM, or Campagnolo drivetrain you want to ride. You can select the gear ratios and the number of teeth per cog.

The Kickr Bike Pro’s incredible ride feel comes from its high-tech flywheel with motor; it adds resistance while simulating the inertia of real-world riding. The Pro provides a coasting feel along with realistic braking and shifting. The system also features a piston-like mechanism that reflects virtual elevation changes by adjusting the angle between the bike and the ground (up to 20% incline and 15% decline).

If the Kickr Bike Pro’s $4,000 price tag is a little out of reach, check out the Kickr Bike Shift. It’s similar to the Pro in adjustment, but ditched the fancy flywheel and gradient-change feature—and it saves you almost $1,500.

Feedback’s Omnium Over-Drive is compact, lightweight (14 pounds), and sets up and breaks down fast. That’s why these portable trainers are ubiquitous in parking lots and team tents at bike races. These same traits also make it a great option for riders with small apartments or training while away from home.

However, this portable trainer isn’t light on features. Two 4-inch magnetic drums provide progressive resistance up to 1,050 watts (at 55 mph). Thanks to its height-adjustable fork mount and sliding base, the Over-Drive accommodates most bikes, wheel sizes, and quick-release or thru-axle configurations. Feedback includes a durable tote bag for storage under a bed, in your garage, or in a car trunk.

The trainer’s compact size makes it easy to carry on a plane as checked luggage (or in your bike bag)—I brought it along many times on trips to Asia and Europe. Plus, the Omnium’s quiet ride won’t disturb neighbors in a hotel room.

Wahoo’s unique-looking Kickr Rollr is a novel approach to indoor trainers. It’s a great option for those who need to install or remove their bike quickly. This makes it easy to use in a pinch, such as when an afternoon thunderstorm rolls in and threatens to cancel your training ride.

At the front, the Rollr features an A-shaped bracket that holds your bike’s front wheel with a tool-free clamp that accommodates tires up to 2.1 inches/53mm wide. At the back, the Rollr’s two drums cradle your bike’s rear tire, and an external flywheel adds resistance.

This design makes it quick and easy to put a bike on the Kickr Rollr, swap out multiple bikes, or share a trainer with other riders. However, we don’t recommend this trainer for riders who do a lot of out-of-the-saddle, high-intensity training or for users who regularly race on Zwift. (A direct-drive trainer will be better suited for these tasks.)

While the Rollr is adjustable for different wheelbases, the adjustment is limited and optimized for road bikes. This means long-wheelbase mountain bikes might not fit (most road or gravel bikes shouldn’t have any issues). Since the trainer doesn’t read power, you must have a power meter to use the Rollr’s smart features.

Direct-drivetrainers attach to your bike’s rear dropouts and replace your rear wheel with a resistance unit. These trainers are typically quieter than other systems, provide more accurate power readings, and are ideal for high-power efforts.

Friction trainers use a roller pressed against your bike’s rear tire. They’re lighter, (usually) more affordable, and more portable than other systems. However, friction trainers can be very noisy and wear out tires.

Rollers are a time-tested indoor riding platform. They use three drums (rollers) that you ride on, so they require balance. While some rollers have resistance, many don’t.

Smart bikes are dedicated indoor training bikes. These trainers are heavy and take up space, but they’re a great option if you have a bigger budget, are tired of taking your bike on/off the trainer, or don’t want to wreck your outdoor bike with sweat and salt.

Typically, a smart trainer is an indoor trainer that can wirelessly communicate power data with a training app on a smartphone or computer. Most smart trainers also work with virtual riding platforms like Zwift by automatically adjusting resistance to simulate changes in terrain.

The popularity of online riding platforms means most newer trainers are “smart” and will both transmit your data and adjust resistance. These features often add to the cost of a new trainer. But prices are falling; you can find connected trainers—such as the Saris M2—for less than $200.

If you want to try Zwift but don’t have a smart trainer, you can still log virtual miles using a Bluetooth speed sensor. Check out our guide to getting started here.

Compatibility: With axle attachment standards and widths frequently changing, check if the trainer you want offers different attachment options (such as thru-axle adaptors, or for direct-attachment trainers, free-hub options). Some trainers come with them. If yours doesn’t, you’ll need to purchase them separately. The Robert Axle Project is my go-to resource for replacement thru-axles and adapters.

Noise: While most manufacturers can get away with using words like “silent” and “virtually silent” to describe the noise level of their trainers, there are other factors to consider, such as the sound your bike’s drivetrain makes as you pedal, and if you use one, the fan that’s whirring away to keep you cool and simulate wind speeds. To get a better idea of how loud “silent” actually is, we used a decibel meter to record the noise levels of each trainer being ridden at 15 and 25 mph. Decibels ranged from 68 (comparable to a vacuum cleaner) to 85 (a diesel truck going 40 mph); the fan alone measured 71. To get an idea of how significant a seemingly minor jump in decibels can be, 70 is twice as loud as 60, and 80 is twice as loud as 70.‌

Stability: Trainer crashes are rare, but not unheard of when you’re going cross-eyed trying to beat your PR on a workout. Typically, the wider the trainer’s base, the more stable it will be. Many have a leveling feature for uneven surfaces.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#8852. The 2026 New York City Marathon Was the Largest Marathon in History

More than 61,000 runners—from ages 18 to 90—crossed the finish line on Sunday.

One of the world's biggest marathons keeps getting bigger. On Sunday, November 1, the 2026 New York City Marathon officially cemented its place in the history books as the largest marathon of all time, surpassing the 2026 London Marathon, which had 59,830 finishers.

According to results released Monday by New York Road Runners (NYRR), 61,146 runners crossed the iconic finish line in Central Park (61,529 started the event). That total blasts past last year’s NYC tally of 59,226 finishers—which followed 2024’s record-breaking field of 55,646—marking the third consecutive year the five-borough race has raised the bar worldwide for mass participation.

This year’s record served as a nice topper for a historic run as it coincided with the 50th anniversary of the five-borough course. When organizers first took the race out of Central Park and onto the streets of Staten Island, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx, and Manhattan in 1976, the event was a bold urban experiment. Five decades later, it is an epicenter of the global running community, with waves of marathoners streaming from the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge from 8 a.m. until well after dark.

While tens of thousands of age-groupers, charity runners, and first-timers chased personal glory, the pro fields delivered plenty of fireworks at the front of the pack:

There were plenty of other milestones as well.

#8851. 15-Minute Beginner-Friendly Yoga, No Flexibility Required

Taylor Lorenz—known online as Taylor’s Tracks—is a certified yoga teacher with more than 800 hours of training in vinyasa, hatha, and yin yoga. Here, she guides you through a practice suitable for any experience level with yoga.

No matter how long you’ve been practicing yoga, returning to the basics is always beneficial. This yoga for beginners practice features a flow full of repeating shapes, including forward bends, side stretches, and gentle twists, all supported by modifications and props, if needed, to ensure that the poses work for any body, regardless of how flexible or inflexible you might be.

Listen to your body, breathe slowly, and enjoy the flow.

Keep two yoga blocks or block-like props (think: thick books) close by. These can help you access poses that your body might otherwise object to so that you can still benefit.

Begin kneeling in Thunderbolt Pose. If this doesn’t feel comfortable for your ankles or knees, slide a block beneath your sit bones to minimize the pressure. If it’s still uncomfortable, you can skip this pose.

Come onto your hands and knees with your shoulders over your wrists, hips stacked over your knees. With your next inhalation, lower your belly, lift your chin and chest, and arch your back in Cow Pose.

Exhale as you round your back and tuck your chin in Cat Pose.

Repeat Cat and Cow 3 times each, moving with the pace of your breath.

As you round into your last Cat Pose, tuck your toes and sink your sit bones back toward your heels.

Shift your shoulders forward over your wrists. Keep your toes tucked and with your next exhalation, lift your knees away from the mat and reach your hips up and back in Downward-Facing Dog. Think of your body being in an inverted V shape.

Feel free to bend you knees as much as you need to for the pose to feel comfortable along your hamstrings and lower back. You can also place blocks underneath your hands.

Stay here for 3 cycles of breath, pedaling out your feet by bending one knee and straightening the other, and then switching. You can also sway a little from side to side or simply stay in stillness.

Walk your feet toward your hands to come into a Standing Forward Bend. Relax your neck and let your head hang. You can let your hands dangle or rest your fingertips on the mat.

You can also place a block beneath each of your hands. You might want to bend your knees slightly to ease the strain on your hamstrings or lower back.

Inhale and start to lift your chest slightly, bringing your fingertips to your shins and lengthening your spine in Halfway Lift. Keep the back of your neck long and stare straight down at the mat. You can also keep your fingertips on your blocks here.

Inhale to rise as you come to standing, sweeping your arms out toward the sides and overhead. Bring your hands together at heart center in Mountain Pose.

With your next inhalation, reach your arms back toward the sky. Grab your left wrist with your right hand and guide your left wrist up and over to the right in a Standing Side Bend. Feel the stretch along your left side body.

Inhale as you come back through center and exhale as you twist toward the right, with your left arm reaching forward and your right arm reaching toward the back of the mat. Gaze toward the right.

When you’re ready, come back through center before repeating Standing Side Bend and Standing Twist on the opposite side.

Inhale to come back through center, exhale to Standing Forward Bend.

With your next exhalation, step back to Downward-Facing Dog.

From Downward Dog, step your right foot between your hands. Lower your left knee to the mat and sweep your arms overhead in Low Lunge.

Use our right hand to grab hold of your left wrist again, guiding it up and over in a side bend while keeping your balance in your Low Lunge. Press through your right foot and your back knee to help find steadiness.

Inhale as you come back through center and exhale as you twist toward the right, with your left arm reaching forward and your right arm reaching toward the back of the mat.

Inhale both arms back to center, palms facing forward. With your exhalation, bring your hands to the ground or to blocks on either side of your front foot. Start to straighten your front leg, sliding your right heel away from you and flexing your right foot in Half Splits.

You can keep your hands underneath your shoulders or slide them forward closer to your feet for a more intense shoulder and side body stretch.

With your next inhalation, come back through Low Lunge. Exhale, Downward-Facing Dog.

Reach your left leg to the sky and repeat the following poses on the opposite side:

Step toward the front of the mat and fold forward in Standing Forward Bend.

Inhale, reaching your arms up and overhead with your big toes touching or hip-distance apart. With your exhalation, reach your arms alongside your head and sit your hips back in Chair Pose.

Keep your arms high and begin to draw your left knee toward your chest, foot flexed. With your exhalation, step your left foot back into a High Lunge.

With your right hand, grab your left wrist, and reaching up and over toward the right side.

Inhale to come back through center. Exhale to open your arms toward the right, left arm forward, right arm back.

Inhale to reach both arms toward the sky. Exhale to straighten the right leg, hinging at your hips and folding your chest toward your right leg with your back heel lifted in a less intense variation of Pyramid Pose. Bring your hands to the mat to frame your front foot, your shin, or blocks on either side of your foot. Take 1 full breath here.

When you’re ready, step your left foot up to meet your right in Standing Forward Bend.

Inhale, reaching your arms up and overhead. With your exhalation, keep your arms high and sit your hips back in Chair Pose.

Repeat the following poses on the opposite side:

Gently land your knees to your mat and move through hands and knee into a seated position. Bring the soles of your feet together and let your knees fall out toward the sides in Bound Angle Pose. If this feels too intense, slide a blocks beneath each knee for extra support.

Stay here, or round your spine and walk your hands forward as you bring your chest toward your toes. Let your body find where it wants to be rather than force the shape. Take 5 breaths in your chosen position.

When you’re ready, move through a seated position to come all the way onto your back in Savasana. Feel free to add blocks beneath your knees for extra support.

Stay here for 3-5 minutes or as long as you’d like.

Push yourself upright to a comfortable seat. Bring your hands together at heart center, bow your head, and thank yourself for showing up on your mat today.

#8850. What Happens When Grief Derails Your Triathlon Training

Rachel Olson wins 2026 Ironman 70.3 São Paulo after struggling to train through the grief of losing her mother in November 2024. (Photo: Romulo Cruz/Ironman)

In late September, Rachel Olson crossed the finish line first at Ironman 70.3 São Paulo, nearly 10 minutes ahead of her nearest competitor. The race, by her own admission, was “not spectacular” for the longtime pro triathlete. But the support that followed was. The crowd embraced her, and athletes and fans who had followed her story cheered a little louder, as though they knew what it took just to get her to the start line.

Because in the months after her mother Janis died in November 2024 of liver disease, Olson could barely bring herself to work out. She did not want to disappear from triathlon. But she’d go to the pool and just sit on the edge and cry. She’d hop on her bike and feel a sudden urge to turn around. Running, always an easy way to manage big emotions, became a chore.

Then her body began to rebel: digestive issues, mysterious inflammation, bone-deep exhaustion, muscles that wouldn’t recover.

“My body was basically screaming at me that something was wrong, like it was constantly fighting something,” said Olson, 35, who lives in Boulder with her fiancé, fellow pro triathlete Andre Lopes. “Your mind is telling you to process, and your body is telling you to slow down.”

For endurance athletes, the instinct after a loss is often to train through the emotional pain. The adage goes that exercise helps with grief: Get outside, move your body, clear your head. Sometimes it does. But for Olson and many others, the very thing that once gave life structure can become one more demand on a body and mind already stretched thin.

“Grief doesn’t just live in the mind. It’s in the chest, in the restlessness, in this low-grade energy that has nowhere obvious to go,” said Kenza Haddock, president and co-founder of Oceanic Counseling Group in Murrells Inlet, South Carolina. “Endurance sport can tip from processing grief into outrunning it, using exhaustion to stay ahead of the feeling rather than move through it. It can just leave you more numb.”

Plenty of endurance athletes have turned grief into a mission. In August 2026, Matthew Hollingham, a 25-year-old doctoral student at Penn State, created an “Arctic Circle to Africa” triathlon in memory of his late fiancée Lovisa Arnesson-Cronhamre, who was killed in a hit-and-run while jogging on campus. Over 61 days and 3,545 miles, he swam in a lake above the Arctic Circle, ran a marathon a day for 37 days, and cycled just over 110 miles a day for 23. He raised more than $40,000 for two charities and kept her memory present.

Others have taken similar routes; at the 2026 London Marathon, Laura Coleman-Day, a 33-year-old mother from Lincolnshire in the U.K., went viral for changing into her wedding dress and running the final miles in it as a dedication to her late husband, Xander.

This kind of public mission can be cathartic, says Hilary Bucell, a psychotherapist and lecturer at Columbia University.

“Engaging in something like triathlon can become a ritualized space where the recognition of the loss is welcomed and at the same time, the sport’s necessity for present moment awareness also helps athletes acknowledge new life experiences continuing now beyond the loss,” she said.

Of course, racing to honor a loved one doesn’t erase grief — it just gives you a place to put it. It can also offer a healthy distraction from the deep ache of a devastating loss.

Some aren’t able to navigate their grief in such a public and profound way. There are those like Olson whose grief hits the body hard enough to derail training. In 2023, Gustav Iden, the 2022 Ironman World Champion, ended his season early to heal and regroup after the death of his mother, revealing “it was very emotional, and it was hard to find joy in training after that.” (He returned to racing about a year later.)

As one of her mother’s main caretakers, Olson spent two years before her death flying to her hometown in Texas for doctor’s appointments. Triathlon took a backseat: She parted ways with her coach and scaled back her training. Even when she did have time to work out, anxiety followed.

“I would think, ‘Am I going to be out on a bike ride and get a phone call saying she’s in the hospital? Are things going to go downhill?’”

After Janis died, that anxiety turned physical. Olson was never diagnosed with one specific issue, but testing showed elevated inflammation markers and low ferritin, requiring an iron infusion.

“Ultimately, I think my body was responding to trauma. It felt like I had an illness,” she said. “Trying to perform in a body that felt completely foreign to me was incredibly difficult. I didn’t understand why my body wasn’t doing what it had done before.”

Research suggests that grief can affect the body as well as the mind. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) lists impaired immune response and increased mortality from heart disease, especially in older, widowed patients, among the physical complications. The effects may vary, as not everyone experiences the same physical response.

Part of the explanation may lie in how the brain processes the loss of a loved one through interconnected systems involved in emotion, threat detection, and the regulation of stress hormones. Grief can flood the body with inflammatory signals. and increase cortisol, the steroid hormone produced by the adrenal glands that regulates the body’s response to stress.

“Grief is a neurological event that impacts your ability to learn and remember things, attend to things, and impacts your mood,” said Wilfred van Gorp, a Manhattan-based board-certified neuropsychologist. “Losing someone keeps your amygdala on high alert and elevates cortisol. It impacts you in your body as well as your mind.”

Grief and stress can also disrupt communication between the brain and the gut, which may contribute to everything from irritable bowel syndrome to acid reflux to ulcers, according to research.

For Olson, whose stomach swelled within days of her mother’s death, that brain-gut link was obvious.

“Only two days after [she passed], I woke up, and my stomach was distended about five inches. And then I kind of exploded in inflammation weight,” she shared. “Trying to get that down is not an easy process.”

Still, Olson pushed on. She’d qualified for her first Ironman World Championship slated for about 10 months after Janis died. She wanted to race there to honor her mom. She also didn’t want to lose her identity as a triathlete. Her training “wasn’t even close” to peak levels. In Kona, her stomach rebelled on the bike. After vomiting for three hours, she pulled out soon after starting the run.

“I held onto triathlon so tightly even though my body wasn’t ready. My mind wasn’t ready,” Olson said. “I kept pushing because I wanted it so badly. I attached too much weight to needing training [and racing] to go well and needing something in my life to be OK. Looking back, I realize I didn’t have to be OK.”

After Kona, Olson took a break. She focused on her other jobs as a triathlon coach and as a sales rep, and on envisioning what her wedding to Lopes could look like without her mom.

“I decided I wasn’t going to think about triathlon for a couple of weeks,” she shared. “If I still wanted it afterward, great. If I didn’t, that was OK, too.”

Spoiler: She still loved it. With the fog lifted, Olson saw a different future in the sport, starting with a new coach, Kasper Pedersen, who could build a sustainable load and understand her fragile state.

“I looked for a coach who understands that life happens,” said Olson. “Kasper is great at helping me push my boundaries, but he also knows that I may need to go at my own pace.”

They’re keeping her training volume relatively low as she re-establishes a baseline and repairs her frayed central nervous system.

“I really wanted to make my body and mind think, ‘This is fun. This is helping us,’ rather than setting off alarm bells every time I went out,” Olson shared. “There are still days where I have to take some time off. … Grief really is a roller coaster. But overall, we’ve done a really good job of figuring out what is working.”

Talking about it helps, too, though it doesn’t come easily. Olson describes her grief as a “cloud over her personal life,” and opening up about it has cost her: One friend drifted away, unable to understand what she was going through. Olson wonders if she was simply too much to handle. Still, she finds solace in speaking out, and in being a voice for others who may be grieving alone.

“As athletes, we want to put difficult things in the back of our minds and keep going,” she said. “But I’m glad I can be a voice for other people who are going through the same so they feel less alone than they think they are.”

If her recent win in Brazil is any sign, Olson is rounding a bend toward healing, with an approach to triathlon (and life) that’s less about control and more about leaning into the process, however unpredictable and messy it may be.

“I feel like I’m a different person than I was before [my mom died]. It will always feel like a part of me has been ripped away. But I also know that there’s literally no pain that hurts as bad as what I went through,” she said. “So I’ll keep telling myself, ‘Yes, I can do this thing.’”

#8848. A 24-Year-Old Runner Died After a Medical Emergency in the Final Miles of the NYC Marathon

Rachel Apa was running her first marathon to raise money for Parkinson's research in memory of her grandfather.

Rachel Apa was nearing the end of her first New York City Marathon when she collapsed in Central Park on Sunday, November 1. The 24-year-old had spent months putting in the work needed to conquer 26.2 miles, but never made it across the finish line. Instead, she was taken to Mount Sinai Medical Center, where she died later that night.

Apa, a Bucknell University alum who lived in central Pennsylvania, came to New York to run with Parkinson's Foundation Champions, raising money in memory of her grandfather, who died from the disease in 2022.

According to reporting from The New York Times, the medical emergency happened around 1:30 p.m. close to Mile 24, around 85th Street, right as runners enter the final stretch through Central Park. Several spectators rushed to help and began performing CPR. New York Road Runners medical staff arrived shortly after, and tried to resuscitate her with a defibrillator before paramedics took her to the hospital.

Her parents had been keeping up with Rachel throughout the race as she made her way through the five boroughs, though from different locations. Michelle Apa, her mother, was in New York and watched Rachel run through Queens at Mile 14, while Steve Apa, her father, was back home in Lewisberry, Pennsylvania, following her progress through the marathon's tracking app.

Steve had been texting his daughter throughout the day. According to messages he shared with the Times, Rachel sent an "Ow" text at Mile 18, followed by a double "Ow ow" at Mile 19. She kept moving through the course, although her dad received no replies after that. As she reached Mile 23 on the app, Steve sent another message: "Final stretch." Rachel never responded.

Michelle eventually made her way to Central Park, reportedly arriving just as the ambulance carrying her daughter was leaving, per the Times. Doctors spent hours trying to save Rachel. Steve told the newspaper she was pronounced dead around 9:40 p.m.

"It's unfathomable," he told the newspaper. "Perfect health, perfect shape, 24 years old."

Steve told the Times that his daughter died from rhabdomyolysis, which occurs when damaged muscle tissue breaks down and releases substances into the bloodstream. The condition can cause serious kidney damage and, according to the Cleveland Clinic, can be triggered by extreme physical exertion.

An official cause of death had not been established as of Tuesday, November 3, with CBS New York reporting that the city's medical examiner was still investigating.

Sunday marked the marathon's first runner death following a medical incident since 2024, according to NYRR. The organization released a statement Monday:

"We are deeply saddened by the death of one of our runners following yesterday's race. Our thoughts and sincere sympathies are with the runner's family, friends, and the entire running community."

Before the marathon, Apa explained her decision to run on her fundraising page, sharing how much her grandfather influenced her love of sports and why supporting the Parkinson's Foundation mattered to her.

"He taught me to stay active, push my limits, and embrace challenges, shaping my love for sports and movement," she wrote.

Apa explained that watching him lose his mobility after his Parkinson's diagnosis had made her want to help others facing the disease. She wanted to use her first marathon to help others affected by it, raising money and awareness in the process “for research, better care, and a cure.”

As of 5 p.m. ET Tuesday, the page had exceeded her $4,000 goal, and reflected more than $28,000 in donations.

Sean Abrams was the Senior Editor, Growth and Engagement at Men’s Health. He’s a former hip hop dancer who likes long walks on the beach and large glasses of tequila. You can find his previous work at Maxim, Elite Daily, and AskMen.

Picture this: you've just landed in Honolulu after a long transcontinental flight. You've got four days on Maui planned, and then a few nights on Kauai before heading home. The problem? Those interisland flights add up fast — Hawaiian Airlines will gladly charge you $150–$250 *per person* for a 20-to-40-minute hop between islands. For a family of four, that's easily $600–$1,000 in airfare just to island-hop, on top of everything else you've already spent to get to Hawaii. Now imagine paying 7,500 HawaiianMiles per person instead — miles you transferred from your American Express Membership Rewards account at a 1:1 ratio just a day or two before booking. Suddenly, that $150–$250 ticket costs you points worth less than a nice dinner. At 3.3 cents per point on the high end, you're extracting extraordinary value from miles that most people leave sitting in an account doing nothing. This is what the ChooseFI community means when we talk about finding pricing inefficiencies in loyalty programs. Hawaiian Airlines prices these interisland segments on a dynamic award chart — but because these are short, regional hops operated almost entirely on 717s and A321s between islands most people aren't cross-shopping for redemptions, the program hasn't inflated the price the way major international carriers have. The sweet spot holds. The math is simple and satisfying: a cash ticket from Honolulu (HNL) to Kahului, Maui (OGG) or Lihue, Kauai (LIH) typically runs $100–$250. You're redeeming 7,500 miles to cover that cost, which means you're getting **1.3 to 3.3 cents per point** in value — above what most programs deliver on domestic redemptions. And because Hawaiian charges **zero fuel surcharges** on its own-operated flights, every mile goes toward the ticket price, not toward fees. For the FI-minded traveler who planned a multi-island Hawaii trip anyway, this redemption doesn't just save money — it reframes how you think about points. These aren't bonuses. They're a currency, and knowing where to spend them is the skill.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: HawaiianMiles prices interisland flights at a flat 7,500 miles in economy, and that price is shockingly stable relative to what these tickets actually cost in cash.

Here's why this works as a pricing inefficiency. Hawaiian Airlines operates a near-monopoly on interisland travel in Hawaii. There's limited true competition for these routes (go! Mokulele operates turboprops on some routes, but Hawaiian dominates the jet service). Because cash demand is inelastic — visitors need to get between islands — Hawaiian charges a premium in cash. But the HawaiianMiles award program hasn't kept pace with those cash price increases in the same aggressive way that programs like United MileagePlus or Delta SkyMiles have. The result: 7,500 miles per segment, consistently, while cash prices climb.

Now let's talk about how you actually get those miles into your account.

The primary transfer path the ChooseFI community uses is American Express Membership Rewards → HawaiianMiles at a 1:1 ratio. If you have the Amex Gold, Platinum, or a no-annual-fee Amex Everyday card earning MR points, you can transfer directly to Hawaiian. Transfer speed is 1–2 days — not instant, so plan accordingly and don't wait until the last minute.

Two other paths exist if you're working with different currencies:

One critical nuance: HawaiianMiles are earned primarily through flying, not credit card spend. Hawaiian does have a co-branded credit card, but it's not a top earner for most people's daily spend. This means your primary accumulation strategy is transfer partners — Amex MR and Bilt are your best levers.

Another key detail: Hawaiian miles never expire. This matters because you can slowly accumulate miles across multiple statement cycles, transfer when you're ready to book, and not feel rushed. There's no expiration clock running against you.

Finally, the no fuel surcharges policy is a genuine differentiator. Many programs — particularly those involving European carriers — tack on $300–$600 in surcharges that gut your redemption's net value. HawaiianMiles charges no fuel surcharges on Hawaiian-operated flights. Your 7,500 miles covers the flight. Taxes and fees on interisland tickets are minimal, often just a few dollars. What you see is what you get.

Go to hawaiianairlines.com and use the 'Book' tool, selecting 'Reward Travel' as your travel type. Enter your route — for example, HNL to OGG (Honolulu to Kahului, Maui) or HNL to LIH (Honolulu to Lihue, Kauai). Plug in your desired travel date and search. You're looking for economy award space priced at 7,500 miles. Availability on interisland routes is almost always wide open — this is one of the best availability scores (5/5) of any sweet spot in this guide series, but it costs nothing to confirm before you transfer.

If you don't have a HawaiianMiles account, create one at hawaiianairlines.com — it takes about two minutes and is free. Note your HawaiianMiles number. You'll need it for the transfer step.

From Amex Membership Rewards: Log into your Amex account, navigate to 'Membership Rewards,' select 'Transfer Points,' and choose Hawaiian Airlines HawaiianMiles as the destination. Enter your HawaiianMiles number and the number of miles you want to transfer (at minimum, 7,500 per person you're booking). Transfers process in 1–2 days.

From Bilt Rewards: Log into your Bilt app or biltrewards.com, navigate to 'Redeem,' select 'Transfer to Airline Partner,' and choose Hawaiian Airlines at 1:1. Same 1–2 day transfer window.

From Marriott Bonvoy: Use this only as a last resort due to the 3:1 ratio. Navigate to Bonvoy's transfer portal and select HawaiianMiles. Allow up to 5 days.

Once your miles land (check your HawaiianMiles account balance), return to hawaiianairlines.com, log in, and re-run your award search. Select the flight you want, confirm the 7,500-mile price, and proceed through checkout. Taxes on interisland awards are typically just a few dollars — no fuel surcharges apply.

HawaiianMiles opens its booking window 330 days out. If you're planning a Hawaii trip far in advance and have specific flight times in mind, you can search and book early. That said, given the excellent availability on these routes, booking 2–4 weeks out is usually fine.

This is rare for interisland routes, but if it happens, try: searching adjacent dates, looking at different departure times on the same route, or checking alternate routing (e.g., OGG to LIH instead of HNL to LIH directly). Interisland availability doesn't fluctuate the way transatlantic business class does.

Card links may earn ChooseFI a commission. See our advertiser disclosure.

Let's make this concrete. You're planning a two-week Hawaii trip for two people. You've booked your Honolulu arrival flight separately, and now you need to connect the dots between islands: Honolulu (HNL) to Kahului, Maui (OGG) mid-trip, and then Maui (OGG) to Lihue, Kauai (LIH) before heading home.

The cash price check: Pull up hawaiianairlines.com and look at what these tickets retail for. On a typical mid-trip travel day, the HNL→OGG segment is priced at $189 per person. The OGG→LIH hop runs $149 per person. For two travelers, that's $676 in cash — before you've bought a single plate of shave ice.

The points price: Each segment costs 7,500 HawaiianMiles per person in economy. Two passengers, two flights: 30,000 HawaiianMiles total, plus roughly $10–$20 in taxes and fees across both bookings. No fuel surcharges.

The CPP calculation: You're replacing $676 in cash spending with 30,000 miles. That's 2.25 cents per point — well above the 0.8–1.2 cpp you'd expect on typical HawaiianMiles redemptions, and solidly within the 1.3–3.3 cpp sweet spot range for this redemption.

What the experience looks like: Hawaiian's interisland product is no-frills — these are 20-to-40-minute flights on Boeing 717s. You won't get a meal or premium service. But you will get a reliable, on-time carrier, clean aircraft, and the undeniable satisfaction of hopping between two of the most beautiful island destinations on Earth without opening your wallet at the gate.

For the ChooseFI traveler, the win isn't the in-flight experience — it's the mental accounting shift. You budgeted for interisland flights; now that budget goes to a sunset sailing charter or a snorkeling excursion instead. The points paid for the planes. The cash funds the memories.

Do: Transfer Points in the Right Batch Size HawaiianMiles doesn't allow you to transfer partial miles back out, so calculate exactly how many you need before initiating a transfer. For two passengers on two flights, that's 30,000 miles. Transfer exactly that amount — or a small buffer — rather than dumping your entire MR balance into a program you may not use frequently.

Do: Use Amex MR or Bilt as Your Primary Earning Strategy Since HawaiianMiles are earned primarily through flying, your accumulation plan should center on transferable currencies. The Amex Gold Card (4x on dining and groceries) and Amex Platinum (5x on flights) are elite MR earners. Bilt's no-annual-fee card earning on rent is underused by the ChooseFI community for exactly this kind of transfer.

Do: Search for Availability Before You Transfer This is worth repeating as a pro tip because new points travelers make this mistake constantly. Transfer speeds are 1–2 days for Amex MR and Bilt. Don't transfer points and then discover the flight you wanted is sold out. Always confirm availability first, then transfer, then book immediately once miles land.

Avoid: Using Marriott Bonvoy for This Transfer At a 3:1 ratio, you'd spend 22,500 Bonvoy points for a 7,500-mile award. Bonvoy points are worth approximately 0.7–0.9 cpp on their own best redemptions. The math doesn't hold here — save your Bonvoy points for hotel redemptions.

Do: Consider the Merger Context Hawaiian Airlines is in the process of merging with Alaska Airlines, and HawaiianMiles may eventually transition into Alaska Mileage Plan. Pay attention to program announcements. This could change transfer partners, award pricing, or program structure. The current sweet spot exists now — book it while the program operates under its current rules.

Avoid: Waiting for a 'Better' Redemption on These Miles HawaiianMiles are a limited-use currency. They're excellent for interisland and mainland-to-Hawaii flights, but they don't transfer to other airlines and don't unlock international business class sweet spots. If you've got miles in this program, use them for exactly what they're designed for — Hawaiian flights — rather than letting them sit hoping for a better opportunity that may never come.

Do: Book Multiple Segments in a Single Trip If you're doing a true multi-island itinerary, every interisland hop is 7,500 miles. Three islands means two hops — 15,000 miles per person. Plan your island sequence to minimize backtracking, and book all segments at once once your miles transfer.

Make multi-island trips affordable with the right points strategy

Most visitors to Hawaii stick to one island because interisland flights add $100-$400+ per person to the trip cost. By using points for these short hops, you unlock a fundamentally different Hawaii experience — island-hopping from Oahu to Maui to the Big Island to Kauai without the airfare costs stacking up. This is a multiplier strategy: you are not just saving on one flight, you are enabling an entirely different type of trip. Combining a points-funded mainland-to-Hawaii flight with points-funded interisland hops creates a nearly free (in cash) multi-island Hawaiian vacation.

Decide which islands you want to visit and in what order. The most common combinations are Oahu + Maui, Oahu + Big Island, or a three-island itinerary. Map out how many interisland hops you need so you know the total points required.

Check Hawaiian Airlines (7,500 miles each way), Southwest (variable, typically 4,000-8,000 points), and United (5,000-7,500 miles) for each interisland segment. Southwest often offers the best flexibility with no change fees and no blackout dates.

For Hawaiian Airlines, transfer Amex Membership Rewards. For Southwest, earn Rapid Rewards directly or transfer from Chase (transfer to Southwest is currently limited). For United segments, transfer from Chase or use Turkish Miles&Smiles for even lower pricing.

Book each interisland hop as a separate one-way award. This gives you maximum flexibility to mix airlines and optimize pricing per segment. One-way awards have no penalty compared to round trips on these short routes.

Align your interisland hops with your arrival and departure flights. Arrive on one island and depart from a different one (open-jaw booking) to avoid backtracking. For example, arrive Honolulu, hop to Maui, depart Maui to the mainland.

Hawaiian Airlines has the most extensive interisland network and offers the most daily frequencies. Southwest Airlines also operates key interisland routes (Honolulu-Maui, Honolulu-Kona, Honolulu-Lihue). United flies select interisland segments as well. Each airline has different award pricing and transfer partner access.

Hawaiian Airlines interisland awards typically price at 7,500 HawaiianMiles each way. Southwest varies by cash fare but generally costs 4,000-8,000 Rapid Rewards points each way for interisland hops. United interisland segments can be booked for 5,000-7,500 miles using various Star Alliance partner programs.

Yes, especially when booking multiple hops. A family of four making two interisland hops at $150 each way would spend $1,200 in cash. Converting that to points frees up significant cash for accommodations, activities, and dining. The per-point value (1.5-2.5 cents) is reasonable, and the trip flexibility gained is substantial.

A popular strategy is to fly into Honolulu (Oahu), hop to Maui for beaches and Haleakala, then continue to the Big Island (Kona) for volcanoes and snorkeling, and optionally finish on Kauai for dramatic scenery. Each hop is 30-60 minutes. Allow 2-3 days minimum per island.

This redemption was built for families and couples planning a multi-island Hawaii vacation — full stop. If you're visiting multiple islands (which most Hawaii first-timers and repeat visitors do), you're already mentally budgeting for interisland flights. This sweet spot simply redirects that cash budget back into your pocket and replaces it with points.

Families get a 5/5 Family Friendly score here for good reason: availability is wide open, booking is simple, and the economics scale beautifully. Four people, two hops = 60,000 miles to cover potentially $1,200+ in interisland airfare. That's an extraordinary displacement of vacation cash.

Beginners are explicitly welcomed by this redemption's design. There's no partner airline complexity, no fuel surcharge math to calculate, no routing rules to decode. You search on Hawaiian's website, you transfer points, you book. The 5/5 Beginner Friendly and Easy to Book scores reflect that this is genuinely one of the simplest award redemptions you can execute.

Minimum points needed: 7,500 HawaiianMiles per person per segment. For a solo traveler doing two hops, that's 15,000 miles. For a family of four doing two hops, that's 60,000 miles.

This is NOT for: Travelers who don't have an Amex MR or Bilt account and no path to earning HawaiianMiles quickly. It's also not ideal for travelers who only need a single interisland flight — the opportunity cost of setting up the transfer relationship for 7,500 miles may not be worth it unless you're already accumulating MR points for other redemptions.

This redemption earns a **Beginner** rating — and it genuinely deserves it. In a world of waitlists, fuel surcharges, routing rules, and phone-only bookings, Hawaiian interisland awards are refreshingly clean. **What makes it easy:** Award availability is consistently excellent (5/5). The booking portal is functional and user-friendly. There are no fuel surcharges to calculate. Miles never expire, so there's no pressure. You can complete the entire redemption — from transfer initiation to confirmed booking — in about 48 hours. **The one genuine friction point:** Earning HawaiianMiles isn't as straightforward as earning Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex MR. Hawaiian doesn't have a widely-used co-branded credit card for most people's everyday spend. This means you're dependent on transfer partners, and the Amex MR and Bilt paths are your primary options. If you don't have either, this redemption becomes harder to access. **Tip 1:** Start with an Amex card that earns Membership Rewards — the Amex Gold is the ChooseFI community favorite for everyday earning. Once you're accumulating MR points, you have a direct path to Hawaiian via a 1:1 transfer. **Tip 2:** Always search award availability before transferring. It takes 30 seconds and protects you from the one mistake that could derail an otherwise smooth booking. **Tip 3:** Don't overthink the merger situation. Hawaiian and Alaska remain separate programs today. Book what's in front of you. If you can earn Amex MR points, you can execute this redemption. It's the perfect first award booking for a ChooseFI member who wants to see how the system works without risking complexity.

Interisland awards are the key that unlocks multi-island Hawaii vacations without the stacking airfare costs that keep most travelers on a single island. At 7,500-10,000 miles per hop, the points cost is modest, and the trip transformation is significant. Whether you use Hawaiian Airlines miles, Southwest Rapid Rewards, or United partner programs, the strategy is the same: let points handle the short hops so your cash stays in your pocket for experiences. Combined with a points-funded mainland-to-Hawaii flight, interisland awards make a multi-island Hawaiian vacation one of the most achievable aspirational trips in travel rewards.

#8845. The 7 Best Jogging Strollers for Every Active Parent

These strollers combine comfort, convenience, and style. They’re perfect for moms and dads trying to get a workout in.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Getting out for a run as a parent of a little one is made infinitely easier with a great jogging stroller. As a running mom, I spent countless hours behind my kids, and now my nieces and nephews lacing up and getting behind a stroller for my own mental and physical health and giving my siblings a much-needed respite (I even bring back treats).

I’ve since made running my job, and have had the opportunity to test dozens of running strollers over the years, and let me tell you, they are not all the same. The range of quality and ride between them can be pretty bananas, and as someone who tends toward higher mileage, it took me a long time to find one that I loved.

Thankfully, jogging strollers have evolved a lot since my first runs with my baby over a decade ago, and now there is a great jogging stroller for everyone no matter your height, running style, surfaces you run on, or miles you’ll be logging. There are strollers that work as both running and everyday strollers, luxury running strollers, multisport strollers that can hit the snow, be towed by a bicycle, or pushed on your own steam, and there are high-tech jogging strollers ready to rack up at the races.

Every year, I dedicate hundreds of hours to testing jogging strollers. I run with kids aged roughly 7 months to 3 years on tracks, pavement, highly groomed trails, boardwalks, and even those charming New York sidewalks. Each stroller clocks at least 40 miles under my watch through all sorts of conditions—rain, snow, sunshine, you name it, we’re out there. Snack testing is a must for cleanability checks, naturally.

Storage? I’ve crammed everything imaginable into the baskets on these. Brakes get a relentless workout. I've folded, unfolded, and hauled these things all over the tri-state area. Airports? Been there, done that (huge mistake, by the way). Here’s my travel tip: check it in a stroller travel bag and thank me later.

Beyond the specs, it’s about the feel. How easy is it to push and steer, even one-handed? And since my nieces and nephews are my precious cargo, their comfort is paramount. We log countless miles, and I see firsthand how happy they are (or aren’t) in each stroller. Some provide a dream ride, others unleash their inner tiny terrors. Basically, I get the real 411 on what works and what doesn't.

Thule makes some of the best tech and outdoor gear on the market, and this stroller is a shining example of the brand. It’s somehow both rugged and elegant, providing the runner with easy, light-touch steering and braking. I was a huge fan of the two previous iterations of this stroller, but this version has surpassed my expectations. I always had issues with the length and size of the canopy, and the tilted position of the seat. But this version sits more upright and has a more generous canopy than its predecessors, making it more comfortable for your little one.

The pneumatic tires are fab and give the stroller a lot of give to glide over difficult terrain like boardwalks, bumpy tracks, and even some trails. I took this beast out on the jankiest boardwalk in all of the land—Rockaway Beach in Queens, New York, and not only did my little nephew fall asleep and stay asleep (and secure) in the stroller even as I almost tripped a dozen times, he fell asleep so deeply that he actually transferred from the stroller to the car seat without a stir.

The storage basket is a decent size, but I do wish it was mesh material, which sand and other dirt could fall through. Also, given that it’s a solid fabric and not mesh, I’d expect it to have a larger weight limit. As it is, 15 pounds is all you can carry beneath. That being said, there are tons of accessories, including handle bags that increase storage capacity and convenience.

I love the twisting hand brake on the Thule. It is a less-abrupt stop than a traditional hand brake, giving you more control. The foot brake is easily operated as well, though disengaging the brakes should not be done in sandals or bare feet.

As for the car seat attachment and available bassinet, both are great, but they do come at an extra price, and the Thule UG3 is bulky for every day. However, it’s such a nice ride, and since the front wheel locks in place and unlocks for easy turning, it is usable as an everyday stroller.

Finding any stroller for under $200 is a feat, especially right now. For families on a budget, the Baby Trend Expedition Jogger is a fantastic option that doesn’t skimp on features. Surprisingly, it includes multiple parent and child drink trays, an accessory often sold separately with more expensive models, adding a bit of convenience. (However, when running, skip the hard cups for the toddlers for safety.)

For the price, the ride is smooth and capable of handling casual jogs and everyday outings. However, it’s worth noting that the overall build quality and components feel a bit flimsier compared to higher-end strollers. The fabrics are a bit scratchier, and the frame and accessories are just not the same.

That said, it’s still a solid stroller with a lot of potential for families. It’s probably not going to withstand the same high mileage or rigorous use as its pricier counterparts, but it’s ideal for those with less intense running routines. Also, it’s specifically designed to be compatible with Baby Trend infant car seats, which is something to keep in mind when considering your overall travel system.

So you don’t want to store a stroller for every occasion? I get it. I live in Brooklyn and understand the limits of small spaces. Enter the solution to your problems: The Guava Roam is a fabulous compact everyday and jogging stroller known for its easy maneuverability and relatively compact fold. It features broad car seat compatibility via its adapters for various brands including Graco, Nuna, UppaBaby, Cybex, Chicco, and Britax. It has one of the smallest footprints both folded and unfolded, and while it’s a bit on the heavy side at 28.5 pounds, the way it folds makes it easy to lug around and stash in your trunk.

But the diminutive size and convenience aren’t the only things that make this an outstanding option for families and runners. My favorite bit about this stroller is the fact that you can lock and unlock the front wheel via a control at the handlebar. It’s genius. I have no earthly clue why more stroller companies aren’t doing this.

I’m also a huge fan of the independent suspension on this stroller that settles and levels as you hit large divots, giving the passenger a smooth, easy ride.

The seat on this stroller is our 3-year-old tester’s favorite, with the five-point harness that’s “not pinchy” and the seat “nice on your booty.” I like the accessory kit near the adjustable handlebar that fits your drink, your phone, your wallet, and at least four mini bags of gummy Nerd clusters (my running fuel of choice).

The stroller isn’t perfect, but it’s so good, you can almost overlook the shallow undercarriage basket and the fact it’s lacking a hand brake. Ideally, I’d love for this stroller to also have pneumatic tires for longer runs and better shock absorption, but the whole thing is just so convenient, its positives easily outweigh its negatives.

I’ve hauled about a gajillion strollers in and out of car trunks, and I know which ones claim to be compact when folded, and which really are. The Cybex Avi Spin is actually a compact jogging stroller. It has a unique way of folding that allows you to either do a basic, one-handed compact fold, or go all the way, and remove the tires first, and then fold it into something that’s around backpack-sized.

The ride is lovely for the jogger, with an adjustable handlebar (it requires two hands to adjust), soft, moisture-wicking grip, and lockable front wheel with an easy deceleration hand brake. It coasts over ruts and bumps really well, but it’s by no means going to hit any trails and remain stable. Jogging strollers aren’t really built for that, by and large.

It cleans up beautifully as well, with removable, machine-washable fabrics, including the UPF 50+-rated canopy. Just pretreat the fabric, wash on gentle, and lay flat to dry.

I do have one gripe, though, and it’s not nothing. The ergonomic, nearly lie-flat seat is fantastic for naps, and the no-rethread, easy-to-adjust harness is great, but younger passengers will lose most of the view if they’re reclined even a little purely because of positioning. This is common on many strollers, but for some reason, is more pronounced on this model. Our tester cared not at all, though, as he was busy looking straight out at the flock of American oystercatchers gathered on the boardwalk at the beach in Queens, New York, where I tested this stroller. My suggestion? Find a running area with dopey looking birds and kids are thrilled. Egrets are also a favorite, I’ve found.

I am a massive fan of this double stroller—Bob gets it right with this one. It’s largely one of the easiest to assemble and to fold, whether or not you take off the wheels. It’s a joy to push, even if you have two large toddlers in the seats. The tires are my favorite of any standard jogging stroller on this list. They are the best aligned, and the adjustable front wheel means you never have to worry if it comes out of alignment, as you can just fix it in a few tweaks.

But oh, how I could write sonnets about the storage. You know what you need a ton of when you’re pushing two kids for a two-plus hour run? Everything. Diapers, wipes, snacks, drinks, extra clothing, sunscreen, snacks for yourself, a few bottles of water, and more. And with the giant storage basket and all the storage cubbies on this beauty, you’ve got the space to hold them. The only thing it doesn’t store is extra patience for when they start fighting at mile 10 and you have 3.1 more miles on your run.

I have run over 200 miles with this stroller, and though I have had to replace the inner tube in the front tire, the stroller is still in great shape. The combination mesh and sealed poly storage basket underneath has seen some things in its life, and it still comes out clean and doesn’t smell, which is a huge accomplishment considering all it has been through.

While lugging it around folded isn't the easiest task, the Bob Revolution 3.0 Duallie’s exceptional performance and ample storage more than compensate. Overall, this double stroller is a top pick for parents who love to run and need the capacity for two little ones. It’s a durable, comfortable, and thoughtfully designed stroller that will make countless runs a joy for both you and your children.

I had heaps of fun testing this stroller out, and recently, I even got on a bicycle (not my thing!) and tried it out in tow mode. This stroller is a beast and, truly, it is only for the most sporting amongst us. If you’re a serious outdoor fanatic, you’ve met your match. It’s designed like a bike trailer, but thanks to its multiple bases/setups, it works as a stroller, a jogging stroller, a bike trailer, and even a stroller on skis for snowshoeing and fun in the sand.

This is technically the double version, but I think it’s worth it to get the wider Chariot Cross 2 over the single version, as it feels a bit more stable than the single, and gives your child some extra space. The seats inside are roomy, and I had no complaints from the Peanut Section about the straps or cushion levels, no matter if the kids were being towed, pushed, or shoved over ice and snow.

Switching the kits out could be simpler, but it’s not especially difficult. I managed to do it pretty easily, and I have a partially paralyzed left hand. Putting it together initially is honestly a bigger pain. It’s easy to clean, though, with removable pads. The materials can take a serious amount of scrubbing and hosing off without showing any wear, which is good considering how filthy a stroller like this could become.

I love the oversized storage bag that affixes to the back. It’s simple to use and clean, and deep enough to fit way more than you’d expect. It’s a slick feature that puts this stroller in a category of its own.

As for the ride, it’s as smooth as it can be over the snow, sand, and ice. This stroller is a bit heavy for an all-out run, but great for jogging slow, easy miles. As a regular stroller, it’s great for myriad applications, but my favorite way to use it is when you’re in a buggy area, as it’s completely enclosed. As a bike trailer, it shines, holding its ground and keeping everything steady. For serious outdoor enthusiasts seeking a versatile and durable multisport option, the Thule Chariot Cross 2 is a top-tier choice that's built to handle almost any adventure.

I’ve pushed the Veer Switch&Jog over 25 miles on all kinds of terrain, and it did well on almost everything. I struggled to push it on mud and sand, but that’s true of just about any stroller. The second I find one that doesn’t? You’ll be the first to know.

My favorite thing about this baby is that you’re able to switch out the jump seat back and forth. Additional pieces are available. The cooler is great, and the booster seat takes about two seconds to set up at a restaurant, which freaking rocks when you think about how dirty restaurant high chairs can get.

During the testing we had a projectile vomit situation. Totally my fault. I overfed the small human treats before the run. My bad, I know better. I took it straight to a self-serve car wash and sprayed absolute crap out of it with the a high-pressure wand. After a little scrubbing, it was totally fine, and the smell came out too (thank god, because it was dairy). I do wish the fabric was machine washable, but it’s attached so firmly to the frame that I get why it’s not.

On runs, it’s stable, and the telescoping handle and handbrake are both easy to use. The front wheel locks for straightaways and unlocks when you’re just wandering around the city.

Folding it is kind of a pain in the you-know-what, not gonna lie. But it’s a convertible tank of a stroller, and it’s very hard to beat at this price.

Given that jogging strollers can be a significant investment, it's crucial to select one that aligns with your needs. To ensure you choose the right stroller, consider these key specifications:

These specs directly relate to your running style. Serious runners will prioritize performance features like wheel type and suspension, while casual joggers might focus on convenience features like car seat compatibility and ease of folding.

To be included on this list, every jogging stroller must meet certain criteria. Key features of a good jogging stroller include a lockable front wheel for safe straightaways at a running pace, excellent build quality for durability, a large canopy for sun protection, and built-in safety features such as a wrist strap, sweat-resistant handlebar grips, and a secure harness system.

And, not for nothing, but they need to feel good when you run behind them. I can’t tell you how many clunkers I’ve tested that made my runs a chore. They need to provide both the runner and the passenger with a comfortable experience. If you’re kicking the storage basket or your hands feel like they’ve become permanently glued to the handlebar, you’re not going to want to use that stroller.

As avid runners who have embraced parenthood, we understand the unique demands placed on jogging strollers. We know that these aren't just tools for transporting children; they are crucial pieces of equipment that must perform flawlessly whether you're engaged in rigorous training for your next marathon or simply navigating the everyday errands with your little one in tow.

For years, the Runner's World team has been committed to guiding runners toward the gear that allows them to achieve peak performance and enjoy their passion for running to the max. This deep-seated expertise extends into our in-depth evaluations of running gear, and jogging strollers are no exception. Our primary objective is to thoroughly test and identify the options available on the market, and to provide informed and reliable recommendations for runners of all experience levels.

When is it safe to run with your child in the stroller?

The general rule recommended by pediatricians is to wait until the baby is at least 6 months old, and has good head, trunk, and neck control. AKA, they can sit unassisted for long periods of time.

What is the best way to clean a jogging stroller?

Honestly, some of these strollers allow you to remove many of the fabrics and wash them in the machine, but for a jogger, it’s kind of a pain. I suggest taking off the canopy, tilting the whole thing upside down and shaking it out before using a damp cloth and wiping it down, and allowing it to air dry. If it’s really gross, hose the thing down, but take off the harness first, as soaking it can reduce its efficacy.

What Should You Avoid in a jogging stroller?

You should be holding your child’s hard sippy cups and snacks and save those for walking breaks. Jogging can jostle, and I’ve seen some pretty gnarly dental injuries on kids who had plastic sippy cup incidents from jogging strollers.

Generally not. Even if they fall within the parameters set by Disney of 31- by 52 inches, I’ve heard of many of them (apart from the Guava) getting rejected at the gates.

Cat Bowen, senior editor of commerce; reviews, is a seasoned runner with more than 20 years of distance running experience, including dozens of marathons, half marathons, and even a few ultra marathons. For over a decade, she has tested parenting, fitness, home, and running gear and written in-depth guides to help readers with their next purchase.
