#8844. Essential Yoga Poses That Deliver Serious Knee Strengthening

The thing about practicing yoga for knee strengthening is you typically don’t know you need to do it until there’s an issue. YouTube yoga teacher Yoga With Kassandra takes you through a routine designed to emphasize the muscles that support knee strength and explains how to modify the poses to suit your needs.

Whether you’re wanting to build knee strength to enhance your everyday functionality or you’re recovery from a knee injury and finally at the point where you can practice yoga, you need strengthening exercises that support all the muscles that support and stabilize your knees. Basically, you want to work on the hip adductors, the quads, the glutes, the hamstrings.

The following poses literally work all of the muscles that contribute to knee stability. You’ll also get to play around a little with some dynamic movement and try some balancing exercises that help you understand how to properly engage the muscles that support the knee. Then you can take that awareness into other yoga poses as well as your everyday movements.

Regularly practicing this yoga for knee strength routine will help anyone build knee strength. I know from personal experience just how frustrating a knee injury can be, so if that applies to you, know that the more you dedicate time towards rehabilitating yourself, and the more diligent you are with your practices, the more likely you’ll feel a difference in your ease of movement. And remember that rest is equally as important as stretching and strengthening.

You will need a block or a block-like item for several of these poses. If you experience pain in any of the poses, slowly come out and skip ahead to the next pose. Always consult with your physician or physical therapist prior to introducing new exercises.

Start lying on your back and bring your feet about hip-distance apart and your heels pretty close toward your glutes. Place the block directly in between the inner thighs and squeeze the block as much as you possibly can. Then push down into all four corners of both feet and slowly lift first the pelvis off the mat, then the lower back, and then the mid back in Bridge Pose. The higher you lift, the harder it becomes to squeeze your block, but keep squeezing it anyway. This helps train your inner thighs, or adductor muscles, to contract. Building inner thigh power can also help you become better at balancing poses.

Take about 3 breaths here, pushing down through your big toes. Then exhale and slowly roll down, inch by inch. Move your block to the side.

From lying on your back, lift your right leg toward the sky and straighten it without locking your knee or hyperextending it. Interlace your fingers behind your right hamstrings. Instead of making this a passive stretch, push your leg against your palms as much as you can, and feel your arms resist. Keep pushing, pushing, pushing with your hamstrings. This should be challenging. You’ll also get a little arm workout. Try to keep your lower back neutral and close to the mat. Continue for a few more breaths.

You might find that your leg starts coming a little closer toward your chest, and that’s fine, but don’t force the stretch. Then release and switch legs.

Re-extend your right leg and bring your hands behind the back of your calf muscles. If that means you need to bend a little in your knee, that’s perfectly fine. If you can’t reach that far, bring your hands to the hamstrings again, but shift them closer to the knee, which creates a different sensation. Same thing, you want to push against your hands and resist. Then repeat on the other side.

This is not a yoga pose, but it’s absolutely amazing for your adductors. Grab your block and place it between your inner thighs again. Instead of keeping your heels close to you as in Bridge, walk your feet out so it feels almost as if your legs are almost straight and there’s about 6 inches between the mat and the backs of your knees.

Flex your feet, push your heels down into the mat, and see if you can squeeze your block and lift your hips off the mat. They’re only going to lift about an inch or so and that’s fine. This is an intense pose. You’re gonna feel it in your legs pretty much right away. If you don’t feel it, it’s because your knees are too bent and you need to straighten them a little more. Squeeze your block, push down into your heels, and try to drag your heels toward your shoulders. Hold here for a few more breaths. Then lower and move your block off to the side.

Come into Downward-Facing Dog. Normally I would suggest some Cat and Cow stretches before going into Down Dog, but if you’re recovering from knee issues you might not be able to apply bring your knees to the mat because of the pressure, so consider those stretches optional or take a seated version of them. You’re pushing into the heels here to stretch your hamstrings, lengthen your arms, and lengthen your spine.

Reach your right leg toward the sky in Three-Legged Dog, then step forward toward the top of the mat. Push down into your feet and come up into High Lunge. You want your feet hip-distance apart for stability. It’s find to bend your back knee if that feels more doable. It’s important that your front knee is going in the same direction as your toes and is stacked over your ankle. You don’t want the knee to be swaying to one side or jutting forward in front of your toes.

Bring your hands to your heart and keep your right knee bent and focus on its stability as you tilt your chest forward into a variation of Warrior 3. Keep the knee of your supporting leg bent as you reach your left leg back and find your balance.

As you inhale, push your right leg straight, and then exhale gently as you bend your right knee again. Think of this as almost like a one-legged squat. So inhale, straighten the leg. Exhale, bend the knee.

Continue for several breaths. Keep your right knee pointing straight over the second and third toes. Last one, inhale to straighten and hold here.

From Warrior 3, reach your left leg straight toward the ceiling and bring your chest toward your right thigh in Standing Splits. You might want to bring your block underneath your hands or fingertips.

Then exhale, bend both knees as much as you can, and see if you can bring your knees together to touch, so you’re in a little ball with your left foot hovering above the mat.

Then inhale, open back up into Standing Splits. Look at your right knee and make certain it’s not shifting to the right or the left. Do that once more.

Bend both knees and bring your left foot to the mat with your big toes together and your heels slightly apart in Chair Pose. If this creates tension in your lower back, you can keep your feet hip-distance apart. Rock your weight back into your heels and keep your tailbone reaching back and your thighs hugging the midline as if you were still squeezing that block. Stay here or reach your arms alongside your head.

Lean more weight onto your right leg, and see if you can pick up your left foot and step it back into your High Lunge. Then very carefully pivot the back foot almost parallel to the short side of the mat, keeping your shin and your knee facing the same direction, in Warrior 2. Your right knee is still bending. Squeezing the glutes helps press that right knee open as it points forward. Reach your arms straight out from your shoulders.

To work on strengthening, inhale as you straighten the front leg and bring your hands together in front of you, and then exhale back into Warrior 2 and reach your arms. Repeat several times. The goal is not to rush this but to do it with control. You want to really feel that knee tracking directly over the second and third toes and not wobbling.

Straighten your right leg, being careful not to lock or hyperextend your knees. Then shift forward into Triangle Pose and reach your left arm upward. Draw your left shoulder slightly back as you open across the chest.

From Triangle, look down at the floor and circle your hands to the mat. Step to Downward-Facing Dog.

Repeat these poses on your left side, starting with High Lunge and continuing to Dynamic Warrior 3, Standing Splits, Chair Pose, Dynamic Warrior 2, Triangle, and Down Dog.

From Down Dog, walk your feet to the top of the mat. Bend your knees a little, grab your block, and come all the way to standing. Come into Mountain Pose with the block in between your thighs, just as you did in Bridge Pose. Squeeze the block and hug in toward the midline. You can feel the adductors engage. Plant down firmly through all four corners of both feet.

As you inhale, stand a little taller. As you exhale, continue to squeeze your block as you lower yourself into Chair Pose. Repeat this movement about 5 times, moving slowly and steadily, continuing to squeeze the block. You might need to adjust your block a little.

Slowly fold forward in Standing Forward Bend. If you need to bend your knees, that’s perfectly fine. Even in this fold, can you squeeze your block? Then bend your knees a little more and release your block.

Slowly roll all the way up to standing. Notice how you feel as you attempt the pose, because if you’re still injured, the shape might not be accessible to you, and it’s fine to skip it. Lean onto your right foot, bend your left knee, and catch hold of the inner edge of your left foot behind you with your left hand. Keep your left hip and knee drawing inward toward the midline. So imagine you’re still squeezing your block in between your thighs. That is really important.

Reach your right arm forward. Instead of dipping the chest down and thinking of lifting the leg up, focus on pushing your foot into your palm. You’re not going super far forward in your Dancer Pose. You’re not working on flexibility, you’re working on strength, although you might feel an intense stretch along the front of your lifted quads.

To help with balance, you can always practice within arm’s reach of a chair or a wall so that you can reach out if needed for extra steadiness.

Then release and repeat on your other leg, foot into the right hand.

Make your way onto your belly on the mat. The shape of this pose is very similar to Dancer, so if this isn’t working for you, work on Locust Pose. If you want to do Bow Pose, bend your knees and see if you can catch hold of your feet and imagine you still have the block in between the inner upper thighs. Squeeze in and start to push the feet against your hands.

If you’re not doing Bow Pose, then bring your arms alongside your body, palms facing the mat, and slowly lift your feet and legs and chest off the mat Focus your gaze forward and down to keep the back of your neck long. Hold here or slowly release and then lift several times.

Flip over onto your back. Grab your block, lift your hips, slide your block underneath your pelvis, and just let yourself settle here. Slow down your breath and start to unwind.

When you’re ready, press into your feet, lift your pelvis, and move your block to the side before lowering yourself down. Maybe you draw your knees toward your belly and bring your arms underneath your calves and stay still or rock a little side to side.

Extend your arms and legs, close your eyes, and notice how you feel now as opposed to when you first started this practice. Let yourself settle into this space.

When you’re ready, begin to lengthen your breath and wiggle your fingers and toes. You can reach your arms up overhead, take a big stretch, and roll onto one side. Come up to take a seat, sitting up tall, maybe closing your eyes for a moment.

Thank you so much for doing this knee-strengthening sequence with me. I hope that it gave you some ideas as to how you can strengthen your knees.

#8843. I Rode My Bike in a Climate Chamber That Can Recreate Almost Any Weather on the Planet—Here’s My Biggest Takeaway

Inside Italy’s Terra X Cube, a Tour de France simulation became a real-world heat test.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

I looked into the giant chamber filled with strategically placed bike trainers and couldn’t help but question what I signed up for. The chamber we were walking into is called the Terra X Cube located in Bolzano, Italy, and is designed to replicate conditions from anywhere on the planet. The chamber can recreate a snowstorm on Mount Everest or a heat wave in the Sahara.

Variables like temperature, humidity, wind, precipitation, and altitude can all be controlled from a small observation room just one door over. I knew immediately when I crossed into the threshold of the chamber and the heat hit me in the face that this would be a rough trainer ride.

I was in Bolzano, Italy for an opportunity to participate in this testing in the Terra X Cube as well as tour the apparel brand Q36.5’s headquarters based in Bolzano. The apparel from Q36.5 quickly became my top choice for cycling apparel after getting the chance to test some pieces from their kit for the last few months. Our hot and humid summer in the Northeast gave a perfect testing ground for the Q36.5 Dottore jersey and bibs—and they shined. When a chance to learn more about this brand by visiting their Italian headquarters came up, I jumped on a plane—the opportunity to experience riding in a climate chamber was a special bonus.

Here I’m going to talk about the unique experience of riding in a climate chamber with the heat turned up and my biggest takeaway that you can apply to your trainer riding this season.

The test course and climate were designed to replicate the last section of Stage 2 from the 2026 men’s Tour de France ending in Barcelona. We rode with a custom workout in Zwift and our data was being tracked across the board: SRM cranks to track power, heart rate data to validate fatigue, and CORE sensors to track our heat strain throughout the workout. The room was set to a balmy 97 degrees Fahrenheit.

There was even a tester from Q36.5 in the room with us with a custom jersey. The jersey he wore was effectively two jerseys cut in half at the zipper and straight down the back. He had multiple CORE heat sensors attached around his body to track which jersey design and material was more effective at thermoregulation. One of those jersey designs will end up in a future product.

The ride was supposed to last for about 45 minutes, but our group was the first of the day and ran into some technical difficulties getting the trainers set up. In one sense this was good because we were able to have an extended warmup on the trainers, but the reality meant we spent an extra 45 minutes warming up in the already heated up chamber.

Thankfully, over the last few months, I’ve been doing heat training protocols with my CORE training sensor. I dove straight in with six weeks of active heat training, then I pivoted to strictly passive heat training with my home sauna. While I was absolutely heating up I was relatively comfortable rolling into the ride.

Once we got through our extended warmup we began the proper ride. Effectively we were shooting for an over-under workout that emulated the end of stage two at this year’s Tour de France. I had my CORE temperature data up on the screen and saw that before we were starting the ride my internal temperature was at about 99 degrees. The giant fans at the front of the room would change power to replicate the airflow during climbs versus descents, but at those temperatures it felt like sitting in front of a massive hair dryer.

As we began the official warmup my temperature steadily climbed—according to my CORE sensor I peaked just over 102 degrees. In the middle of the test I looked around the room and everyone looked like they were putting out high effort, even when we were supposed to be sitting in our recovery phase. The heat was taking its toll and our views did not inspire a boost in energy. Staring at the metallic walls while pedaling on our hamster wheel bikes did not give inspiration for an extra push for our final sprint. But as we finished up our not-so-cool cooldown I couldn’t help but think I would do it again.

After our group left the chamber the second group queued up for their turn on the bikes. The technical difficulties were overcome with our group, so they were able to jump straight into the ride after a five-minute warmup. That night we all regrouped to go through the data and we were able to see our data versus the data from some of the professionals in the stage we recreated. My biggest takeaway from the comparison to the professionals was their core temperature data. The professionals we were comparing against showed very little heat strain compared to even the fittest in our group. It’s worth noting the professionals had also already ridden over 60 miles before our route even started—those professionals were extremely heat adapted.

My biggest personal takeaway was how I could recreate this at home. When I talked to someone else in my group we discussed the similarities to this experience and heat training at home. When I do an active heat session at home I layer up in three layers top and bottom, a painter’s suit with the shins and feet cut off (so it doesn’t get caught in the cranks), and a hat or beanie for good measure. My active heat session numbers at home are surprisingly similar to this experience: typically a 45-minute warmup gets me into zone three of the heat strain index in the CORE app and then I spend about 45 minutes in this zone. This shows you don’t need a massive climate chamber to get the training benefits of heat training. Some warm layers, a painter’s suit, a CORE sensor, and a bike trainer can give you the benefits you need to develop this component of training.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

#8842. Here’s How to Train From Now Through the New Year to Maintain Your Hard-Earned Marathon Fitness

A run coach and an exercise physiologist break down the weekly mileage and workouts you need to preserve your speed, strength, and endurance.

You’ve spent months training for your fall marathon, so the thought of losing that hard-earned fitness after race day probably stings. But at the same time, you can’t simply continue logging miles and workouts like you’re in race mode. Trying to stay razor-sharp year-round can lead to injury and burnout; your body needs rest after training for peak fitness.

So, instead, put your marathon fitness on ice. Freeze the adaptations you’ve gained and the endurance you’ve built. Then, you can pick up where you left off on, say, January 1, or whenever it’s time to lock back in for a spring marathon.

If you train right in the weeks between now and the new year, you won’t feel like you’re rebuilding fitness from scratch. Instead, you’ll preserve the key aerobic, muscular, and endurance adaptations you’ve worked so hard to develop.

To do that, we explain the minimum miles you need for maintenance and how speed, strength, and cross-training keep you in prime condition. Expect to return to race training feeling well-rested, confident, and ready to tackle another marathon cycle this spring.

In the first two weeks immediately following your marathon, you’ll want to focus more on rest and easy time-based jogging. Once you’ve recovered, however, you can return to tracking your miles more closely.

The bare minimum mileage you’ll need to maintain will vary from runner to runner, Heather Milton, CSCS, lead exercise physiologist at Primary MD and cofounder of Master My Run, tells Runner’s World. Much of it depends on how many miles you regularly put in over the weeks of your marathon training cycle.

“Science does not give us an exact number of what percentage of your marathon volume to decrease to that still allows you to maintain the same amount of aerobic fitness,” Milton explains. From her coaching experience, however, she’s found this number is likely around 50 percent of a runner’s typical weekly mileage.

David Hall, an RRCA- and USATF-certified run coach and founder of Running Coach CT, agrees. When planning his athletes’ schedules for the off-season, he looks at their typical running volume during marathon training and reduces their weekly mileage to no less than half. Every fourth week, however, mileage can drop to as low as 20 percent of their average to help facilitate recovery.

“A runner who was running 60 miles per week during their marathon build could definitely cut that in half,” Milton says. Or, take a runner who averaged around 40 miles per week. This individual could reduce their weekly mileage to 20, add in some cross-training, and expect to maintain much of their progress.

In fact, Milton adds, every runner can benefit from incorporating more of those cross-training sessions in the off-season. “Other forms of exercise can decrease the repetitiveness of the running motion and help you develop more well-rounded fitness, so I do prefer more variety from cross-training in the down-season,” she explains.

At the same time, Milton wants people to do the exercise they enjoy and, of course, runners love running. “I have to be reasonable about what a runner is willing to do and what keeps them healthy while they’re doing it,” she says. If you want to keep running four days per week in the off-season, that’s still workable—with one important caveat: You need to prioritize strength training.

When you’re in the thick of marathon training, running is your main focus. So while you’re still doing strength work during this time, it mostly helps maintain the strength you already have, rather than increase it, Milton explains. The off-season provides an ideal time to really build up and strengthen your muscle mass and bone health as much as possible.

Each week, Milton says to aim for two to three resistance training sessions that focus on heavier weights with a low to moderate number of reps. (You can do more than three weekly sessions as long as you’re not working the same muscle groups two days in a row.) This sets you up for a stronger return to your spring training cycle because it helps improve running economy, your overall neuromuscular health, and your fast-twitch muscle fibers, which help power you through fast bursts of running or hill climbing.

“Plus, when you start training for your next marathon, you’ll be in a stronger position to increase your running volume again because you’ve strengthened all of the areas of your body that were impacted by your previous race, which can help prevent injuries,” Milton adds.

During the off-season, you certainly don’t need to run every day to maintain your fitness. In fact, you can preserve key fitness markers—such as your VO2 max—with as little as three workouts per week.

“The goal is to maintain at least three to four aerobic days per week to maintain your fitness level,” says Milton. You can opt to run as little as once per week, as long as you continue to cross-train on the remaining days, she adds.

Aim for 30 to 60 minutes of whichever aerobic exercise you most enjoy—hit the gym for the elliptical or indoor pool, or get outside for skiing and cycling.

Similarly, the number of running days per week for Hall’s athletes varies, but many have success with three because it allows more time for strength and flexibility work. He also adds a second rest day to the schedules of his runners who typically train six days per week during a marathon block. But in both cases, consistency is crucial—you don’t want to go a week without doing anything. “Do something every other day at a minimum to stay active,” Hall says.

One of your runs each week should be a bit longer than the others, but it doesn’t need to match the lengths of your true marathon long runs. Milton typically recommends a long run between five and 13 miles, depending on the individual’s training volume.

If you don’t want to worry about tracking mileage in the off-season, that’s fine, too. Running for time instead of miles provides the same endurance benefits, Hall says. Around four weeks postmarathon, his athletes will typically start with one-hour long runs. “Then, they’ll go up to 75 minutes, then to 90 minutes, and then maybe up to an hour and 45,” he explains.

Over several weeks, this gradual progression sets his runners up with a solid base to build from when they start their spring marathon training. “But don’t push the pace,” he emphasizes. “These are easy, conversational efforts.”

Whether you run for time or miles, make sure you’re not increasing either too quickly. “Keep the same rules in mind as when you’re building mileage in marathon training,” Milton says. “Aim to increase by no more than 10 percent each week.” Recent research suggests that, to reduce injury risk, you can apply this rule to the distance of any single run, as well.

What does this look like in practice? Let’s say a runner is doing five aerobic sessions per week, which includes about 20 miles of running. Two are cross-training days and the remaining three are running days. They might choose to run three to five miles one day, five to seven miles another day, and then five to 13 miles for their long run. You also don’t need to increase distance as quickly as you would in marathon training, Milton explains.

Over three weeks, she says a runner might balance their mileage as follows:

Week 1: 4 miles, 6 miles, 10 milesWeek 2: 5 miles, 6 miles, 9 milesWeek 3: 3 miles, 7 miles, 11 miles

In the four weeks immediately following your marathon, don’t worry about fast workouts or hitting paces, says Hall. During those first two weeks postrace, he advises his athletes to go for 20- to 30-minute daily walks. In the third and fourth weeks, he reintroduces easy running and a touch of speed.

“The general rule I apply is: no hard running for the number of days that’s equal to the number of miles in the race. So for a marathon, we’re talking about 30 days of walking and conversational effort running—maybe dipping into tempo pace a bit—but certainly nothing above lactate threshold.”

After that time, Hall says runners can start to add back intensity. In fact, he encourages it, suggesting you incorporate either a 20-minute run at threshold pace or an interval session for the same amount of time. He also recommends alternating one mile at your threshold pace, followed by one minute of easy jogging or brisk walking, until you reach 20 minutes.

“Training at lactate threshold pace can make conversational effort feel easier and can help you run faster while still remaining mostly in an aerobic zone,” Hall explains. In other words, your body adapts so running at any pace starts to feel like it requires less work.

Another way to get in some speed during the winter season? Sign up for a holiday race like a Turkey Trot or Jingle Bell Jog, he says. “It can get boring if all you do is train. Racing a 5K keeps the interest alive and lets you put in a hard effort.” Keep in mind, though, you did just run a marathon, so you don’t need to race all out or cross the finish line with a PR.

According to both Hall and Milton, the golden rule that will help you maintain your hard-earned gains is consistency. Once you’ve recovered physically and mentally from 26.2, get back into a routine that keeps you moving. “Doing something is always better than doing nothing,” Hall says—because you can lose 8 percent of your VO2 max in four to six weeks if you pull the plug on activity completely.

Similarly, you’ll want to avoid “stop-and-go” training. “If you’re running two to four days per week, keep running two to four days per week, every week—within reason, because life gets in the way sometimes,” Milton says. But running 30 miles one week, doing nothing for three weeks, and then trying to get back into it can lead to a real struggle, she adds.

As long as you do your best to stay consistent—and don’t stress when the holidays, travel, or other engagements inevitably interfere—you’ll find your fitness quite close to where you left it after your fall marathon. All that’s left for you to do? Thaw it out with a fresh marathon training cycle this spring.

Morgan is a gear editor who has been with Runner’s World since 2017. She started as an intern ghostwriting The Warmup, a bygone version of the daily RW newsletter. Now, she tests and reviews anything you might find on runners’ feet-from crew socks and compression boots to carbon-plated super shoes.

A lifelong runner and shoe geek, Morgan has been chasing the perfect pair of kicks since she joined her grade school cross-country team. Since then, she ran as a Division I walk-on for the cross-country and track & field teams at the University of Delaware, where she studied English and Biology. She has one full marathon under her belt, and has raced more halfs and 5Ks than she can count.

#8841. Are High-Intensity Workouts Messing With Your Cortisol?

If you’ve scrolled through social media lately, you’ve probably seen wellness influencers claim high-intensity exercise increases cortisol, the infamous “stress hormone” that, in excess amounts, can lead to fatigue, weight gain, trouble sleeping, high blood pressure, and elevated blood sugar.

Many influencers say to switch to a no-stress, low-sweat regimen. And while low-intensity exercises such as Pilates, treadmill walking, or yoga are valid ways to work out—and serve as excellent cross-training activities for runners—HIIT workouts (like hill repeats, sprint intervals, and tempo runs) are key if you’re training for a race or looking to build speed and power.

But are high-intensity runs actually messing with your hormones, or is the wellness side of the internet spreading misinformation? We’re here to separate fact from fiction.

Cortisol is a hormone made by your adrenal glands, which are located on top of your kidneys and are part of your body’s endocrine system.

“Cortisol helps regulate metabolism, blood pressure, and the immune response, and it makes energy available when the body is under stress—including during exercise,” says Dr. Aysegul Eren, M.D., endocrinologist and medical director of the Adrenal Program at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center.

This hormone rises when your body faces increased physical or metabolic demand, such as exercise, illness, fasting, low blood sugar, or psychological stress, Eren explains. During exercise, cortisol naturally spikes as a way to provide energy to your body so it can perform. Viewed through that lens, cortisol is an important part of your body’s response to exercise and your ability to complete workouts.

“Higher-intensity exercise reliably causes a temporary cortisol rise, generally related to exercise intensity,” Eren says. “This is normal physiology, not something harmful to prevent.”

How long cortisol remains elevated depends on the stressor, according to Dr. Feyza Erenler, M.D., an endocrinologist at Tufts Medical Center. It may be minutes to hours for a brief stimulus like exercise, she explains.

A 2021 meta-analysis of 10 studies on HIIT, published in the Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports, found that cortisol increased immediately after exercise, often fell below baseline about two hours later, and returned to baseline within 24 hours.

“There’s no evidence that a specific number of HIIT sessions causes chronically high cortisol,” Eren says. “The more relevant concern is overtraining—chronic training without adequate recovery—which can lead to persistent underperformance. ‘Too much’ is individual, depending on training load, sleep, nutrition, recovery, and other stressors.”

In fact, research shows physical activity can actually lead to lower cortisol levels. A 2026 study in the Journal of Sport and Health Science found that those who did 150 minutes of moderate- to vigorous-intensity aerobic exercise (50 to 85% of their max heart rate) every week for a year saw a reduction in long-term cortisol levels.

Symptoms frequently attributed to “high cortisol,” such as fatigue, poor sleep, anxiety, or difficulty losing weight, don’t indicate that a person has high cortisol, according to Erenler. “These symptoms are extremely common and nonspecific and can occur for many different reasons,” she says.

Signs of true high cortisol—not the brief, self-resolving spike during exercise—include bruising, muscle weakness (particularly in the upper legs), wide purple stretch marks, worsening high blood pressure or diabetes, and sometimes changes in fat distribution, according to Eren.

If you’re experiencing any of the above symptoms, Eren recommends discussing them with your healthcare provider rather than trying to diagnose yourself with high cortisol all on your own (or with the help of a chatbot). Chronic high cortisol levels that are undiagnosed can cause high blood pressure, diabetes, muscle and bone loss, higher infection risk, and cardiovascular complications.

But rest assured, cortisol disorders are rare. For instance, Cushing syndrome, a condition where you have too much cortisol in your blood for a long period of time, only affects 10 to 15 people per million each year, according to the Endocrine Society. Cushing syndrome is caused by a tumor on the pituitary gland at the base of your brain, not too much high-intensity exercise.

“During exercise, cortisol temporarily rises in response to the physiological stress and then decreases as the body recovers and the stressor resolves,” Erenler says. “In Cushing syndrome, cortisol exposure remains inappropriately elevated over time, and the normal regulatory mechanisms—including the normal circadian pattern and suppression of cortisol production—are disrupted.”

For most healthy people, there’s no need to try to suppress the normal cortisol response to exercise. Instead, the goal should be a sustainable training program that includes adequate recovery, sufficient sleep and nutrition, and variation in workout intensity.

“Don’t worry about the temporary rise in cortisol that occurs with exercise,” Eren says. “It’s a normal part of the body’s response to physical activity, not a sign that exercise is harming you.”

Erenler agrees and says the goal isn’t to eliminate cortisol—it’s to challenge your body appropriately and give it enough recovery to adapt to the stress you’re placing on it.

#8839. The 10 Best Running Shoes for Wide Feet and Big Toes

Don’t subject yourself to cramped feet—these running shoes are the comfiest and roomiest.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

I’m four miles out on my run when I feel angry blisters forming between my toes because they’re overcrowded in my shoe’s toebox. Add that to a long list of annoying things going on with my feet: mild plantar fasciitis, black toenails, gnarly calluses that make me ashamed to wear sandals. I am a card-carrying member of the wide-foot club, yet I’ve resisted wide-width running shoes for years. Mostly because around the time I found I had wide feet (over 15 years ago), the only colors available in wide-widths were black, white, or gray.

Today, running shoes for wide feet have become more accessible, more visible, and less boring. Perhaps with the dawn of foot scans at specialty running shops, store owners and brands are finally realizing just how common wide-footed runners are—and why it’s so important runners stop squishing their feet in standard-sized shoes.

I’ve run 28 marathons and vet all kinds of gear, from sports bras to smartwatches, as RW running reviews editor. For research, I visited Aardvark Sports Shop, a local run store in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, to get the lowdown on running shoes for wide-foot runners from Aardvark Footwear Lead Trainer Kate Egging. Egging, a former RW wear-tester, has worked at Aardvark for four years and is a lifelong wide-foot runner, like myself. I also spoke with A. Stacie Page, PT, DPT, of Johns Hopkins Running Program at Johns Hopkins Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation, who discussed the risks of wearing too-narrow shoes and how this can affect running performance.

Besides gear expertise provided by our staff, we also have a team of 300-plus local shoe testers who log at least 100 miles per pair of running shoes. They provide valuable feedback on fit, feel, and ride to help us determine the best trainers, ensuring our selections are all-inclusive. We also enlisted the help of Egging, because she gets to try on shoes at Aardvark and help runners make footwear decisions.

Compared to the Brooks Ghost, the Brooks Glycerin is broader in the midfoot area, resulting in a more accommodating fit for wider foot shapes. The new triple jacquard knit also provides a stretchier upper that houses wide feet.

The midsole foam provides a supportive, high-energy-return ride stacked at 38 mm in the heel. Brooks added 2 mm of DNA Tuned in the forefoot. What you get is more balanced cushioning throughout the shoe and a lower heel-toe drop.

I’ve worn the Glycerin 23 for base miles and long runs. My feet fit securely in the shoe thanks to the padded border on the interior of the heel collar. The softness underfoot and overall cozy fit make the Glycerin 23 a preferred everyday shoe in my testing pile and one I can depend on when I’m scheduled for hours on the road, according to my training plan.

Shop Men’s at brooksrunning.com | Shop Women’s at brooksrunning.com

It was a tough choice for Senior Editor Pavlína Černá, when she had to choose a shoe to wear for a 75K march south of Prague in the Czech Republic. Her decision: the On Cloudmonster 3.

“The signature CloudTec sole absorbs the impact of my steps like it’s a tiny trampoline that pushes me off right away and rocks me forward, doing half the work of running (or walking) for me,” she said in her shoe review (link below). “The toebox is wide and slightly stretchy, accommodating my foot as it swells over time.”

At Aardvark, Egging noted how On’s shoes have a surprisingly wide but secure fit. Several of our testers also praised the shoe for its roomy toebox.

The shoe has a Speedboard to promote propulsion. The source of its high rebound comes from its Helion foam and CloudTec system. We liked the overall comfort of the shoe on walks, long hikes, and daily runs.

“[The shoe] is super comfortable, excellent cushioning, nothing pinched rubbed or anything,” said tester Dave Brattley. “Definitely, the best pair of shoes that I have had the chance to run in.”

One thing to note: The shoe is only available in standard size. But we found the broad platform and lacing system make the Cloudmonster 3 accessible for both wide- and narrow-foot runners.

Shop Men’s at on.com | Shop Women’s at on.com

What? A Nike shoe on our Best Running Shoes for Wide Feet list? Expecting the brand’s usual narrow fit when I got my pair of Vomero 18s to test I was shocked how accommodating the fit felt wrapped around my wide feet.

Nike updated the lasts of its popular franchises—the Vomero, Structure, and Alphafly—basing the wider foot shape on women’s feedback. Turns out both women and men liked the end result.

The shoe is mega plush with 46 mm of ZoomX and ReactX foams, making it an ideal pick for long runs. The ride is soft and responsive, like a Brooks Glycerin or Saucony Triumph—but with PEBA.

“I really enjoyed how incredibly comfortable the Vomero 18 was,” said Editorial Assistant Michael McDonough. “Once the shoes were broken in, the sheer volume of cushion made longer runs much more enjoyable and pain-free. They helped me increase my mileage without hurting my feet, which has been an issue for me in the past.”

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com

The Gel-Kayano 33 introduces a new stability system: FluidSupport. Replacing the 4-D Guidance system, FluidSupport involves the dual-foam midsole—FF Blast Max and FF Blast Plus—working in tandem with the shoe’s geometry to help guide your form when you need it. The shoe is more flexible with FluidSupport, despite the 40 mm of beefy cushioning.

The shoe only comes in standard size, but it offers plenty of space for runners with high insteps, along with a snug fit in the midfoot area. I found the shoe to have ample toe room. My wide feet didn’t feel squeezed nor did my instep feel any pressure on my runs. Running in the Gel-Kayano 33, you won’t have to stop to loosen the laces.

Our wide-foot testers shared similar feedback. “I like the upper; the collar has lots of cushion that didn’t irritate my ankle bone,” said Lorenzo Molina. “The lacing system was smooth and the overall fit is great because my foot fits better in a wider shoe.”

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com

Just about everything about the Guide 19 is accommodating. It preserves the same soft, cushioned feel as its predecessor with the same unobtrusive stability tech for, yes, guiding erratic running form.

CenterPath tech lends stability with higher sidewalls and a broader base. The Pwrrun midsole provides max-cushioning, making the Guide 19 a terrific long-run and recovery shoe of choice.

One tester gave the trainer his highest rating because of “its strong comfort, support, and cushioning, and the fact that it had no major weaknesses.”

“I was lucky enough to test this shoe’s predecessor, the Saucony Guide 18, and I enjoyed that shoe immensely for the same reasons,” said our tester, Dave Block. “But I think this model has even more cushioning and softness.”

Shop Men’s at saucony.com | Shop Women’s at saucony.com

The Torin 9 showcases several updates that make the daily trainer an even more welcoming intro to zero-drop shoes. The 28 mm stack height houses the brand’s P35X foam, with a dense core and soft carrier that softens landings without masking ground feel.

“I generally prefer cushioning that provides protection without disconnecting me from the running experience, and the Torin strikes that balance exceptionally well,” said tester Don Kuntzman. “The cushioning felt evenly distributed from heel to forefoot, creating a smooth, balanced ride that never felt overly soft, mushy, or unstable.”

The outsole has Vibram rubber, making the shoe’s ride tackier and more versatile. Our testers weren’t afraid to traverse onto the trail after hitting pace on the road.

The non-gusseted tongue provides more room for high insteps. Altra’s signature wide toebox is a bunion-prone, wide-foot runner’s dream. No need to worry about rubbing or hot spots.

Shop Men’s at altrarunning.com | Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com

Last year, Egging said the Clifton 10 was a pleasant surprise in terms of fit for wide feet. Unlike the Bondi 9, which has a narrower fit than past iterations, she found the Clifton 10’s sidewalls non-intrusive and the midfoot non-constrictive. The same goes for the Clifton 11. Hoka didn’t narrow the shoe’s fit, and it feels just as comfy and accommodating as its predecessor.

The shoe has Hoka’s Active Foot Frame to cradle your foot and help with stability. This means you can run and walk in the Clifton 11 confidently without rolling your ankles or feeling confined and stiff with extra stability features.

The compression-molded EVA foam isn’t as responsive as other supercritical foams you see in running shoes, but the Clifton 11 still has a high energy return ride that boosts everyday runs, long runs, and run/walks.

Shop Men’s at hoka.com | Shop Women’s at hoka.com

Egging wants everyone to know the Echelon 10 is not like the old Echelons Saucony was known for. Formerly a clunky run/walker for runners who need orthotics, the tenth iteration is lighter and more nimble, yet still orthotic-friendly. The shoe has the brand’s highly responsive Pwrrun midsole, which is the same foam in the Guide 18.

According to Egging, the Echelon 10 is an excellent choice for underpronators, or supinators (when your foot rolls inward less than 15 percent while running), because of its broad base and comfy cushioning.

“The Echelon gets a little bit overlooked because it falls into such a ‘comfort customer’ category,” Egging says. “But if you’ve got that new runner that has a high volume foot, maybe that 4E runner who needs the extra wide, who supinates and they need a broader base, this shoe is very runnable.”

If you are having issues with other trainers or are a new runner with specific needs, don’t discredit the Echelon 10. It could be your ticket to a great ride

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com

Brands tend to make super shoes more tapered in the midfoot, like the spiked shoes on a track. But the Rocket X 3 has an accommodating, broad platform that you could slide an orthotic into.

The shoe has dual-density PEBA foam and a winged carbon plate to promote propulsion. The upper is single-layer engineered mesh, which allows for breathability over the course of a sweaty, foot-swelling marathon. It was tester Shane Houghton’s favorite feature.

“The mesh upper is a great part about Rocket X 2,” he said. “When you tighten the shoe it stays securely in place and wraps around your foot perfectly. And it’s so airy and breathable because the holes in the netting are so big. There is no chance of your feet getting hot in these shoes no matter how tight you’re wearing them. I appreciated the padding around the heel. It was nice to have that there when a lot of racers don’t.”

The Lone Peak 9+ offers both a comfy fit with a roomy toebox, providing ample room for toe splaying. “Fit and comfort is something that the Lone Peak 9+ has dialed in,” says Rip Cantelmi, who previously tested the Lone Peak 7 and Brooks Divide 5. “Laced up, the foot feels relaxed, strong, and sensitive. I have observed that the shoe is wide enough to accommodate toe spacers if you use them. The padding around the collar remains optimized for comfort and flexibility. Heat management remains positive.”

The Altra Lone Peak 9+ has an Altra Ego midsole, which provides just enough supportive cushioning as well as some ground feel, which testers like Cantelmi appreciated.

“Ground feel is something that many trail shoes ignore for the pursuit of comfort in the form of high-stacked foam, but the Lone Peak 9+ finds the perfect balance of cushion, protection, and feel,” says Cantelmi, who describes the shoe’s cushioning as neither minimalist nor marshmallowy.

Shop Men’s at altra.com | Shop Women’s at altra.com

Misconceptions About Wide-Foot Runners and Shoes

“I’ve had my feet measured before; I don’t need to do it again”

Getting your foot measured is not a once-and-done kind of deal. Your foot size changes throughout your life, due to aging, work, and having children. “Sometimes when people get pregnant their feet sizes change dramatically,” says Page. “An injury could also cause an arch to drop if you don’t have that same muscle activation.”

She references a study on incorrectly fitted footwear published in 2018, which found a large proportion of the population was wearing the incorrect size shoe and how this can be associated with foot pain and foot disorders. Her recommendation is simple: get a comfortable shoe that fits properly.

Another reason to have your foot scanned: Some runners may think they have a wide foot when in actuality they have a high arch or instep. “That’s when they need a shoe measuring that high profile,” says Egging.

“I’ve worn this shoe forever; the newest version will fit the same”

“I think it might be even more important for a wide-footed runner to revisit a run specialty store for a fit because the models as they update, don’t always fit the same,” says Egging.

The Hoka Bondi 9, for example, fits narrower than the previous iteration. This is because of Hoka’s sidewalls which are built up to hug your foot, which can result in a tighter fit for wide-foot Bondi lovers.

Altra also requires some probing. Even though the brand is known for its accommodating footshapes and roomy toeboxes, some Altra shoes can fit narrower in the midfoot due to updates. Upper “upgrades” to look out for in any kind of shoe when you’re a wide-foot shopper are gusseted tongues, which can make the fit tighter due to more material on the instep, and overlays.

“Getting black toenails is a rite of passage”

Black toenails are not a badge of honor. Egging is an ultrarunner and she’s never lost one toenail because she received a proper shoe fitting early in her run career. Other signs of needing to get refitted and change your shoe size: numbness, tingling, Achilles tendonitis, and plantar fasciitis.

“Movement is good!” Egging says, when runners are concerned about a little looseness in a road shoe. “A lot of plantar fasciitis in wide-foot runners is coming from that arch being crunched by tight-fitting shoes.” (Trail shoes are a different story; you’ll want a more secure hold around your foot.) Tightness and constriction can also negatively affect your performance. That kind of discomfort, Page warns, can change your running pattern and lead to pain or injury.

When it comes to choosing running shoes, you want some wiggle room. If you see bruising, blood blisters on the tops of your toes, or experience toe curling, you probably need a wider toebox—this also includes runners with hammertoes, bunions, bunionettes, and Morton’s neuroma.

With your bare foot, step on a blank piece of paper. Outline your foot with a pen or pencil. Use a ruler to measure the widest part in inches of your stencil horizontally (across the ball of your foot); be aware you’ll need a wider toebox if you have bunions or bunionettes. Write this number down and refer to the men’s or women’s chart to find your width

Related: How to measure your feet: A guide for runners

What can I do when the shoe I want to buy isn’t available in wide?

If you’re a bra wearer, you may have heard the term “sister sizes.” Shoes also have sister sizes. For example, I wear women’s 5.5 in street shoes, but most of my running shoes are 6.5 because they’re the standard width (B). I size up for foot swelling (it’s recommended to size up your running shoes) and size up again for width. I’m actually a size 6, C width in women’s running shoes.

It’ll take several try-ons to get the right feel and the right shoe, but it can be possible to find a women’s B or men’s D size shoe if there are no wides available, or wide if your foot is extra wide. Women can also pivot to a men’s size, but be forewarned: men’s shoes tend to run longer and have more space in the heel area.

“Socks are super, super important,” says Egging. “I think people neglect that. The price point is frightening at first. You’re like, $18 for one pair of socks? That’s insane! But eight years later when you still have that same sock and that six-pack you got at T.J. Maxx has come and gone in the meantime.” She recommends Injinji, Blister Resist, and Balega.

At RW HQ, we’ve been testing Wide Open, a company that specifically designs socks for wide feet—and that’s been a game changer. Instead of getting blisters in between my toes or second-guessing the wide toebox of an Altra or Topo Athletic shoe, I’ve discovered just how much socks can affect your run like Egging says.

What racing shoe options are there for wide-foot runners?

Wider width options for racing shoes are still a rarity. I’ve found through personal experience that the New Balance SuperComp Elite v6, Hoka Rocket X 3, and Hoka Cielo X1 3 have the most accommodating lasts compared to other super shoes, which taper in the midfoot resulting in narrower fit. A major thing to consider is that your feet swell over time as you run, especially on a hot day. Consider sizing up, but take into consideration most racing shoes are unisex, so they may run longer or be wider in the heel.

Amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

#8836. How Warrior 1 Can Help Relieve Your Tight Hips and Lower Back

(Photo: Andrew Clark; Design in Canva by Laura Harold)

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about how to do Warrior 1 first appeared in the June 2007 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

When you have only a short time for your daily practice, which poses do you choose? Whether you opt for a simple Adho Mukha Svanasana (Downward-Facing Dog), the paired inversions Sirsasana (Headstand) and Sarvangasana (Shoulderstand), or a restorative pose to counter your hectic day, consider including another pose consistently: Virabhadrasana I (Warrior I).

I often sing the praises of this challenging pose to skeptical students who feel that it’s a lot of work without a lot of noticeable benefit, so let me explain my enthusiasm for it. In my work as a physical therapist and yoga teacher, I’ve noticed that many people in our sedentary society have tight hip flexors, which they don’t stretch much, if at all. I’m convinced that short, tight hip flexors are a major factor in many cases of chronic or recurring back pain that so many people experience in the West.

The hip flexors become tight when the hips are constantly placed in a flexed position—think sitting, driving, or sleeping in the fetal position. Like any other muscles, hip flexors will shorten structurally if they are not stretched. However, if you incorporate Virabhadrasana I into your regular practice, you’ll stretch the hip flexors, helping them gradually return to their normal length and easing a source of backaches.

The hip flexor muscles include the iliacus, psoas, rectus femoris, tensor fasciae latae, sartorius, and, in some situations, the short adductors pectines and adductor brevis. All of these muscles (except the adductors mentioned) cross the front of the hip and are active in hip flexion, which pulls the femur (thighbone) and torso closer together. The hip flexes when you perform a sit-up or lift your leg toward your chest while standing. (Each of these muscles has other actions, too, but we’re focusing here on their hip-flexing ability.)

Of the whole group of muscles, the iliacus and psoas are the strongest hip flexors. They are often referred to as the iliopsoas because they both follow the same path and have exactly the same action. Although they have different origins, the psoas originates on the lumbar spine, while the iliacus originates on the inner surface of the ilium, one of the large bones of the pelvis—they come together in the very back of the lower abdomen and run across the floor of the pelvis, over the outer part of the pubic bones on each side, and dive deep through the inner upper thighs to attach to the inner upper femurs.

The iliopsoas is powerful partly due to its size—each psoas is nearly as big around as your wrist—and partly because its position so close to the hip joint gives it excellent leverage. It is such a strong muscle, in fact, that it can influence the tilt of your pelvis and therefore the position of your spine during your daily activities. In other words, when the iliopsoas gets very short and tight, it can pull your pelvis into an anterior (forward) tilt. This type of tilt—when the top rim of the pelvis tips forward and down and the coccyx (tailbone) lifts up—usually puts the lumbar spine into hyperextension, also known as a swayback. (A posterior or backward pelvic tilt happens when the top of the pelvis moves backward, the coccyx moves down and tucks under, and the lower back flattens.)

Strong abdominals help pull the pelvis into a posterior tilt, but you might be surprised to hear that even if you have strong abdominals, a tight and strong iliopsoas muscle can win the battle and tilt your pelvis forward.

A chronically hyperextended lumbar spine puts the lower back muscles in a shortened position, causing them to ache. If the only thing that relieves your lower back discomfort is to lie on your back and pull your knees to your chest (therefore flattening the curve), you might have a hyperextended lumbar. Hyperextension also puts a greater percentage of your upper body weight onto the small facet joints on the posterior aspect of the vertebrae instead of on the solid vertebral bodies and disks, where it’s meant to be.

Enter our hero Virabhadrasana I, which can stretch the hip flexors, correct an anteriorly tilted pelvis, and help decompress your lower back. But remember to focus on practicing it with a strong posterior pelvic tilt. If you don’t, and your psoas and iliacus are tight, they will pull the lumbar spine into hyperextension and you’ll eventually feel lower back compression and pain in the pose.

There are several ways to learn how to hold a posterior tilt, but it’s best to learn the action first before integrating it into the pose. Try this: Stand with your back to a wall, with your heels about a foot away from it and your knees slightly bent. Feel an anterior tilt by moving your frontal hip points (the two bony knobs on the front of your pelvis, each known as the ASIS, or the anterior superior iliac spine) down toward your thighs, your coccyx up the wall, and your lower back away from the wall. To move from an anterior to a posterior tilt, lift your ASIS (hip points) up away from your thighs, take your tailbone down the wall, and feel your lower back move onto or toward the wall.

Now that you’re familiar with the action of a posterior tilt, here’s how to incorporate it into your Virabhadrasana I.

Set up the pose with your back to a wall, right foot forward, left heel pressing into the wall. Place a strap over the upper thigh in the crease of your right hip and hold it down with one hand on each side of the thigh. Be sure to keep your chest lifted and your shoulders down. If you are in an anterior tilt, your hip points will drop down toward or even onto the belt. To counter that, bend both knees a little and strongly lift your hip points up off the strap and into a posterior tilt. With the hip points lifted, gradually straighten the left knee, pressing the heel into the floor but keeping the lift up on the hip points, in order to stretch the iliopsoas across the front of the left hip.

Keep in mind that for most students, when the front knee bends more deeply, up to the ultimate goal of 90 degrees, it’s hard to hold the posterior tilt. If that’s the case for you, try coming only partway into the pose.

You can deepen the iliopsoas stretch a bit more by minimizing the external rotation of the left hip. When you do this, your left knee will turn out less. The iliopsoas is an external rotator, so it will try to reduce the stretch by externally rotating as you do a posterior tilt. To lessen this, be sure to turn your left foot 6o degrees away from the wall. (In standing poses like Warrior II, you turn your foot out more, so that it’s parallel to the bottom edge of your mat.) Once you’ve done that, square your pelvis toward the wall across from you as much as you can by pressing the left inner heel down firmly, lifting the left inner knee, and using the strength of the left leg to help bring the left half of the pelvis forward. You’ll not only deepen the iliopsoas stretch, but you’ll also protect your left knee from a twisting injury.

As your iliopsoas stretches and lengthens, it will pull less on your lumbar spine and pelvis, and you’ll be able to lift your lower back up out of the pelvis, thereby decompressing it and relieving discomfort. You may also notice that your posture, both standing and walking, improves, and you might enjoy a new sense of space in your hips and lower back. And you can rest assured that you’re helping prevent arthritis in your lower back.

I hope I’ve made a convincing case for consistently including hip flexor stretches in your home practice. It’s especially important to work them on sedentary days and before practicing backbends—if you’re stuck in an anterior pelvic tilt, you can imagine the compression in the lower back while you do Setu Bandha Sarvangasana (Bridge Pose), Ustrasana (Camel Pose), or Urdhva Dhanurasana (Upward Bow Pose). When you consider adding Warrior I as your iliopsoas stretch, know that you’re setting the stage for a strong and healthy back in the years to come.
