#8834. Cycling Metrics Guide: What to Measure for Better Rides

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Confused about all the data? Learn what numbers to track to see your progress and improve your performance.

My favorite metric has always been feel. I trained for two Ironman, including World Championships in Kona and entire mountain bike stage races like Cape Epic and Brasil Ride tracking nothing but time, distance, speed, and how I felt. I’d trained enough with heart rate and power to know how they worked, but I always reverted to feel.

That said, there have certainly been races where I’ve blown up—where the implosion probably could have been prevented had I been watching my watts. And the times I did spend training with power, there’s little question my sessions were more precise and likely more productive. It can be easier to stay on track with training when you have measurable goals and quantifiable sessions.

Today, I strike a compromise between luddite and tech-geek, tracking my resting heart rate and heart rate variability with an Oura ring, and recording heart rate for most rides so I can keep an eye on how fatigued and/or fresh I am.

Ultimately, I think that’s the best process when it comes to using data. Start with the basics, then add on as you get more experience. Most riders end up settling on a handful of metrics they rely on most.

Here, a primer to get you started tracking your cycling metrics.

Obviously, tracking cycling metrics generally means you need a device to capture that data. Most of the metrics, such as speed, distance, time, and elevation, mentioned here can be captured with a GPS-enabled bike computer like a Garmin, Wahoo, Lezyne, or Hammerhead. The deeper you want to dive into the data, the more sensors you need.

Great for: The satisfaction of seeing your pace pick up

Equipment needed: Any basic bike computer

Your miles per hour (or kilometers per hour, depending on where you live) is a fun metric to track, and it can tell you broadly high much fitter you’re getting. The catch: It’s not very reliable to use in training because so many factors influence it. For example, you may be cranking out World Pro-level wattage but if you’re doing so into a 30-mph block headwind, you’re not going to be setting any land speed records.

Your average speed is best used as an indicator of how your training is going overtime: If you are now consistently averaging 16+ mph on a loop that you used to average 15+ mph, you can see you’re getting fitter and faster.

You can track your average time with and without your stopping time factored into the pace. Most people don’t factor stoppage (or “café time”) in because they want to see moving time only. But if you’re training for a big event like a gravel race, it’s important to know your average speed including that stoppage time, because races often set cut offs based on a 10-mph pace, which includes rest stops. Once you see how long those “short breaks” really are, you can learn to keep them quick and avoid missing time cuts. You’ll also know how fast you need to ride to allow yourself the stoppage time you plan to take.

Great for: Watching your endurance increase

Equipment needed: Any basic bike computer

We all like to see how far we’ve gone, especially on a big ride. Distance can be a motivational metric to track. If you’re averaging 50 to 80 miles a week, can you make it 100? Can you set an annual goal of hitting 5,000 miles or more? When tracking distance, it’s important to take into consideration what type of riding you do. Riding 60 miles on flat roads is very different from 60 miles of singletrack. One might take three to four hours while the other takes the better part of a day.

Distance is also important to track if you’re training for a ride of a specific distance. If you want to ride a century in the fall, you’ll want to work up to it by hitting 50-mile and 75-mile rides as the event approaches.

Great for: Learning pacing for eventsEquipment needed: Any watch will do, but a bike computer can automatically track moving time and stoppage time

Most cyclists train by time because that’s our most finite resource. How much time you have each week to ride determines how to best use that time if your goal is to improve performance. Riders with a tight time budget are best served doing polarized training that emphasizes short, hard interval workouts during the week and longer rides as time permits on the weekend.

Great for: Bragging rights and building strength (hills make you stronger!)

Equipment needed: A GPS enabled bike computer

Elevation gain in cycling is the total amount of feet (or meters) you climb over the course of a ride. Climbing is good training, because your body must work harder in the effort to overcome the pull of gravity. If you’re the kind of rider who routinely avoids inclines, setting climbing goals and tracking elevation can give your cycling fitness a boost. If your goal is to focus on elevations, start by aiming to hit an average of 500 feet per 10 miles. Work up to what some climbing lovers call the “golden ratio” of 1,000 feet of vertical gain per 10 miles of riding.

Equipment needed: Apps like Strava will estimate your calorie burn, but for more accurate data, use a heart rate monitor and/or power meter

A calorie is a unit of energy provided by food. The calorie metric provided on your cycling computer or smartwatch is how many of those units you used to complete your ride. But calorie calculations are an imperfect science.

Some devices will provide estimates based on algorithms, which are just that—estimates. Past research has shown that devices can have a wide margin of error: A Stanford study published in 2017 reported that not one of the seven devices they tested—including the Apple Watch, Fitbit Surge, Mio Alpha 2, Basis Peak, Microsoft Band, PulseOn, and the Samsung Gear S2—delivered an accurate number for calories burned. The most accurate one, the Apple Watch, was off by 27 percent. The least accurate one? Off by 93 percent.

A more recent meta-analysis published in The British Journal of Sports Medicine echoed these findings, indicating that though devices that measure your heart rate along with your movement are more accurate, they all have a pretty significant margin of error.

Apps like GarminConnect, Strava, and other training apps might be a bit better, but they’re not perfect, either, and the number they give you depends heavily on the information you give the app. The more detailed data you input about yourself, such as age, height, weight, gender, and max heart rate, the more accurately their internal algorithms can calculate your calorie burn. Wearing a chest-based heart rate monitor that is synced to your device also helps make your calorie count more accurate.

Ultimately, the best way to know how many calories you burn on a ride is by using a power meter. Power meters measure the work you’re performing and display it in kilojoules, which is a unit of work that takes into account that the human body isn’t 100-percent efficient when turning energy from your fuel stores into physical work, like pedaling a bike.

“Kilojoules and calories burned in cycling convert to a 1:1 ratio,” explains USA Cycling elite coach Daniel Matheny, head coach at Matheny Endurance in Colorado Springs. If your ride file says you performed 800 kJ of work, you can feel confident within a 5-percent margin of error that you burned about 800 calories.

Tracking calories is useful for helping you fuel for rides. Some riders underestimate the number of calories they’ll burn on a three-hour group ride and end up falling off the back on the verge of bonking three quarters of the way through. Properly fueled riders ride faster and happier.

Just note that the goal is not to replace every calorie you’re burning as you ride. Your gut can’t take that. “Replace about half the calories you’re burning per hour for rides lasting longer than three or four hours to keep fuel levels topped off,” says sports physiologist and SkratchLabs founder Allen Lim, Ph.D.

You may also notice that the fitter you become, the fewer calories you burn on a given ride at a given pace. That’s because your body has become more efficient at using oxygen.

Great for: Training leg strength and speed; watching fitness improve for new riders

Equipment needed: A cycling computer and cadence sensor

Cadence is the number of revolutions you spin per minute as you pedal. If you have a cadence sensor you can watch your cadence in real time on your bike computer and track your average cadence for each ride.

It’s debatable how useful it is to track and/or train cadence. Coaches used to recommend athletes aim to pedal 90 rpm, but research doesn’t really show benefits from forcing yourself to do so. In 2019, a team of British researchers found that not only did amateur riders not get any added benefit from high cadence cycling, but they also became less efficient, so they were wasting energy.

Hunter Allen, CEO of Peaks Coaching Group, and author of Training and Racing with a Power Meter explains that your cadence will be determined by two things: your main muscle fiber type and your level of cardiovascular cycling fitness. The balance of those factors (which, of course, can change over time) determine your ideal cadence.

Newer riders tend to pedal more slowly because their cardiovascular system can’t handle the higher heart rate that comes with high cadences. As fitness improves, cadence generally rises.

While you probably don’t need to track your cadence from ride to ride, if you have a cadence sensor, it can help you do cadence drills, such as low gear/high cadence and high gear/low cadence drills that can help build cardiovascular fitness, leg speed, and leg strength.

Great for: Learning what sustainable (and unsustainable) efforts feel like and tracking fitness improvement

Equipment needed: Your heart, lungs, legs, and brain

It doesn’t get any more basic than RPE, your rate of perceived exertion. Put more simply, it's a measure of how hard you feel like you’re working. On a 1 to 10 scale, 1 is coasting along on a flat road with a tailwind, and 10 is full gas, willing yourself not to vomit.

You can also think of this as your “breath analyzer,” because a monitoring your breathing is an easy way to rate your efforts. Your muscles use more oxygen the harder you push, so breathing rate is a direct indication of work. If you’re able to sing and recite poetry, you’re not working very hard. If you’re gasping uncontrollably, you are maxed out.

Research shows RPE works just as well as any scientific equipment for measuring your actual effort at any given time, but it doesn’t tell you much more. For instance, you may be huffing and puffing and battling burning legs, but barely producing any power; or you could be feeling chainless while cranking out major wattage. Though you can train by “feel” alone, you get a more complete picture of your daily sessions and progress if you pair it with other metrics like heart rate or power.

It also takes discipline to train by feel because you have to remain tuned in, and it’s all too easy to slack off when you should be pushing or push too hard on a recovery day.

Great for: Creating specific training zones and tuning into your freshness and/or fatigue

Equipment needed: A heart rate monitor and compatible bike computer or watch

As your effort increases, your heart pumps more oxygen and nutrient-rich blood to fuel your muscles. The result: Your heart rate goes up. Monitoring your heart beats per minute (BPM) with a heart rate monitor will tell you just how hard you’re working.

To use heart rate, you need to first determine your max heart rate (MHR)—or the highest number of BPM you can hit. Forget the generic 220 minus your age formula for determining max heart rate and take a field test instead:

Warm up thoroughly, then do a 10-minute time trial as hard as possible, kicking it into full throttle for the final 60 seconds, aiming to full on sprint the final 20 seconds. Cool down and check your data for MHR. Repeat two more times (with rest days in between) to find your true max. Once you have your max, you can break down various levels of training efforts according to percentages of that number. As you get fitter, you’ll be able to ride faster at lower heart rates.

Overall, heart rate monitoring is an excellent training tool—but there are a few downsides. For one, it’s a little fickle. Your BPM can drift up or down depending on how much coffee you’ve had (caffeine raises it); ambient temperature; your hydration status; your plasma volume; how rested you are; and where you are in your menstrual cycle. It can also drift up within the same ride, especially when it’s hot.

Pairing HR and RPE tracking gives you a more complete picture of your effort. If you’re performing tempo intervals at a target heart rate of 150 BPM and your RPE is around 5, you’re on the money. If you’re performing those same intervals but working at an RPE of 8 to hit that same heart rate, that’s a sign that you’re not recovered and should do an easier workout. There’s also some lag time between the moment you increase intensity and the moment your heart rate reflects it, so it’s not the best tool for high-intensity efforts.

You can monitor your heart rate with a chest strap or wrist-based heart rate monitor via your sports watch. Wrist-based sensors on smartwatches and fitness trackers can be less accurate for cyclists, according to some research. That may be due to the optical sensors having less consistent contact with our wrists as we bend it to grasp our bars.

Great for: The most accurate measure of your effort

Equipment needed: A power meter and a compatible bike computer

Power equals work over time. In cycling, your work rate is described as watts of energy produced: Being able to produce a lot of power for your size makes you faster on the bike. Monitoring your watts with a power meter gives you instant feedback about how hard you’re working.

Power training generally revolves around your functional threshold power, or the wattage you can produce for a one-hour time trial, which is a fundamental benchmark for fitness. A common protocol for determining your FTP is performing a 20-minute time trial and multiplying that average wattage by 0.95, since your hour-long wattage would be about 5 percent lower, according to Allen.

The beauty of power is that it is absolute: You are either producing 350 watts on those hill repeats, or you’re not. If you’re not hitting your intended watts for a given workout, it’s time to rest.

Though power is more precise than heart rate, it’s worthwhile to combine the two, as heart rate represents your body’s response to the work you’re doing. Your heart rate should rise and fall in line with your power output. When your power is low and your heart rate is high, it’s recovery time. If you’re serious about training to the point that you’ve hired a coach, a power meter is a good investment.

Great for: Understanding when you need more recovery time

Equipment needed: An Oura ring, Whoop strap, or specific HRV tracking device

HRV is a relatively new player in the performance tracking sphere. Unlike heart rate, which you watch in real time, HRV is one that you track once a day, preferably first thing in the morning (or if you wear an Oura ring or Whoop strap, you’ll see your average overnight score).

HRV is a good indicator of your recovery and/or readiness. It may seem counterintuitive, but a fit, rested, healthy heart should not beat consistently like a metronome. Instead, it should nimbly respond to input from your sympathetic (fight or flight) and parasympathetic (rest and digest) nervous system.

High variability (reflected in a higher HRV score) shows that you’re ready to go and capable of adapting to your environment and respond to exercise demands to perform well. Low variability between beats can be a sign of stress, fatigue, and inflammation—all things that can follow training too hard with too little recovery.

HRV is specific to each person and naturally declines with age. Though high numbers are considered “better,” high is relative to your own baseline. One person’s high HRV might be 125 while another’s high might be 55.

Referenced regularly, HRV scores will help you track fitness gains. For example, you’ll typically see HRV measurements decrease (become more negative) during long, heavy training blocks. Then you should see a rebound, where your HRV is significantly higher, after a recovery period. An upward trend over time means you’re getting fitter. A downward trend means you’re training too hard and or under too much stress without proper rest and recovery. When using HRV, it’s important not to put too much weight on a single day’s reading, but rather to look at trends and averages over a few days.

You can buy individual HRV monitors like straps and finger clip sensors, but if you’re going to track HRV, you should also track resting heart rate, sleep, and training load and/or activity levels, so you can put it into context. So, a device like a Whoop strap or Oura ring are the way to go, because they automatically put HRV into context of the whole picture. (If you work with a coach, they can as well).

Do you need to track HRV to become a better rider? Of course not. You can generally tell when you need a rest day by feel. But if you routinely train hard and like to dial in your training and lifestyle habits for optimum recovery and training readiness, this is a useful metric to use. It can be especially helpful if you’re trying to establish healthy habits like cutting back on alcohol and getting more sleep, because those types of lifestyle factors show up quickly in HRV scores.

All this measuring and monitoring doesn’t do much good unless you apply it to specific training purposes—that is, training at different effort levels to build specific types of fitness. That’s where training zones come in. Different coaches break down training zones differently, but in general you’ll see effort levels spread out over five to seven zones that range from recovery to max effort. For example, here are five classic training zones:

You need to ride easy so your body can heal, adapt, and get stronger and fitter. Zone 1 rides should feel ridiculously easy. Your only goal is to boost your circulation and promote repair and recovery. These rides hover at one or two on the RPE scale.

Zone 2 is all about aerobic effort. Endurance rides require enough energy to feel like exercise, but still let you carry a conversation, cruise for hours, and enjoy the ride. These efforts stimulate mitochondrial growth and build capillaries and fat-burning capacity. Zone 2 rides are done at an RPE of three to four.

Efforts in Zone 3 are just above your comfort level, so you’re breathing faster and working harder than you would on a typical aerobic, endurance ride. You’re not working so hard, however, that you can’t sustain your effort for a long period of time. Steady Zone 3 tempo efforts improve your body’s ability to clear and use lactic acid, so they also help raise your lactate threshold. They’re done at an RPE of five to six.

If VO2 max is your roof, lactate threshold—the point at which you start working anaerobically—is your drop ceiling. Training in Zone 4, which is right at that point, helps you hit higher intensities before you bump into that overhang. These efforts are done at an RPE of seven to eight.

To raise your VO2max, the maximum amount of oxygen your body can use, you need to push yourself as far into the red as you can go. Zone 5 efforts are done full throttle—a nine to 10 on the RPE scale. Because they’re so hard, they’re also very short, generally lasting three to five minutes.

Here is a sample of basic training zones that incorporate the metrics above. Some coaches will break these down and expand them further or use other metrics such as percent of lactate threshold heart rate as a guide.

#8833. Unlock Your Full Potential by Fixing These Common Triathlon Body Imbalances

Triathletes can face muscle imbalances. These off-season exercises help build proper strength to prepare for next season. (Photo: Brad Kaminski/Triathlete)

Triathlon training is all about repetition, with hours upon hours spent catching and pulling in the pool, turning the pedals on the bike, and turning the legs over on the run. With that repetition comes natural imbalance, with some muscle groups getting overworked while others get neglected (or even weaken with age).

Over time, these imbalances can impact performance directly or indirectly by contributing to injury development. That’s why taking time to identify and address these imbalances now will help keep you healthy in the long run.

By pinpointing areas of weakness or asymmetry early on, athletes can target the stabilizing muscles, improve biomechanical efficiency across all three disciplines, and significantly reduce the risk of overuse injuries that often arise from repetitive strain. Here’s how.

While swimming is generally thought of as the “safest” discipline in triathlon, issues can and do occur, often manifesting as “swimmer’s shoulder.” Swimmer’s shoulder is a bit of a catch-all term for pain in the front of the shoulder that encompasses several pathologies, including rotator cuff issues.

Typically, underlying laxity and instability exist. One factor that can contribute to shoulder problems is a strength imbalance between the shoulder internal and external rotators, with the internal rotators becoming disproportionately strong in comparison to the external rotators. This makes sense, as the shoulder internal rotators are active throughout the catch and pull, working to rotate the arm in and push against water.

But the external rotators still play an important role, as they help to stabilize the shoulder joint, keeping the ball of the joint centered in the socket to help prevent impingement and pain with overhead use and shoulder abnormalities. To decrease injury risk, external rotators should have about two-thirds of the strength of the internal rotators.

The most reliable, valid ways to check this involve specialized dynamometry equipment that measures force. But if you’re just looking to get a general idea, check how many reps of each of the below motions you can do until fatigue.

In this case, the test (lying prone, rotating the back of the arm up) can also be used as an effective strengthening exercise for external rotation. Start with higher reps, lower weights to learn the motion (3 sets of 10-12), then work up to higher weights, lower reps (4 sets of 6-8) to build more strength.

If this position causes pain or is too difficult at first, a side-lying shoulder external rotation is also a good option.

While the incidence of overuse injuries attributed to cycling is generally lower than those attributed to running, they can and do occur, most commonly impacting the knee and lower back. Although singling out contributing factors is difficult, the prolonged posture and muscle activations associated with cycling predispose athletes to overdeveloped quadriceps and an undeveloped posterior chain (glutes, hamstrings, back extensors) and lateral hip muscles.

Cyclists need strong quads – these are the predominant muscle used to power the pedal stroke. But the glutes and hamstrings do assist, so neglecting those leaves some power on the table. Plus, that injury-prone lower back needs adequate strength and endurance to withstand hours spent in a forward-flexed position.

Also, because muscle weakness and tightness often go hand-in-hand, related limitations in mobility throughout the posterior chain limit a cyclist’s ability to comfortably hold more aggressive aero positions. Those quads of steel will only help so much if you’re sitting up to ease back and glute discomfort by the end of a long ride!

The strength and endurance of the posterior chain (and also the lateral hip, which can play a role when it comes to knee pain on the bike) can be checked using a single-leg bridge hold.

The single-leg RDL is a good choice for eliciting both high force and stretch in the hamstrings and strengthening the gluteal muscles, back extensors, and lateral hips. Isolating each leg can also help with side-to-side imbalances.

When it comes to muscle strength and running, the glutes have been frequently implicated as the cause of (and solution to) many issues. But, while the glutes do play an important stability-related role in the run gait and deficits have been linked with injury, the true workhorse of the run gait – the calves – often gets overlooked and under-strengthened.

The soleus (one of the calf muscles) experiences forces of up to eight times body weight and produces up to 50% of forward propulsive power while running. Because the calves insert onto the heel via the Achilles tendon (which acts as a spring during running), the two are linked, with decreased calf strength seen in athletes with Achilles issues compared to healthy controls.

Strong calves can also help to protect against tibial bone stress injuries. Masters athletes lose calf strength (and Achilles tendon stiffness) disproportionately to other muscle groups with age, leading to both a reduction in propulsion and step length and an increased risk of lower leg soft tissue injuries such as strains and tendinopathies. So, when it comes to both performance and helping to guard against many common lower leg injuries, first check the powerhouse muscles below the knee!

Calf strength can be tested with a single-leg calf raise test.

The test here can again be used as the exercise – just load it up!

So, while the different disciplines and repeated motions of triathlon might lend athletes to certain imbalances, not all is lost! Triathletes can make themselves stronger, more resilient, and faster with some awareness and work – so don’t neglect those details.

Imagine checking into a Park Hyatt — marble floors, a sommelier who remembers your name by day two, a room that costs $400 a night — and knowing you paid for it with points you earned by writing your rent check. Not by flying 100,000 miles. Not by spending on a business credit card. By paying the bill you were already going to pay anyway. That's the emotional core of this sweet spot, and it's one of the most powerful entry points into travel rewards for the ChooseFI community. Rent is typically your single largest monthly expense, and for years it was a dead end — money out the door with zero return. Bilt Rewards changed that equation entirely. Here's the math that should stop you mid-scroll: a single night at a Category 4 Hyatt — think Hyatt Place in a major city or a solid Park Hyatt property in a secondary market — costs around $150–$250 in cash. With World of Hyatt points, that same night runs 15,000 points. Transfer your Bilt points at a 1:1 ratio, and you've just redeemed at roughly 1–1.7 cents per point at the low end. But at a Category 6 or 7 property — a Grand Hyatt in Tokyo, a Alila in Bali, an Andaz on the Sunset Strip — cash rates climb to $350–$600 per night while the award chart holds steady. That's where you hit **4–8 cents per point**, the upper end of what any hotel currency in the world delivers. The CPP range for this redemption runs **2–8 cents per point**, with a retail value of **$100–$400 per redemption unit**. In loyalty currency terms, that's elite-tier performance. Most hotel points deliver 0.5–0.8 cents. Hyatt points, earned through your rent payment and transferred instantly, routinely deliver 3–5x that value. This is a **pricing inefficiency built into Hyatt's fixed award chart**. Hyatt hasn't aggressively devalued the way other programs have. The chart still prices aspirational properties at points levels that don't reflect their true cash cost — and Bilt gives you a direct pipeline to those points through the expense you can't avoid. For anyone on the path to FI, that's not a hack. That's just math working in your favor.

Why rent-to-hotel is one of the most accessible travel rewards sweet spots

The core insight here has two parts, and understanding both will change how you think about every dollar of rent you pay going forward.

Part One: Bilt Is the Only Card That Earns Points on Rent With No Fee

Most landlords don't accept credit cards. Those that do typically charge a 2–3% processing fee, which instantly erases any rewards value. Bilt solved this by partnering directly with property management companies and creating a system where you pay rent via the Bilt app, and the payment processes as ACH (no fee to you or your landlord), while Bilt credits your account with points. You earn 1x point per dollar on rent, up to 100,000 points per year. On a $2,000/month rent payment, that's 24,000 Hyatt points annually from a bill you were paying anyway. Zero incremental spend. Zero fees.

The one rule to know: you must make at least 5 transactions on your Bilt card each statement period to earn points on rent. Five purchases — even five $1 transactions — unlocks the rent earnings. This is a simple, low-lift requirement.

Part Two: World of Hyatt's Fixed Award Chart Is the Unlock

Once your Bilt points are sitting in your account, you transfer them to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio, and the transfer is instant. No waiting 3–5 business days. No points in limbo while availability disappears. You search, you find availability, you transfer, you book — in a single session if you want.

Hyatt's award chart is category-based, fixed pricing from 3,500 points (Category 1) to 45,000 points (Category 8) per night. This is the inefficiency. When a Park Hyatt in a major international city costs $500 in cash but only 30,000 points (Category 6), you're extracting 1.67 cents per point at minimum — and in peak season when cash rates hit $700, you're at 2.3+ cpp. The chart doesn't move with cash prices.

What makes this particularly powerful for the ChooseFI community is the no fuel surcharges policy — Hyatt charges zero fuel surcharges on award stays, so 15,000 points always means exactly 15,000 points out of your account. No surprise $75 "carrier fees" tacked on at checkout.

The transfer path is: Bilt Rewards → World of Hyatt at 1:1, instant. Chase Ultimate Rewards also transfers to Hyatt at 1:1 instantly, which means if you hold a Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve, you have a second pipeline to the same program — an important redundancy for maximizing this sweet spot.

For 5,000 points — a single night at a Category 1 or 2 property — you're looking at a $100–$150 night that might cost you 2.5 months of coffee purchases on the Bilt card. That's the entry point. The ceiling is a $400+ night at a Category 5–7 property for 20,000–30,000 points. Both ends of the spectrum represent exceptional value, which is rare in any loyalty program.

Head to biltrewards.com and apply for the Bilt Mastercard (issued by Wells Fargo). The card has no annual fee. Once approved, add the card to your Bilt app and register your rent payment. If your building is in the Bilt Alliance (a growing network of partnered properties), setup is seamless. If not, you can still pay rent through the Bilt app via ACH transfer — Bilt mails a check to your landlord on your behalf, and you still earn points.

Key setup rule: Activate rent rewards in the app before your first payment cycle.

Before rent points post, you need five qualifying purchases on your Bilt card that statement period. Set up small recurring charges — a streaming subscription, a coffee shop, a weekly grocery run — and you'll hit this automatically. Don't forget this step; missing it means forfeiting that month's rent points.

Go to world.hyatt.com and use the award availability search. Select "Use Points" and search your destination and dates. Hyatt's search shows availability up to 395 days in advance — one of the longest windows in the hotel loyalty space. Identify your property, confirm the points price and availability, then — and only then — proceed to transfer.

Never transfer points without confirmed availability. Even though Hyatt availability is generally strong, you want to lock in what you see before moving irreversible points.

In the Bilt app, navigate to "Redeem" → "Transfer Points" and select World of Hyatt. Enter the exact number of points you need. The transfer is instant — points appear in your Hyatt account within minutes, not days. This is one of Bilt's most underrated features and means you can act on last-minute availability without risk.

Return to world.hyatt.com, confirm your points balance has updated, and complete your booking. You'll pay zero fuel surcharges — the points cost is the only cost. You can also call the World of Hyatt reservations line if you need help with a complex booking or want to stack a free night certificate.

If your first-choice property is sold out on points, try these tactics:

Hotel loyalty programs use "award charts" that assign each property a category level with a fixed points price. When a hotel's cash rate rises due to demand or location, the points price stays the same. This creates the value gap that makes points redemptions worthwhile. Hyatt's chart is considered the most generous among major hotel chains because it has resisted the aggressive devaluations that Hilton and Marriott have implemented. A Category 7 property might cost $500-$800 per night in cash but only 30,000 points. That gap is where your 4-8 cents per point value comes from.

Let's make this concrete. You've been paying $1,800/month in rent for the past year, diligently hitting your five monthly transactions. Your Bilt account holds approximately 21,600 points (1x on rent, plus some bonus earning on the card). You're planning a long weekend in Nashville with your partner.

The Property: Hyatt Place Nashville Downtown. Category 3, costing 12,000 World of Hyatt points per night. Cash rate for a Friday–Sunday stay: $189/night, totaling $378 for two nights before taxes and fees. With taxes, you're looking at roughly $430 out of pocket.

The Points Play: Transfer 24,000 Bilt points to Hyatt instantly, book two nights. Total points spent: 24,000. Total cash paid: $0 (Hyatt charges no fuel surcharges, no award fees).

The CPP calculation: $378 cash value ÷ 24,000 points = 1.58 cents per point at the conservative end. Factor in the taxes you're also avoiding (most properties don't charge taxes on award stays), and your effective CPP climbs closer to 1.8–2 cents per point.

Now scale up. Apply the same 24,000 points to a single night at Park Hyatt Chicago — a Category 7 property. Cash rate: $550–$700/night on a peak weekend. Points cost: 30,000 per night (you'll need to save a couple extra months). At $600 cash value for 30,000 points, you're at 2 cents per point — but if you hit a $700 night, that's 2.33 cpp.

The experience itself? Park Hyatt properties deliver: floor-to-ceiling windows, complimentary minibar items, a spa, and a level of service that genuinely doesn't feel like a "points hotel." You're not using a coupon at a budget chain — you're staying at the same property business travelers expense at full rate, experiencing everything they experience, funded almost entirely by the rent check you wrote anyway.

If you hold Hyatt Globalist status, suite upgrades on award stays are available based on availability — turning a 30,000-point redemption into a $900+ suite night. That's where the CPP ceiling of 8 cents per point becomes real.

World of Hyatt awards include a fifth-night-free benefit on standard award redemptions when you book five or more consecutive nights. On a five-night stay at a Category 5 property (20,000 points/night), you'd normally pay 100,000 points — but with the fifth night free, it's 80,000 points for five nights. That's a 20% improvement in value with zero extra effort. Plan longer trips to unlock this.

Do: Book 395 Days Out for Peak Destinations

Hyatt opens award inventory at the same time as cash inventory — 395 days in advance. For high-demand properties (think Park Hyatt Maldives at Hadahaa or Alila Ventana Big Sur), availability at standard rates disappears quickly. Set a calendar reminder and search early.

If you hold a Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve, your Chase Ultimate Rewards points also transfer to Hyatt at 1:1, instantly. This means you have two separate point pools feeding the same program — Bilt for rent earnings and Chase for everyday spending. Together, you can accumulate Hyatt points significantly faster and take on higher-category properties.

Avoid: Transferring Points Before Confirming Availability

Bilt-to-Hyatt transfers are instant and irreversible. If you transfer 30,000 points and then can't find the availability you thought you saw, those points are now in Hyatt — and if you don't use them, they expire after 24 months of account inactivity. Always search Hyatt first, confirm dates and property, then transfer.

Avoid: Missing the 5-Transaction Monthly Minimum

This is the most common Bilt mistake. If you forget to make five purchases on your Bilt card in a given month, you earn zero points on rent — not reduced points, zero. Automate five small recurring charges to the card and never think about it again.

Do: Target Category 4–6 Properties for Best Value

Category 1–3 properties offer solid value, but the CPP accelerates meaningfully in Categories 4–6 (15,000–25,000 points/night) where cash rates are $200–$400 but points costs haven't kept pace. This is the sweet spot within the sweet spot.

Do: Watch for Hyatt's Points + Cash Awards

Hyatt offers a Points + Cash option at roughly half the standard award rate, combined with a cash co-pay. If your Hyatt balance is small, this lets you access properties without waiting to accumulate a full award.

This redemption was built for renters — specifically, renters who are already on the path to FI and feel the friction of paying rent every month with nothing to show for it. If you pay at least $1,000/month in rent, this sweet spot is generating meaningful Hyatt points from dollar one. At $2,000/month, you're accumulating 24,000 Hyatt points per year from rent alone — enough for two nights at a Category 5 property or a single aspirational night at a Park Hyatt.

Minimum to make it work: You need at least 5,000 Hyatt points for a Category 1 redemption — easily achievable after 5–6 months of rent payments on a $1,000/month lease. For aspirational Category 6–7 stays, you're targeting 25,000–30,000 points, which takes planning but is absolutely achievable.

This isn't the right fit if you own your home (no rent to earn on), if you're already deep into a competing hotel loyalty program, or if your primary travel goal is international business class flights — in that case, transferable airline currencies deserve more of your attention first. But for hotel stays, especially in the U.S., this is the single most frictionless on-ramp into the Hyatt ecosystem available anywhere.

This redemption earns a **5/5 for beginner friendliness**, and that rating is accurate — but it helps to understand exactly *why* it's easy, so you don't accidentally make it harder than it needs to be. **What makes it easy:** - Earning is passive. Once your Bilt card is set up and rent is registered, points accrue automatically with no behavior change required (beyond five small monthly transactions). - The transfer is instant — no waiting, no uncertainty, no risk of availability disappearing while points are in transit. - Hyatt's award chart is fixed and transparent. You can see exactly what a property costs before you transfer a single point. - No fuel surcharges means no unpleasant surprises at checkout. **The one area that trips beginners up:** forgetting the five-transaction monthly minimum. This is the single most common Bilt mistake, and it's entirely preventable. Set up five small autopay charges on your Bilt card — a $5 streaming service, a recurring Amazon purchase, anything — and you'll never miss it. **Tip for the first redemption:** Start with a Category 3 or 4 Hyatt Place or Hyatt Regency for a domestic weekend trip. The points requirement is low (8,000–15,000 points), availability is widely open, and the booking process is identical to any other Hyatt stay. It's a low-stakes way to see the entire system work from earning to booking. If you can pay rent, own a smartphone, and make five purchases a month, you can execute this redemption. The ChooseFI community has embraced this one for good reason — it's genuinely the most accessible entry point into premium hotel travel rewards available today.

No. Bilt works with any landlord that accepts payment. If your building is not in the Bilt Alliance, Bilt processes the payment via ACH. The only difference is Alliance buildings may offer additional perks like bonus points or rent credits.

You will still pay your rent through Bilt, but you will earn zero points on that month's rent payment. The five-transaction requirement resets monthly. Set up autopay on small recurring charges to prevent this.

Bilt caps rent earning at 100,000 points per month (equivalent to $100,000 in rent at 1x). For the vast majority of renters, this cap is irrelevant. There is no annual cap on total points earned.

The Bilt-to-Hyatt pipeline is the most accessible travel rewards sweet spot available today. You are already paying rent. The Bilt card has no annual fee. Hyatt points deliver 2-8 cents in value. The transfer is instant. If you rent and you are not earning Hyatt points from that rent payment, you are leaving hundreds of dollars in annual hotel value on the table. #8831. The Brooks Launch 12 Helps You Run Fast—and Save Big

This affordable trainer has racing shoe DNA.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

The Launch 12 is cushier than a racing flat but can handle hard workouts on the track and on the road. The affordable trainer—a bargain buy for $120—won’t break the bank, but it doesn’t feel cheaply made. The Launch has that Brooks touch; the comfy fit that securely locks your foot inside an airy mesh upper.

We included the Launch 12 in our Best Affordable Shoes guide because it’s an excellent choice for runners wanting a designated trainer for fast days. It’s also a sweet, cheaper lower-stacked alternative in a sea of towering, high-cushioned models.

For the runner who says the Brooks Ghost is too bulky and boxy, the Launch 12 could be your sole mate.

I’ve added track workouts to my training this year after finally overcoming my fear of the dreaded all-eyes-on-me oval. It’s fun to go balls-to-the-wall in today’s super trainers and high stacks during speed sessions, but I sometimes desire a more grounded, minimally designed trainer to really test my fitness. The Brooks Launch 12 is that shoe.

Finding out there’s DNA Flash v2 foam in the Launch 12 is like finding an Easter egg in a movie. It’s a callout to the Hyperion Elite 4, Brooks’s premium racing shoe model. The shoe originally had nitrogen-infused DNA Flash v2 foam to pump up your ride before switching to DNA Gold (PEBA, baby) in the Hyperion Elite 5. But it can’t be ignored that DNA Flash v2 was a form of Brooks’s original super foam.

This gives the shoe a firm, snappy ride with plenty of padding for shock absorption. It’s not max-cushioned, and certainly not super trainer height at 35 mm, but it packs plenty of support for hard and long efforts.

“Typically, I’m a fan of the middle ground when it comes to trainers,” said Content Hyper Editor Ashley Tysiac. “I like to have a shoe with enough cushioning that I feel like my feet are supported, but not too much that I feel like my feet are being weighed down by bricks. This shoe was a pleasant break from some of the heavier, maximalist trainers that I’ve tried in the past couple of years. It’s a lightweight shoe that provides a firm ride.

“There’s not a ton of give to the shoe or spring in its step, but I didn’t mind that. The firm, easy ride was something I could enjoy on regular runs, long runs, and even some runs with faster-paced segments in the middle.”

The Launch 12 is built like a track shoe with its narrow, streamlined last. Tester Ricky Snyder said he had no issues with the fit, saying everything was “perfect, no hot spots or cramping in the toe box, no hard or rubbing plastic parts.”

However, Tysiac—and I—found the Launch 12’s midfoot a wee too snug.

“I wasn’t a huge fan of the lacing system,” she said. “No matter how many times I loosened and re-laced my shoes, it always felt too tight through the midfoot area, causing some noticeable discomfort.”

As a runner with wide feet, I couldn’t agree more with Tysiac. Compared to Brooks’s Hyperion 3, which also has DNA Flash v2 foam along a knit upper that hugs your foot, I felt the Launch 12 was much narrower and constrictive. The Hyperion 3 costs $20 extra, and speaking from experience, it could be worth the spending if you have wide feet like mine.

The Launch 12 is a shoe for runners looking to find a cheaper alternative to the more costly speedwork ones on the market, but it’s also for runners who miss shoes pre-super foam. The shoe may have an older midsole version of Brooks’s special sauce, but the ride takes you back to simple days, when a firmly cushioned trainer was all you needed to get in a run.

“I took out the Brooks Launch 12 on a variety of runs, including regular runs, regular runs with pickups in the middle, and long runs. Perhaps the shoe’s best feature that stands out is how light it is, providing a ride that doesn’t feel too bogged down. They felt light enough to rip off some faster-paced fartlek segments during the middle of a regular run, but still supportive enough to make it through a longer run.”

For $120, you’ll find a trainer that can take on multiple workouts. The Launch 12 is a good deal for the runner looking to save.

#8830. Don’t Let a Flat Tire End Your Ride. Here’s What I Carry in My Ride-Rescue Kit

A practical guide to building a flat kit that gets you home without overloading your bike.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

There are so many options out there when setting up a flat tire kit. During my time in bike shops I sold every flat kit you could imagine—from the basic prepackaged flat repair kits to repair kits that could fix almost anything on the bike. When you have the right pieces of gear, it can make the difference between an easy roadside fix and finding a plan B to get home.

Building the right kit can make the difference between fixing the bike mid-ride and needing an unexpected pickup. One key is bringing the things you need and not what you don’t—then knowing how to use the tools in your kit.

Even on bikes you’ve had for a while it can be worth revisiting what’s sitting in your flat pack. Below I’ll walk you through what’s in my basic flat kit, why I pick those pieces, and why you should intermittently check out your flat pack to prevent any roadside surprises.

The tire levers are the foundation of any good flat repair kit—after all, you won’t be able to fix a flat very well if you can’t get the tire off and back on. I’ve gone through many different lever options over the years in my own flat kits, as well as from my time running a bike shop. The tire levers I swear by are the Pedro’s yellow tire levers. They are burly enough to be reliable and durable—I’m rarely worried about snapping a Pedro’s lever even on a tight tire.

The one thing many people don’t think about with levers is that sometimes you drop them or put them down when you’re trying to manage the roadside repair. The Pedro’s levers are easy to find thanks to their bright yellow color.

One runner-up is the tire lever from Muc-Off. They are similar in size, durability, and come in bright and easy to find colors. Personally I have not had the same amount of time using Muc-Off levers compared to the Pedro’s levers. One final tip: don’t use metal levers. Yes, they are burly, but they can easily damage rims when trying to get a tire off—especially carbon.

The traditional tube you may have gotten the last time you stopped in your local shop while picking up a tube to fix a flat at home is a great option to put in your flat pack, but there are other options. TPU and latex tubes are popular because of their light weight and small packed size.

I typically go with a standard tube on most of my flat kits. This is because I typically ride all year round and some of those lighter and more packable materials for tubes are more sensitive to temperature. If you’re a fair-weather rider, however, it can be worth considering a TPU or latex tube. Just remember to double-check that both the tube and valve size are correct for the wheels you are using.

One note on checking out your tubes: check to make sure the tube is in good condition every few months. I was on a ride recently where someone got a flat and his multitool was against the tube in his saddle bag. The multitool rubbed a hole into the side of the tube making it useless. He said he had not inspected that tube in at least a year. Luckily we had an extra tube for him and could keep rolling, but a quick check could have prevented him pulling a tube from someone else’s flat kit.

Similar to tire levers, I’ve used many different inflators over the years. My favorites to use are either the PDW CO2 inflator or the Muc-Off Inflator. These two options are durable and are easy to use with gloves on—which is especially helpful as we get into some cooler temperatures.

I carry two cans of CO2 because I’ve run into several experiences before where one ends up not being enough. It could be because I used one to try to add a burst of air in the hopes my tubeless system would fill the hole with sealant and I could go on my way. I’ve also had user error experiences where I simply didn’t get the canister on correctly and most or all of the air rushed out of the canister. In any case, they don’t take up much space, but having a backup is a key piece of the flat kit.

There are other inflation options you can go with too. Electronic pumps have been growing in popularity over the last few years, with test editor Dan Chabanov recently calling out the Cycplus AS2 Ultra Electric Inflator as his inflator of choice. I typically add a frame-mounted pump on longer rides, because these can’t run out of battery and as long as you can still pump you won’t run out of available air.

You’d be surprised what you can fix with a few zip ties. I’ve used these packable and inexpensive additions to fix issues like broken bottle cage bolts and broken cable and housing guides. I’ve had friends who have reattached things like derailleurs and saddle bags with a few strategically placed zip ties.

When I ride I typically carry a $10 bill and a single dollar bill. I know $11 seems like a random amount of money to carry on the bike. But the single and the ten serve two different purposes. A single dollar bill works as a great tire boot if you have a large gash in your tire. Simply put the dollar bill inside the tire against the gash before putting the tube in. If you run tubeless you can apply a little sealant from inside the tire to the dollar bill to help it stick better against the tire. Then when you inflate your tube, the pressure of the tube inside the tire will keep the dollar bill in place. The dollar bill will protect the tube from the elements and the road surface outside the tire.

The ten-dollar bill is your backup plan. I’ve been on rides before where I underestimated the amount of hydration and nutrition I needed to get through an effort. Having a few dollars for a gas station or convenience store refuel stop has dragged me out of the hole more than once. Most places these days take digital forms of payment like Apple Pay, but if you’re riding in more remote areas cash can be king.

A multitool that has the basic Allen keys and screwdriver that you’ll need is essential. If it has sizes 4, 5, and 6 you’ll be able to take care of most roadside fixes or adjustments you might ride into.

I personally like to bring a multitool with a chain breaker because I’ve had to fix a chain more than once on a ride. If fixing a chain is something you want to be prepared for on your ride, consider bringing a quick link that is compatible with your chain. They are another small and relatively inexpensive addition to your flat kit that can save plenty of headaches. A broken chain doesn’t have to be the end of your ride if you have the tools and the knowledge to piece it back together.

Different bikes have different ways to carry all this stuff. Some bikes have internal frame storage, some saddles have integrated mounts for certain bags, and some bikes have dropper posts that are only compatible with select saddle bags. On really short road rides I’ve even just thrown the basics of my flat kit in a jersey pocket. Personally, I typically put my flat repair kit into a frame bag, saddle bag, or utilize the internal frame storage so I can keep the extra weight and bulk off my body. If you have any essentials in your flat kit that I don’t include in mine let me know in the comments below.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

#8829. How to Master the Run/Walk Method: Tracking Your Intervals

Proper tracking and workout structure can lead to success using this training technique.

Whether you’re aiming for a 16-minute or 8-minute mile pace, utilizing a balanced run/walk interval structure makes for more efficient workouts, better fitness progression, and stronger race performances.

It’s not necessarily how fast you’re going, but the intention behind your intervals that dictates your training and racing success with the run/walk method. Your walk breaks shouldn’t feel like a casual stroll through the park, nor should your run intervals translate to an all-out sprint effort. With the Runner’s World program, How to Master the Run/Walk Method, you’ll learn how to best manage your efforts, organize your intervals, and track your sessions.

From nailing your interval durations to finding your preferred training tracker, you’ll discover how to implement the run/walk method consistently into your routine—and start seeing results in your fitness and race performances.

In Runner’s World’s How to Master the Run/Walk Method: Tracking Your Intervals, we’ll teach you:

While you can use either time or distance to log your run/walks, we recommend starting with time-based intervals, especially if you’re new to running or the run/walk method. You’ll split your running and walking intervals into specified periods of seconds or minutes, rather than distance logged.

If you’re using a training plan such as Runner’s World Start Running or Run Nonstop plan, you’ll gradually increase your run time while shortening your walk time until your walk breaks disappear altogether. But with the run/walk method, you’ll always have walk breaks built in, and you’ll adjust your run interval based on your current goal or race pace.

Notice that no matter your overall pace, you can allot 30 seconds of walking. It’s an ideal interval duration for reaping the recovery benefits of walking without significantly affecting your pace.

As your pace increases, the larger your run-to-walk ratio will become, translating to more time spent running. For example, you may run for two minutes and walk for 30 seconds to hit a 9-minute mile, but when your goal is to shoot for an 8-minute mile, you’ll run for longer (four minutes) to hit a quicker pace.

Instead of focusing on a specific number or pace, use feel to guide your walk intervals. Be intentional with your walks, keeping them brisk but allowing your heart rate to drop and your muscles to enjoy some recovery. Your walk effort should feel significantly less intense than your run portions.

“I tell my runners you should be walking not like you’re looking for sharks’ teeth on the beach or cracks in the sidewalk. You should feel like you’ve got someplace to be, but you shouldn’t get into the race walking motion that you would see in the Olympics,” says Chris Twiggs, chief training officer at Galloway Training.

As you get faster as a walker, you’ll take some of the pressure off of having to run faster to stick with your goal pace. You may also notice more efficient transitions from walk to run, and vice versa, as you improve your speed.

Because run/walk sessions require meticulous tracking, you’ll want to use an interval timer for optimal results. Your smartwatch or fitness tracker may have interval capabilities, but an interval timer is the best tool for accurately structuring your run/walks. Set your run/walk ratios on the timer before your workout, and attach it to your jacket or waistband. The timer will buzz to alert you during your workout when it’s time to run or walk.

If you’re logging your workouts on a fitness tracker or app like Strava, don’t worry about pressing pause during your walk intervals. Keeping the clock going during your entire workout gives you a more accurate representation of your effort, which makes tracking your fitness progress clearer. After each session, write down your total distance, interval ratio, and how you felt during the workout to measure both your objective and subjective progress.

The last component to consider before heading out the door? Shoes. Lace up a pair of comfortable and supportive shoes to power your run/walk workouts. While most run/walkers should rely on run shoes that transition smoothly between intervals, your shoe choice depends on your preferences and experience. Find your ideal shoe by consulting our run/walk shoe guide, curated by Runner’s World gear experts after putting a variety of models through extensive wear testing.

“The main things to look for [in run/walk shoes] are cushioning, support, and durability,” says Carissa Galloway, RDN, certified personal trainer and race commentator. “If you’re just starting out, a shoe with higher stability is important.”

Ashley is Editor of Content Hype at Hearst’s Enthusiast & Wellness Group. She is a former collegiate runner at UNC Asheville where she studied mass communication. Ashley loves all things running; she has raced two marathons, plus has covered some of the sport’s top events in her career, including the Paris Olympics, U.S. Olympic Trials and multiple World Marathon Majors.

#8828. These Alignment Tips Are the Key to Balancing in Half Moon Pose

(Photo: Andrew Clark; Design in Canva by Laura Harold)

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about how to do Half Moon Pose first appeared in the January-February 2003 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

Every yoga pose is but a wrapper for its unique internal gift. Ardha Chandrasana (Half Moon Pose) gives you the license to fly. With only one hand and one foot touching the ground, the rest of your body is free to soar. Your body stretches from head to heel, creating a sense of wide-dancing euphoria. Your heart center opens, expanding to embrace all the world. Among the standing poses, Ardha Chandrasana offers unique access to this vast, unbridled freedom of the heart.

Yet to achieve this unbounded freedom, we must first ground ourselves in a myriad of details. I am frequently asked, “Why are there so many details to attend to in each pose? Why should I make a conscious effort to straighten my legs, rotate my hips, or lift the inner arches of my feet in Ardha Chandrasana? Why not just switch off my brain, relax, and feel?”

I have found that attending to detail actually deepens the ability to feel, rather than hindering it, and makes it possible to receive the inner gifts of yoga. Though details can sometimes be overwhelming, attention to them refines your evolution and gives you great fulfillment and joy.

On the most basic level, details protect you during your practice. On another level, details ensure that you receive the benefits of the pose; detailed instructions help you bring the specific energetic gift of the pose into yourself. For energy to flow correctly, precise alignment is required. Without alignment, energy drains away and the pose collapses.

Of course, refinements can be carried too far, and you can become so focused on details that you lose sight of the large energy flows that circulate through the whole body. The general rule is that you need enough detail so that there will be no injury to the body *and* so that the pose serves its unique function. A useful approach, especially at first, is to work on just one or two details each time you practice the pose, gradually adding more subtle details after you attain the basics of the physical alignment. Trying to do subtle inner work before becoming physically aligned will lead to a collapse in the posture and a sense of frustration.

Details have more profound purposes as well. When you work on generalities, your mind is dull. When you start to focus on detail—in Ardha Chandrasana or in any pose—your awareness is refined. And awareness is the essence of yoga. Through the attention to detail in your practice, through the cultivation of refinement, and through the constant and ever more careful attention to your existence, you will slowly become aware of the soft, inner voice that will guide you to your spirit and to your fulfillment.

Supta Padangusthasana II (Reclining Hand-to-Big-Toe Pose, side variation) prepares you for Ardha Chandrasana, since it contains all the major movements of Ardha Chandrasana but does not require you to bear weight or to balance. Working on this pose will prevent strain in the buttock muscles as you later try to hold the leg up in Ardha Chandrasana.

To do Supta Padangusthasana II, lie on your back with both legs straight. Bend your right leg and catch your right big toe with the first two fingers of your right hand. (Use a belt around the instep of the foot if you cannot reach your toe.) Exhaling, slowly straighten your right leg completely, fully contracting the thigh muscles of both legs. You should maintain this quadriceps contraction throughout the pose. On your next exhalation, press your right sitting bone away from your head and bring your right leg out to the right side and down toward the ground; if possible, rest the outer right ankle on the floor.

Rather than letting your left hip rise, work to make both iliac crests (front hip bones) equidistant from the floor. This will create flexibility in the adductors and release tense muscles in the front of your pelvis so that when you do Ardha Chandrasana, the pelvis will rest evenly on the head of the standing-leg femur (thighbone). Press your left thigh into the floor. Placing your left hand on your left frontal pelvis, pull it to the left to help open it (Figure 1). Stay for three to nine deep breaths. Exhaling, bring your right leg up so that your arm is once again perpendicular to the floor. Release your right foot, bringing it back down beside the left. Repeat on the other side.

Yoga practitioners move into Ardha Chandrasana from Trikonasana (Figure 2) because the pelvis and the front-leg thighbone are in similar positions in both poses. If you can maintain their placement as you move into Ardha Chandrasana, the pose becomes much easier.

In Trikonasana, take a deep inhalation and visualize your body moving to the next step. Slowly bend your right knee, keeping the right hip externally rotated. Reach forward with your right hand and place the fingertips on the floor about one-and-a-half feet in front of your right foot and slightly to the little toe side (Figure 3). On an exhalation, shift more weight onto your right hand, lifting the left leg toward the ceiling until it becomes parallel to the floor. If you cannot lift your left leg directly from Trikonasana, slide your left foot closer to your right before coming up. Keep your left hand stable and reaching up toward the ceiling throughout your transition. This will greatly improve your balance.

As you move into Ardha Chandrasana, spread the toes and toe mounds of both feet as far apart as you can. This will energize your feet, bring vitality to your brain, and stabilize your movement. Straighten the right leg, powerfully rotating your hip externally so that the right kneecap continues to face your right toes. Even after your right knee is completely straight, continue to rotate the right hip externally. This is the most important action for maintaining safety in the pose, since it protects your inner knee ligaments, a place where many people have searing pain from hyperextension. This rotation also places the head of your femur accurately into joint so that when you lift the left side of your pelvis, you will place your weight evenly on the right hip joint.

Once in Ardha Chandrasana, distribute your weight evenly between the inner and outer foot of your supporting leg. You will notice that your weight tends to drop to your outer foot. To counteract this, consciously press the big toe mound and the inner heel into the floor while lifting your arch. This action will improve your sense of balance because your foot is the foundation of your pose; its lateral stability will determine the stability of your knee and hip.

If your right knee has rotated internally and you find it difficult to rotate it externally, bend your knee a bit. This action will release your hip and make rotation easier. If your standing-leg knee hyperextends, press the calf muscle forward toward your shin, microbend your knee, and press the top of your thigh (the upper quadriceps) back toward your hamstrings. Maintaining both these movements realigns your leg and prevents your knee joint from locking and distorting.

Now lift your left ilium (hip bone) toward the ceiling. Be careful not to press it back, for this will jam your sacroiliac joints and may eventually cause a compression injury. Another point of caution: Lifting your left ilium will tend to make your right leg rotate internally, and this must be resisted to prevent the damage to your inner knee ligaments. Your right leg’s external rotation must always take priority over the lift of your left ilium. When you do become able to lift your left ilium while maintaining the right hip’s external rotation, you will find that the weight of your body will rest on the center of the hip joint, thereby relieving tension in the outer muscles of your right leg, where many beginners get cramps. For additional stability of your right hip, hug your right outer thigh toward your inner thigh before lifting the left ilium.

The outer right ankle bone, the outer right knee, and the greater trochanter of the right leg (the bony knob at the top outer edge of the thigh) should be in one straight line perpendicular to the floor. If your standing leg is leaning toward your head, there will be compression in the rear of that hip joint and excessive weight in the hand and head. Alternately, if your standing leg is leaning toward your back leg, there will be compression in the front of your standing-leg hip joint and your back leg will then feel sluggish and heavy.

Your standing leg should also be perpendicular when viewed from the side. The right sitting bone tends to fall behind you, which collapses your right groin and puts tension in your outer right hip. Press the outer right hip forward until your right sitting bone is directly above your right heel. Simultaneously, lift your right outer ankle and outer leg toward your hip.

To add a more rigorous element of truth to the alignment of your legs, practice this pose with a wall behind you, placing the little toe of your right foot next to the wall and your right heel approximately a half-inch away from the wall. This makes the pose more difficult because your standing leg is now prevented from dropping backward. In this position, you must squeeze your outer right leg inward and lift your left pelvis straight up in order to do the pose.

Energize the muscles throughout both your legs, creating a sense of compactness, as if all the flesh of your legs is being drawn into your bones. This will create a feeling that your right leg has become a pillar supporting your body; it will also make your left leg feel much lighter.

Ardha Chandrasana not only strengthens the legs but also uses the standing leg to bring energy up from the earth. This upward drawing of energy is a foundational principle in yoga and in many martial arts; it is why you contract your quadriceps in the standing poses. When your quadriceps are relaxed, energy does not lift up your inner legs; when you pull the quadriceps up, they become “pumps” that bring the energy from the earth into your pelvis, where your root chakra and second chakra reside. These chakras cannot function well without a flow of energy. Ardha Chandrasana gives you an opportunity to create this flow.

There are other actions that assist this process of lifting energy. I have found that only through combining the lift of the arches and the lift of the quadriceps can the energy of the earth be transmitted into the pelvis and transmuted into corporeal energy. Lift the arch of your standing leg, suck energy up your inner leg through your groin, and feed the energy into the pelvis via a slight lift of your perineum (Mula Bandha). To accomplish these actions, begin by pressing down the mound of your big toe and the inner heel of your standing leg. To create stability, the outer edge of your standing foot also has to be pressed down strongly.

Thus, you will create arches both lengthwise and widthwise, between your big toe and heel as well as between the inner edge and outer edge of your foot.

Now turn your attention to the left leg. As you continue to rotate the right hip externally (so your knee points directly toward the middle of your foot), externally rotate your left leg so that your left kneecap faces front. Once your left kneecap is facing front, do not rotate your left hip any further.

The next action in your left leg should be to press the top of your thigh back toward your hamstrings; then lengthen the back of your leg into your heel. Simultaneously, draw the left side of the pit of your abdomen—the region of your belly just above your pubic bone—toward your head, creating a stretch across your left groin. This will prevent your left thighbone from falling forward and your left buttock from over-contracting.

To prevent fatigue in the left leg, press it down as if you were resting it on a big balloon. Instead of hanging the upper leg from the outer hip muscles, contract your inner thigh muscles toward your outer thigh. This will take the tension out of your outer hip muscles and strengthen your inner leg, including your adductors.

Two primary actions that are involved in Ardha Chandrasana are the “stacking” of the pelvis and the lifting of the pit of the abdomen. The stacking of your pelvis on your right hip joint not only ensures your safety but also aligns your pelvis to receive energy from your right leg. When the left side of your pelvis moves away from the right foot in Ardha Chandrasana, you will get the sense of your pelvis as an ever-widening bowl. This widening makes the pelvis available for the energy that rises from the earth through your standing leg.

Similarly, the lift of the pit of your abdomen aligns your pelvis with your rib cage, making the floor of your pelvis and your diaphragm parallel. This alignment charges the energy of your abdomen and nourishes your kidneys. As you draw the pit of your abdomen toward your head, your tailbone will move toward your perineum and your sitting bones will tuck toward your top leg heel. Do not tighten or flatten your stomach. Instead, lengthen from your pubis to your chest. This action realigns your pelvis and extends your lower back, preventing strain and cramping around the lumbar spine.

If you have stiff hamstrings or are perhaps new to Ardha Chandrasana, place a block underneath your right hand. This will increase your stability in the pose and take stress off your right leg, thereby allowing you to lift your left pelvis and pull the pit of your abdomen upward without distorting your spine.

As you continue to work in the pose, attempt to make your left kneecap, belly button, and sternum face front by spinning the left side of your chest and abdomen back. This action prevents the abdominal organs from falling into the front of your belly (their state in most daily activities) and makes them instead fall toward your right side. This massages your abdominal organs and relieves stress in your lower digestive system.

In Ardha Chandrasana, once you have filled your pelvis with life force from the earth, draw this energy up into the heart center for inner reflection and inner work. This movement of energy is one of the foundational elements in the way I teach standing poses.

When you do Ardha Chandrasana to your right, your tendency will be to make the right side of your torso shorter than your left side. Instead, work to keep both sides of the waist equally long. To lengthen your right side, press your right armpit forward, opening the right side of your chest by working your right kidney toward the front of your body. Drawing your outer right hip toward your left heel will also help balance the two sides of your waist and your spine.

In addition, press both shoulder blades toward the buttocks and away from each other. These actions release the congested sensation and cramping that can occur in the upper back behind the heart center. The shoulder blade actions also free your shoulders and neck so that your head can turn without tension.

Try to bring both arms in one straight line perpendicular to the floor. To do this, press your left shoulder blade away from your head more strongly than the right. Also, you should counteract the tendency of the upper arm to drop behind you as you open and turn your chest to face forward. Restrict this tendency by lifting the back of your arm up through the nails of your fingers. The upper arm should now be perpendicular to the floor as viewed from the front and side of the room. Lifting your back arm will stabilize it and prevent it from falling backward. The more stable your upper arm, the more stable your pose.

Your bottom arm, like your bottom leg, lifts energy from the earth into your heart. Placing the pads of your fingertips on the floor, form a cup with the right hand. Suck energy up from the earth through this cup into your chest.

All through out your practice of Ardha Chandrasana, always keep your upper-arm palm wide and facing forward, with your fingertips and thumb tip pointing straight up toward the ceiling and with your fingers and thumb pressing together. These actions align your hand energy and develop concentration. You should pull equally into your thumb and little finger to keep both sides of your wrist even.

Do not let your body fall into a backbend; doing a backbend in this pose dissipates the energy from your kidneys through your belly and chest. In contrast, moving the body into one plane aligns the internal flows of spinal energy from your perineum to the crown of your head. When carefully combined, the following three actions will prevent your body from doing a backbend: Stretch from your left sacrum and right sitting bone into your left heel, from the pit of your abdomen into your diaphragm, and from your kidneys into your front upper chest. These stretches will additionally help move your spine toward your head, while pulling your coccyx and left leg toward your left heel.

Once you have incorporated all of these details into Ardha Chandrasana I (see Figure 4), your brain will have given out all the instructions necessary to create alignment in your physical body. After you reach and hold the alignment, your brain’s job is over. Next, you will have to separate your consciousness from your brain, moving it out of your head and into your heart while you perform the internal actions of the pose. To facilitate this separation of consciousness from your brain, relax the muscles of your face, jaw, and tongue.

As you inhale, bring vitality from your lungs into your whole body; as you exhale, make any necessary adjustments to your alignment. You will find that inhalations draw life force into your body, whereas exhalations channel that force through your body. Keep your breath soft and long, breathing only through your nose with the softness of Ujjayi Pranayama (Victorious Breath): Drawing your breath audibly across the back of your throat, inhale with a slight “s” sound and exhale with an “h.” All these actions will help your breath connect your brain to your heart and the world outside you with the world within.
